questions.explanation: BigQuery integrates with Cloud KMS, allowing you to secure your datasets using Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) for compliance and cryptographic control.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud NAT is a networking service and has no role in managing database storage encryption keys.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Google-managed encryption keys rotate automatically according to Google's internal lifecycle policies and cannot be directly managed or configured by customers.
wrongOptionNotes.D: BigQuery does not support Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK); it supports Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) via Cloud KMS.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A production Compute Engine instance was recently compromised. As part of your incident response protocol, you need to temporarily disable access for all users and service accounts associated with that specific instance without deleting the instance or its disks. What is the most effective action to take immediately?

options.text: Reset the instance and modify its SSH keys metadata.
Disable the service account attached to the compromised instance or remove its IAM bindings.
Downgrade the project to a free tier billing account.
Delete the default service account attached to the project.

questions.explanation: Disabling the specific service account associated with a compromised resource immediately halts active API access and token generation, mitigating further risk during an incident.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Modifying metadata SSH keys does not revoke IAM permissions or service account access tokens that might have already been compromised.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Changing the billing account does not revoke active API credentials or stop compromised workloads from running.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Deleting a project-level default service account can break other dependent applications and services across the entire project.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are managing a Google Cloud project that contains sensitive financial data. To prevent accidental data exposure, you want to ensure that no Cloud Storage buckets within this project can ever be made publicly accessible via public IAM bindings or allUsers/allAuthenticatedUsers permissions. Which feature should you configure?

options.text: VPC Service Controls perimeters around Cloud Storage
Cloud Armor security policy blocking external IP addresses
Disabling the Cloud Storage JSON API in project settings
Public Access Prevention on the Cloud Storage buckets

questions.explanation: Public Access Prevention is a security feature that ensures a Cloud Storage bucket and its contents are never exposed to the public internet, regardless of IAM settings.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC Service Controls protect against data exfiltration across project boundaries, but Public Access Prevention is the specific tool designed to block public bucket access.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud Armor protects HTTP(S) load balancers, not Cloud Storage bucket access configurations.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Disabling the API would block all storage operations entirely, rather than specifically preventing public access configurations.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team suspects that an internal user has been improperly reading sensitive logs and exporting them outside the organization. You need to verify which users or service accounts have accessed Cloud Logging read APIs over the past week. Where should you look for this evidence?

options.text: Data Access audit logs
Compute Engine Serial Port logs
VPC Flow Logs
Admin Activity audit logs

questions.explanation: Data Access audit logs record API calls that read resource data and configurations, providing the necessary audit trail to investigate data access and potential exfiltration.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Serial port logs capture operating system boot and console output, not Google Cloud API access.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC Flow Logs capture network traffic metadata (IP addresses and ports), not API-level data access activity.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Admin Activity logs record configuration changes and administrative writes, not read operations on data.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your company uses Google Cloud, and you need to grant a data science contractor temporary permissions to analyze logs stored in a central Cloud Logging bucket. The contractor must only be able to view log entries and should not have access to other project resources. Following the principle of least privilege, how should you configure this access?

options.text: Grant the roles/storage.objectViewer role on the logging export bucket.
Grant the roles/logging.viewer role at the project level to the contractor's Google account.
Add the contractor as an Owner of the project for the duration of the contract.
Assign the roles/viewer role at the project level to the contractor.

questions.explanation: To grant access to specific Google Cloud services like Cloud Logging while adhering to the principle of least privilege, assign service-specific roles (such as roles/logging.viewer) rather than broad project-level roles like Viewer or Owner.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While logs might be exported to Cloud Storage, granting access to the storage bucket bypasses Cloud Logging IAM and doesn't grant correct log viewer permissions if they use the Log Explorer.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Project Owner grants full administrative control over all project resources, which severely violates the principle of least privilege.
wrongOptionNotes.D: The roles/viewer role is too broad because it grants read access to all resources in the project, not just Cloud Logging.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your development team needs to deploy a custom internal web application to Compute Engine. The application requires access to read configuration files from a specific Cloud Storage bucket. Security policies dictate that you must not store permanent service account keys on the instances. How should you provision access?

options.text: Generate a JSON service account key, embed it in the application source code, and deploy the code to the instance.
Grant the default Compute Engine service account Project Editor permissions.
Create a custom service account with roles/storage.objectViewer on that bucket, attach it to the Compute Engine instance, and run the application.
Configure the bucket to be completely public so the instance can download files via unauthenticated HTTP requests.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine instances should use service accounts to securely authenticate to other Google Cloud services. Avoid using static JSON keys by leveraging attached service accounts, which automatically rotate credentials and integrate with the instance metadata server.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Embedding service account keys in source code violates security best practices due to the risk of credential leakage.
wrongOptionNotes.B: The default service account with Project Editor permissions is overly permissive and violates the principle of least privilege.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Making configuration files public exposes sensitive operational data to the entire internet.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You manage multiple Google Cloud projects organized under a Resource Manager folder structure. You need to ensure that no users outside of your corporate domain can be granted IAM roles on any resources within a specific folder. Which feature should you implement?

options.text: Revoke all project-level Owner permissions and only use basic roles.
Apply an Organization Policy constraint restricting domain sharing (constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains) on the folder.
Write a custom shell script that runs hourly to scan all IAM policies and delete external user bindings.
Configure VPC Service Controls perimeter around the folder.

questions.explanation: Organization Policy constraints—specifically constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains—allow administrators to restrict identity domains that can be added to IAM policies, enforcing centralized compliance and security governance.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Basic roles do not restrict the identity domains that can be added to IAM policies.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Custom scripts are reactive, prone to race conditions, and do not provide proactive governance like Organization Policies.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC Service Controls protect against data exfiltration across project boundaries via API, but domain restrictions for IAM principals are managed via Organization Policies.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An application running on a Compute Engine instance needs to call Google Cloud APIs. To ensure maximum security, the security team requires that the instance does not have an external IP address, but it must still be able to reach Google APIs privately. How should you configure this?

options.text: Assign a temporary external IP address whenever the application needs to make an API request.
Deploy a Bastion Host with an external IP address to forward all API calls.
Configure Private Google Access on the subnet where the instance's network interface resides.
Attach a Cloud NAT gateway to the VPC network.

questions.explanation: Private Google Access enables VMs without external IP addresses to send traffic to Google APIs and services through the default gateway of the VPC network, keeping traffic internal to Google's network.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Dynamically attaching and detaching external IPs is operationally inefficient and violates the security requirement of having no external IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Routing API calls through a bastion host introduces unnecessary complexity, latency, and single points of failure.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While Cloud NAT allows instances without external IPs to reach the public internet, Private Google Access is the direct and preferred method specifically for reaching Google APIs internally.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team requires that all data written to a specific Cloud Storage bucket be encrypted using a key that your organization fully controls, rather than a Google-managed key. You need to manage the key lifecycle yourself in Google Cloud. What should you use?

options.text: Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) with Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK).
Identity and Access Management (IAM) conditional role bindings.
Google-managed encryption keys with default settings.
Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK) where you provide raw encryption keys on every API request.

questions.explanation: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) via Cloud KMS provide the ideal balance of organizational control, key rotation management, and integration with Google Cloud services like Cloud Storage.

wrongOptionNotes.B: IAM conditions govern who has access and under what context, but they do not provide cryptographic data encryption mechanisms.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Google-managed keys are controlled entirely by Google, which does not meet the requirement for organizational key management and control.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While CSEK gives full control, Google does not store the keys, meaning if you lose the key, the data is permanently unrecoverable, and it complicates ongoing application operations.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are troubleshooting a connectivity issue where an application inside a private subnet cannot connect to a Cloud SQL instance. The security team has blocked all public IPs. How should you enable secure connectivity between the Compute Engine instances and the Cloud SQL instance?

options.text: Configure Private Services Access by establishing a private IP connection between your VPC network and Google's producer network.
Install the Cloud SQL Proxy on a public-facing load balancer.
Assign a public IP address to the Cloud SQL instance and restrict access via authorized networks.
Create a VPN tunnel from your VPC back to the same VPC to force traffic encryption.

questions.explanation: Private Services Access uses VPC Network Peering to allow Google Cloud managed services (like Cloud SQL) to be accessed via internal IP addresses within your VPC.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud SQL Proxy is a great tool, but placing it behind a public load balancer does not solve the private network requirement efficiently compared to native Private Services Access.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The security team explicitly prohibited public IPs, ruling out authorized networks over public internet.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Creating a VPN tunnel to the same VPC is unnecessary and unsupported for internal Cloud SQL connectivity.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your company's compliance framework requires that all Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy changes across your organization's folder hierarchy must be centrally tracked and audited. Which service should you configure to capture these changes?

options.text: Cloud Monitoring uptime checks.
VPC Flow Logs configured on the default VPC network.
Compute Engine serial port logging.
Cloud Audit Logs with Admin Activity logs enabled.

questions.explanation: Cloud Audit Logs automatically record Admin Activity logs, which capture administrative operations such as creating resources or changing IAM policies, providing a complete audit trail.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Monitoring uptime checks verify service availability, not security and audit configurations.
wrongOptionNotes.B: VPC Flow Logs record network packet metadata flowing through VM instances, not control-plane IAM modifications.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Serial port logs capture console output from virtual machine operating systems, not project or organization IAM grants.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You need to grant an external auditor temporary permission to view billing reports and cost management data for a specific Google Cloud project without granting them permissions to modify any infrastructure. Which role should you assign?

options.text: roles/viewer
roles/browser
roles/billing.viewer
roles/resourcemanager.folderViewer

questions.explanation: Billing-specific roles such as roles/billing.viewer allow organizations to delegate financial visibility securely while adhering to the principle of least privilege.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The roles/viewer role grants read access to all Google Cloud resources in the project, which is much broader than billing access.
wrongOptionNotes.B: The browser role only allows viewing the project hierarchy and resource names, not billing or cost details.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Folder viewer grants permissions to view folder hierarchy and metadata, not billing data.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team mandates that developers must not be allowed to create service account keys across any projects in the organization. How can you enforce this requirement globally?

options.text: Remove the Service Account Admin role from all developer IAM bindings.
Delete the default service account in every project manually.
Set up a Cloud Monitoring alert that notifies you when a key is created.
Enforce the 'Disable service account key creation' organization policy constraint (constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation).

questions.explanation: Organization Policy constraints like constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation provide preventative security controls to block unauthorized credential creation at scale.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While removing IAM roles reduces direct permissions, organization policies provide robust, preventative guardrails that are harder to bypass.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Manually deleting default service accounts does not prevent users from creating new service accounts and associated keys.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud Monitoring alerts are reactive and detect key creation after the fact, whereas the security team requires a preventative control.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An application running on a Compute Engine instance needs to validate user credentials against Google Cloud Identity or Firebase. However, the security policy dictates that the VM should not store long-lived credentials. How should the application securely obtain an identity token for authentication?

options.text: Store user passwords in plain text inside a public Cloud Storage bucket.
Use the Google Cloud SDK CLI tool interactively inside the application code by spawning a shell prompt.
Query the local instance metadata server to generate an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity token for the attached service account.
Hardcode the master administrative password in the application configuration file.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine instances can leverage their attached service accounts to request identity tokens (OIDC) or access tokens directly from the metadata server, ensuring secure, ephemeral authentication.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Storing passwords in plain text in a public bucket exposes sensitive user data to the public internet.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Spawning interactive CLI sessions inside production application code is brittle, insecure, and non-scalable.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Hardcoding credentials is a critical security vulnerability and violates fundamental cloud security standards.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are designing a secure environment where developers can deploy workloads, but they must not be allowed to assign public IP addresses to any newly created Compute Engine instances. How should you enforce this control efficiently?

options.text: Enforce the 'Require external IP addresses to be disabled' organization policy constraint (constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess).
Instruct developers via a policy document to never click the external IP checkbox in the Cloud Console.
Remove the Compute Engine Network Admin role and only give them Storage Admin.
Delete the default VPC network where external IPs are enabled by default.

questions.explanation: Organization Policy constraints (such as constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess) provide automated, preventative governance to stop users from allocating external IP addresses to VMs.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Relying on manual documentation and user compliance without technical guardrails invariably leads to policy violations.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Developers need Compute Engine instance creation permissions, so removing network roles entirely would block their core workflow while still not preventing external IPs if they use permitted subnets.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Deleting the default network does not prevent developers from creating custom networks that provision external IP addresses.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team is deploying a containerized application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) in a newly created Google Cloud project. During the pipeline deployment, the cluster creation fails with an error indicating that the default service account lacks permissions to pull images or interact with Google Cloud APIs. What is the most likely root cause and immediate remediation?

options.text: Billing has not been linked to the project, causing all API calls to timeout immediately.
The VPC network lacks a default route to the internet, preventing nodes from downloading packages.
The GKE API is disabled in the project, and you need to enable it using the gcloud services command.

The Compute Engine default service account has been disabled or stripped of its default roles at the project level, and you must restore roles/editor or use a custom service account with correct scopes.

questions.explanation: Google Kubernetes Engine clusters use the Compute Engine default service account by default for node operations. When configuring new projects, hardening scripts or manual permission adjustments often strip this account of essential roles, preventing nodes from initializing correctly.

wrongOptionNotes.A: An unlinked billing account typically results in quota or billing errors rather than generic permission failures during node bootstrapping.
wrongOptionNotes.B: A missing default route causes network timeouts or connection failures, not the specific API permission errors associated with service accounts.
wrongOptionNotes.C: If the GKE API were disabled, the cluster creation command itself would fail immediately with an API-not-enabled error, not a node bootstrapping permission error.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: An administrator attempts to create a new Compute Engine instance in a custom VPC network, but the creation fails with an error stating that the subnet does not have enough available IP addresses. However, checking the instance count reveals very few active VMs. What is the underlying cause?

options.text: Compute Engine requires an external IP address for every instance, and the regional external IP quota is exhausted.
Google Cloud reserves the first and last four IP addresses of every subnet, leaving no usable IPs in a standard subnet.
The subnet range is too small (e.g., /29), and secondary IP ranges allocated for GKE pods or services have exhausted the subnet space.
The project quota for regional IP addresses has been reached across all regions.

questions.explanation: Subnet IP exhaustion often occurs when CIDR ranges are inadequately planned or when secondary IP ranges for containers and services consume the available address space within a subnet.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Instances can be created with internal IP addresses only, so external IP quotas do not restrict internal subnet IP allocation.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Google Cloud reserves only the first two, broadcast, and last IP address (4 total) per subnet, which does not prevent standard instance creation unless the block is tiny.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Project quotas govern global or regional address limits, whereas subnet exhaustion is localized to the specific CIDR block assigned to that subnet.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You configured a Cloud Storage bucket export for your billing data, but after 48 hours, the BigQuery dataset linked to it remains empty. Which troubleshooting step should you take first?

options.text: Recreate the Cloud Storage bucket with uniform bucket-level access enabled.
Manually run a cron job to trigger the billing ingestion pipeline using the Google Cloud CLI.
Grant the BigQuery Data Owner role to your personal user account on the target dataset.
Verify that the billing export configuration correctly points to the active billing account and that the project containing the dataset has the Cloud Billing budget export enabled.

questions.explanation: Cloud Billing exports are managed asynchronously by Google. Ensuring the correct billing account linkage and dataset permissions for the Google-managed billing service agent resolves most ingestion failures.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Uniform bucket-level access is a security setting and does not prevent automated billing export ingestion into BigQuery.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Billing exports are managed entirely by Google Cloud backend processes and cannot be manually triggered via standard gcloud commands.
wrongOptionNotes.C: User permissions do not prevent the automated Google billing service account from writing data into the dataset.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team is troubleshooting a newly deployed application on a Compute Engine instance that cannot connect to a Cloud SQL PostgreSQL database in the same region. The application logs show connection timeouts. What is the most effective troubleshooting sequence?

options.text: Restart the Compute Engine instance to force a refresh of its DHCP lease and DNS resolution tables.
Assign the Owner role to the Compute Engine default service account on the Cloud SQL instance.
Verify that the Cloud SQL instance has an authorized network or private IP configured, and check VPC firewall rules to ensure outbound traffic on port 5432 is not blocked.
Upgrade the Cloud SQL instance tier to a higher CPU and memory configuration to handle incoming connections.

questions.explanation: Database connectivity issues in Google Cloud are almost always related to VPC networking rules, Private Service Access configuration, or Cloud SQL authorized networks rather than instance sizing or IAM.

wrongOptionNotes.A: DNS resolution or DHCP issues rarely cause persistent connection timeouts to Cloud SQL instances addressed via private or public IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud SQL connections are authenticated via database users and passwords, not IAM roles assigned to the compute service account.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Connection timeouts indicate network or access blockages rather than performance throttling due to hardware specs.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are deploying a web application behind an HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Users report intermittent 502 Bad Gateway errors when accessing the site. Your backend instances are running and healthy according to your local checks. What should you investigate first?

options.text: Rotate the SSL certificates attached to the target HTTPS proxy.
Check the Cloud CDN cache hit ratio to ensure static assets are being cached properly.
Verify that the load balancer health check paths match the application endpoints and that backend instances respond with an HTTP 200 status within the timeout window.
Increase the maximum transmission unit (MTU) size on the VPC network interfaces.

questions.explanation: HTTP(S) Load Balancers return 502 Bad Gateway when the proxy cannot establish a valid connection to backend instances or when instances fail health checks, causing them to be removed from the active backend pool.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Expired or invalid SSL certificates cause client-side browser warning errors (e.g., ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID), not 502 Bad Gateway errors.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cache hit ratios affect latency and bandwidth costs, not HTTP 502 proxy gateway errors.
wrongOptionNotes.D: MTU mismatches cause packet fragmentation issues and connection drops, not systematic 502 Bad Gateway application response errors.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: A junior engineer accidentally deleted a critical custom VPC network containing active production subnets. The deletion failed, but the network is now stuck in a disconnecting state. How should you resolve this operational block?

options.text: Run the gcloud compute networks update command with the --force flag.
Submit a Google Cloud Support ticket to forcibly purge the VPC network from the backend database.
Identify and delete all dependent resources (such as active VM instances, VPN gateways, and static routes) attached to the VPC network before retrying the deletion.
Disable the Compute Engine API and re-enable it to reset all network states.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud maintains strict dependency checks. A VPC or subnet cannot be deleted until all dependent resources like VM instances, load balancer forwarding rules, and VPN tunnels are completely removed.

wrongOptionNotes.A: There is no --force flag for network deletion in the gcloud CLI to protect against accidental data loss.
wrongOptionNotes.B: VPC cleanup must be performed by removing dependent resources; Google Cloud support cannot bypass resource dependency safety checks.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Disabling the Compute Engine API is destructive and does not automatically purge dependent VPC objects in a hung state.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your security team reports that a Compute Engine instance in a private subnet has been communicating with an external unauthorized IP address. The instance has no external IP address assigned. How is this possible?

options.text: The VPC firewall rules have been misconfigured to allow public traffic via an internal gateway.
Compute Engine instances automatically receive a temporary ephemeral public IP address during peak hours.
The instance is leveraging VPC Network Peering to route traffic through another project's public internet gateway.
The instance is using Cloud NAT configured for the subnet, allowing outbound internet access without requiring an external IP address.

questions.explanation: Cloud NAT is a managed service that provides outbound internet connectivity for private instances. Instances without external IPs can still egress traffic if their subnet is associated with an active Cloud NAT gateway.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC firewall rules control packet filtering between instances and networks, but do not provide NAT translation for private VMs to reach the internet.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Instances without external IPs never receive public IPs unless explicitly configured during creation or via instance attachment.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC Network Peering does not automatically share internet gateways or NAT services between peered networks unless explicitly configured with custom proxy routing.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your application deployment pipeline fails when attempting to push container images to Artifact Registry. The error message indicates 'Denied: Unauthenticated request'. The CI/CD runner is executing on an external server outside of Google Cloud. What is the correct authentication setup to fix this?

options.text: Grant the Storage Object Viewer role to the project's default service account.
Authenticate the Docker client using a JSON key file for a service account granted the Artifact Registry Writer role, or use workload identity federation.
Configure the local Docker daemon to use the Google Cloud CLI with sudo privileges.
Enable public read access on the Artifact Registry repository via IAM bindings.

questions.explanation: External systems interacting with Google Cloud APIs must authenticate securely. For Artifact Registry, service account keys or Workload Identity Federation combined with gcloud credential helpers are required.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Artifact Registry stores images in Google-managed storage buckets behind its own API; granting storage roles directly does not authenticate the Artifact Registry API client.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Running gcloud auth configure-docker is necessary, but external runners still require valid credentials (like a service account key or token) to authenticate API requests.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Making repositories public violates security policies and still does not authorize unauthenticated push operations.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are managing a Google Cloud project where users report that they cannot access a Cloud Storage bucket, receiving a 403 Forbidden error, despite having been granted the Storage Object Viewer role at the project level. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The Cloud Storage API has not been enabled in the user's home project.
Project-level IAM roles take 24 hours to propagate across Google Cloud global datacenters.
Cloud Storage requires users to have the Compute Instance Admin role to browse bucket contents.
The bucket has uniform bucket-level access disabled, but individual object ACLs restrict access, or the bucket is protected by a VPC Service Controls perimeter.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage permissions are governed by IAM and ACLs. When project-level IAM roles are present but access is denied, ACL overrides or VPC Service Controls perimeters are the usual culprits.

wrongOptionNotes.A: APIs are enabled at the resource project level, not the user's home project level.
wrongOptionNotes.B: IAM role propagation typically takes effect within a few minutes, not 24 hours.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Compute roles are entirely unrelated to Cloud Storage data access permissions.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your database administrator needs to connect to a Cloud SQL instance using the Cloud SQL Auth proxy from a local workstation for emergency maintenance. The connection attempt hangs and eventually times out. What should you check first?

options.text: Ensure that the user running the proxy has authenticated via the gcloud CLI (gcloud auth login) and has the Cloud SQL Client role.
Restart the Cloud SQL instance in maintenance mode to clear active locks.
Assign the Project Editor role to the database administrator's personal Google account.
Configure the workstation's local firewall to open inbound port 3306 to the public internet.

questions.explanation: The Cloud SQL Auth proxy requires proper authentication via gcloud and authorization via the Cloud SQL Client role to create a secure encrypted connection to the database instance.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Connection timeouts during proxy startup relate to authentication or local network egress restrictions, not database locks.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Broad project-level roles like Editor are unnecessary and violate least-privilege principles when specific roles like Cloud SQL Client suffice.
wrongOptionNotes.D: The Cloud SQL Auth proxy initiates outbound connections to Google Cloud on TCP port 3307, eliminating the need to open inbound ports on local firewalls.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: An application running on Compute Engine instances needs to read metadata from the instance metadata server. Recently, the application began throwing errors stating that it cannot reach the metadata server address `169.254.169.254`. How should you troubleshoot this?

options.text: Enable the Compute Engine Metadata API in the Google Cloud Console API library.
Attach a public IP address to the instance so it can query the metadata server over the internet.
Renew the instance's DHCP lease by restarting the metadata proxy service in Google Cloud Console.
Verify that custom startup scripts or local firewall configurations have not blocked local routing to the special IP address 169.254.169.254.

questions.explanation: The metadata server is accessed via a non-routable link-local IP (`169.254.169.254`). Issues reaching it are typically caused by local OS network configuration changes or host-level firewalls blocking the address.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The metadata server is an internal infrastructure service available by default on all Compute Engine VMs and cannot be disabled via the API library.
wrongOptionNotes.B: The metadata server is entirely internal and does not require or accept public internet traffic.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The metadata server IP is a fixed link-local address built into Google Cloud hypervisors and does not rely on standard DHCP lease renewals.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team deployed a new microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine. Users report that the service is intermittently dropping requests. Upon inspecting the Kubernetes logs, you find numerous Out Of Memory (OOM) killer events. What is the appropriate configuration fix?

options.text: Increase the disk size of the persistent volumes attached to the GKE cluster.
Modify the VPC firewall rules to increase maximum packet size limits.
Switch the GKE cluster mode from Autopilot to Standard to gain root access to kernel parameters.
Review and increase the container memory resource limits in the Kubernetes deployment manifest, and ensure node sizing is adequate.

questions.explanation: Kubernetes terminates containers when they consume memory beyond their specified limits. Adjusting container resource requests and limits in the pod specification is the direct remediation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Persistent disk storage capacity is unrelated to RAM memory consumption and OOM termination of application containers.
wrongOptionNotes.B: VPC firewall rules manage network traffic filtering, not application memory allocation.
wrongOptionNotes.C: OOM events are controlled by container memory limits, not the choice between GKE Standard and Autopilot modes.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You have configured a Cloud Logging log sink to route security-relevant logs to a Cloud Storage bucket in a centralized logging project. However, new logs are not appearing in the destination bucket. What is the most likely missing configuration?

options.text: The unique writer identity service account associated with the log sink has not been granted the Storage Object Creator role on the destination bucket.
The Cloud Logging API must be disabled and re-enabled to flush the sink buffer.
Log sinks only support routing to Pub/Sub topics; Cloud Storage requires manual batch exports.
The destination bucket must have versioning enabled for log sinks to write data.

questions.explanation: When creating a log sink, Google Cloud generates a unique writer identity service account. You must grant this service account permissions to write to the destination Cloud Storage bucket or Pub/Sub topic.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling APIs does not resolve missing permission bindings on log sink destinations.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud Logging natively supports exporting logs to Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and Pub/Sub topics.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Object versioning is a data protection setting and is not a prerequisite for receiving exported logs.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: An administrator created a custom VPC firewall rule to block all inbound traffic from a specific malicious IP range. Despite the rule having the highest priority (lowest numerical value, e.g., 100), traffic from that IP range is still reaching the backend VMs. What is the likely reason?

options.text: Google Cloud firewall rules require an explicit system reboot of all target VM instances to take effect.
The destination IP addresses on the VM were configured with static external reservations.
A higher-priority (lower numerical value) ingress allow rule (such as a default-allow rule or VPN allow rule) is overriding the block rule.
VPC firewall rules only apply to egress traffic; inbound traffic filtering must be managed via OS-level iptables.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud VPC firewall rules are evaluated based on priority numbers (lower number = higher priority). If traffic matches a higher-priority allow rule first, subsequent deny rules are bypassed.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC firewall rules are implemented at the software-defined networking hypervisor level and apply instantly without requiring VM reboots.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Static IP reservations do not bypass VPC firewall rule evaluations.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC firewall rules support both ingress and egress traffic filtering natively.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team deployed a multi-tier web application where frontend instances cannot reach the backend database instances located in a separate subnetwork within the same custom VPC. Pings between the instances fail. What should you verify first?

options.text: Enable VPC Network Peering between the frontend subnetwork and backend subnetwork.
Check VPC firewall rules to ensure there is an ingress allow rule permitting traffic from the frontend instance tags or service accounts to the database instances on the required database port.
Attach an external IP address to every database instance so internal routing tables can locate them.
Configure Cloud VPN to bridge the two subnets together within the same VPC.

questions.explanation: Subnets within a single VPC can communicate by default, but traffic is subject to VPC firewall rules. Ensuring proper ingress rules matching tags or service accounts is essential for tier-to-tier communication.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC Network Peering connects separate VPC networks, not subnets within the same VPC network.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Internal communication across subnets within the same VPC relies on internal IP addresses, not external IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Subnets within the same custom VPC are automatically routed together without requiring VPN or peering.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your security team mandates that developers must never be assigned broad primitive roles like Project Editor across production projects, but they still require permissions to deploy and manage Cloud Functions. How should you assign permissions following the principle of least privilege?

options.text: Grant the primitive Project Editor role at the project level, but use IAM conditions to restrict access to specific times of day.
Create a custom role with wildcard permissions (*.functions.*) and assign it at the organization level.
Add the developers to the Owners group for the Google Cloud project to allow seamless code deployments.
Assign the predefined Cloud Functions Developer role and Service Account User role to the developers at the project level.

questions.explanation: Adhering to the principle of least privilege requires avoiding primitive roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) and instead utilizing predefined or custom roles tailored to specific operational tasks, such as Cloud Functions Developer combined with Service Account User.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Project Editor is a primitive role that provides overly broad access across all services, violating the principle of least privilege regardless of IAM conditions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Wildcard permissions in custom roles at the organization level create a massive security risk and violate least-privilege best practices.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Project Owner is the most privileged primitive role and should be strictly avoided for routine developer workflows.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your enterprise organization requires that all Google Cloud Storage buckets created anywhere within the corporate organization must enforce bucket-level public access prevention. Which approach guarantees this compliance automatically for all future projects?

options.text: Configure a cron job using Cloud Scheduler to scan all buckets daily and disable public access via gsutil.
Apply an IAM binding removing `allUsers` and `allAuthenticatedUsers` from the project-level IAM policy.
Rely on developers signing a security compliance document before provisioning new Google Cloud projects.
Set an Organization Policy constraint restricting the `storage.publicAccessPrevention` constraint to enforced at the organization node.

questions.explanation: Organization Policy constraints are the primary mechanism for enforcing compliance guardrails globally across all projects within a Google Cloud organization.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Scanning via cron is reactive, introduces a time window of vulnerability, and does not prevent creation of public buckets in real time.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Project-level IAM policies do not override bucket-level public ACLs or domain-wide sharing settings as effectively as the specialized storage public access prevention policy.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Relying on manual documentation and human compliance checks is prone to human error and policy drift.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: An external security auditor needs read-only access to view audit logs and security configurations in a specific project. Security policy dictates that no long-term credentials or service account keys can be exported. How should you grant this access?

options.text: Grant the predefined roles Viewer and Logging Viewer directly to the auditor's corporate Google Workspace identity.
Temporarily elevate the auditor to Project Owner for the duration of the audit engagement.
Create a shared IAM user account with a password stored in a text file inside a public Cloud Storage bucket.
Generate a long-lived service account key for the auditor and share it securely via encrypted email.

questions.explanation: Access should always be granted directly to federated user identities using predefined least-privilege roles like Viewer and Logging Viewer, completely eliminating the need for service account keys.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Project Owner grants full write and administrative control, drastically exceeding the read-only requirement.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Shared accounts and public credentials represent severe security vulnerabilities.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Exporting and sharing long-lived service account keys violates modern cloud security standards due to theft and leakage risks.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your company's compliance framework requires that all Compute Engine instances must not have external IP addresses assigned by default. You need to configure a preventative guardrail across the entire organization. What should you do?

options.text: Enforce the Organization Policy constraint `constraints/compute.disableSerialPortAccess` across the organization.
Delete the default VPC network in every project so instances cannot attach to public interfaces.
Write a custom Cloud Monitoring alert that notifies security whenever a VM with an external IP is created.
Enforce the Organization Policy constraint `constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess` at the organization level with a denied list.

questions.explanation: Preventative guardrails in Google Cloud are implemented using Organization Policy constraints, such as `constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess`, which blocks the creation of VMs with public IPs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Disabling serial port access restricts debugging capabilities, but it does not control whether instances receive external IP addresses.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Deleting the default VPC does not prevent developers from creating custom VPC networks with external NAT or instance public IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud Monitoring alerts are detective controls, whereas the requirement calls for a preventative guardrail.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your security team discovers that a custom service account used by a data processing pipeline has been overly privileged with broad permissions across multiple production projects. You need to scope down its permissions immediately. What is the best practice approach?

options.text: Leave the permissions as they are, but monitor the service account logs daily using Cloud Logging.
Disable the service account and share a single user personal credential for the pipeline execution.
Delete the service account entirely and recreate it with the exact minimum required IAM roles.
Upgrade the service account to an administrator service account to simplify permission inheritance.

questions.explanation: When a service account is overly privileged, you should strip unnecessary roles and apply only the specific predefined roles necessary for the workload to function.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Monitoring does not remediate an existing excessive permission risk.
wrongOptionNotes.B: User credentials should never be shared for automated headless pipelines.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Upgrading to an administrator account increases exposure and violates the principle of least privilege.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your organization mandates that all Google Cloud resources must reside within specific geographic boundaries (European Union) to comply with data residency regulations. How should you enforce this restriction?

options.text: Rely on project naming conventions to remind engineers to select EU regions.
Manually inspect each resource creation request submitted to the Google Cloud Console.
Configure a firewall rule blocking all egress traffic originating from non-EU IP ranges.
Enforce the Organization Policy constraint `constraints/gcp.resourceLocations` specifying allowed EU macro-regions.

questions.explanation: Data residency compliance is effectively enforced through the `gcp.resourceLocations` Organization Policy constraint, which prevents resources from being created in unauthorized regions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Naming conventions are easily ignored and provide no technical enforcement.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual inspection does not scale and leads to compliance breaches.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC firewall rules control network packet flows, not where GCP storage or database underlying data is provisioned.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: A temporary contractor needs access to deploy resources into a staging project. Security policy states that the contractor's access must automatically expire after 14 days without manual intervention. How should you grant this access?

options.text: Create a dedicated service account key and configure the contractor to use it indefinitely.
Create a calendar reminder to manually delete the IAM binding after two weeks.
Assign the Project Owner role and share the account password with a 14-day self-destruct script.
Grant the role using IAM conditional bindings with a time-based expiration condition.

questions.explanation: IAM conditions allow you to define attribute-based access control, including time-based expiration, which is ideal for temporary contractor access.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Service account keys do not expire automatically and pose a long-term security risk if not rotated.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual reminders are unreliable and prone to administrative oversight.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Sharing credentials and assigning Project Owner violates core security controls.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your security team requires that all customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) used to encrypt BigQuery datasets must be managed via Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) with an automatic key rotation schedule. How do you verify compliance across projects?

options.text: Use Cloud Asset Inventory to query and audit encryption key configurations and associations across all projects.
Run a traceroute from BigQuery to the Cloud KMS endpoint to verify network connectivity.
Log into every individual BigQuery dataset UI and check the encryption settings manually.
Review the monthly billing statement to ensure Cloud KMS charges are present.

questions.explanation: Cloud Asset Inventory is designed to export and query asset metadata, security configurations, and compliance states across an entire organization.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Traceroute tests network paths, not policy compliance or key rotation configurations.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Manual checking across hundreds of datasets is inefficient and prone to human error.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Billing statements show costs, not specific configuration compliance or key rotation settings.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: An internal application running on a Compute Engine instance requires access to secret credentials stored in Secret Manager. What is the most secure method to grant the application access to the secret?

options.text: Hardcode the secret string directly into the application source code repository.
Store the secret in a plain-text configuration file located on the root directory of the VM disk.
Attach a custom service account to the instance and grant it the Secret Manager Secret Accessor role on that specific secret.
Grant the instance default service account the Project Owner role.

questions.explanation: To securely access secrets, instances should use a dedicated service account granted the `Secret Manager Secret Accessor` role scoped strictly to the required secret resource.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Hardcoding secrets in code repositories exposes them to anyone with read access to the code.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Plain-text configuration files on disks can be accessed by anyone with OS-level privileges or snapshot access.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Project Owner grants excessive privileges far beyond reading a specific secret.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your organization wants to prevent users from sharing sensitive internal data outside of the corporate Google Workspace domain via Google Cloud services. Which policy control should you implement?

options.text: Configuring Cloud NAT with restricted port mappings.
Enabling OS Login on all Compute Engine instances.
VPC Service Controls perimeter blocking all outbound traffic.
Domain Restricted Sharing organization policy (`constraints/gcp.domainRestrictedSharing`).

questions.explanation: The `constraints/gcp.domainRestrictedSharing` Organization Policy restricts which accounts can be added as IAM principals, preventing external or unauthorized accounts from gaining access.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud NAT manages network address translation, not data sharing or IAM principal restrictions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: OS Login manages SSH access to virtual machines, not IAM sharing policies for cloud resources.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC Service Controls protect against data exfiltration across API perimeters, but identity-based sharing policies are controlled via Domain Restricted Sharing.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your security architect wants to isolate a set of sensitive BigQuery datasets and Cloud Storage buckets into a secure perimeter to prevent data exfiltration over public APIs, even if a service account is compromised. What Google Cloud feature should you implement?

options.text: Cloud Armor Security Policies.
Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) Firewall Rules.
Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP).
VPC Service Controls.

questions.explanation: VPC Service Controls create security perimeters around Google-managed services (like BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and Bigtable) to mitigate data exfiltration risks.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Armor protects HTTP(S) load balanced web applications from DDoS and web attacks.
wrongOptionNotes.B: VPC firewall rules control packet flows within VPC networks, not Google Cloud API service boundaries like BigQuery or Cloud Storage.
wrongOptionNotes.C: IAP controls access to web applications and VMs running inside Google Cloud, rather than data exfiltration perimeters for multi-tenant APIs.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are managing a Google Cloud project and need to ensure that no user can create service account keys, as your organization mandates the use of Workload Identity Federation or attached service accounts instead. How can you enforce this requirement?

options.text: Configure a firewall rule blocking traffic to the IAM credentials API endpoint.
Delete all existing service accounts across the project.
Enforce the Organization Policy constraint `constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`.
Revoke all IAM roles from every user in the project.

questions.explanation: Organization policy constraints like `constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` provide direct, preventative controls against the generation of long-lived service account keys.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Firewall rules operate at the IP/port network layer and cannot filter specific Google Cloud API method calls.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Deleting service accounts would break running applications and workloads.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Revoking all roles prevents any work from being done and is not a targeted policy control.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your compliance team requires that all administrator activities and data access audit logs for a sensitive project must be retained indefinitely and cannot be modified or deleted by any user, including project owners. What is the recommended feature to achieve this?

options.text: Storing the log files on the local root disk of a temporary Compute Engine instance.
Standard IAM permissions denying delete access to project owners via custom roles.
Cloud Storage Bucket Lock using Object Retention policies in compliance mode.
Cloud Storage object lifecycle rules set to delete objects after 30 days.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage Bucket Lock allows you to configure a WORM (Write Once, Read Many) policy in compliance mode, preventing modification or deletion of audit logs for a specified retention period.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Local disks are ephemeral and do not provide centralized, durable, or compliant audit log retention.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Project owners can modify IAM policies and override custom restrictions unless protected by compliance-locked storage policies.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Lifecycle rules set to delete objects would destroy audit logs, violating retention and compliance requirements.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: An engineer needs to inspect network traffic passing through a subnetwork for security troubleshooting. You want to capture IP packet headers and metadata without exposing payload data. Which feature should you enable?

options.text: Cloud Armor Packet Mirroring.
Cloud DNS Query Logging.
Cloud Audit Data Access Logs.
VPC Flow Logs.

questions.explanation: VPC Flow Logs sample and record network flow data (source/destination IPs, ports, protocols, bytes) for monitoring and troubleshooting network security.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Armor provides web application firewall protection, not packet mirroring.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud DNS query logs capture domain resolution requests, not general subnetwork traffic headers.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Data Access logs record API calls that read or write resource data, not raw network packet headers.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your organization requires that all database instances running on Compute Engine must have their boot disks encrypted with keys managed by Cloud KMS rather than Google-default encryption. How can you enforce this requirement?

options.text: Rely on developers remembering to specify the KMS key flag during `gcloud compute instances create` commands.
Enforce an Organization Policy or audit configuration to ensure disk encryption complies with customer-managed keys (CMEK).
Enforce the Organization Policy constraint `constraints/compute.restrictIsolateResource`.
Enforce the Organization Policy constraint `constraints/compute.requireVpcFlowLogs`.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud provides specific Organization Policy constraints and detective controls to mandate and verify that customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) are used for storage and disk resources.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Relying on manual flags leads to human error and policy drift.
wrongOptionNotes.C: This constraint is not related to customer-managed encryption keys for disks.
wrongOptionNotes.D: This constraint enforces VPC flow logs on networks, not disk encryption keys.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team is deploying a high-throughput, latency-sensitive data ingestion pipeline on Compute Engine. The processing instances need to handle variable workloads with predictable performance while strictly optimizing costs. Which combination of Compute Engine configurations should you choose?

options.text: Deploy custom machine types using the N2 family, purchase 1-year Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) for baseline capacity, and use Spot VMs for elastic scaling peaks.
Deploy e2-medium instances with custom machine types and standard pricing.
Deploy standard n2-standard-4 instances with preemptible VMs to maximize cost savings.
Deploy n2-standard-8 instances with sustained use discounts and spot VMs for non-critical fallback workers.

questions.explanation: For steady-state high-throughput workloads, Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) offer the highest level of predictable discounting for baseline capacity. Spot VMs provide deep discounts for flexible, fault-tolerant scaling peaks, and custom machine types prevent resource over-provisioning.

wrongOptionNotes.B: E2 instances are designed for cost-optimized general-purpose workloads and shared-core characteristics, making them unsuitable for high-throughput heavy data ingestion.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Preemptible VMs can be terminated at any time with a 24-hour maximum lifespan, which disrupts a high-throughput latency-sensitive ingestion pipeline.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Sustained use discounts are automatically applied to older machine families like n1, but modern C2, N2, and E2 families rely on committed use discounts or flexible pricing rather than automatic sustained use discounts.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your organization runs a batch processing workload on Compute Engine that executes every night for 4 hours. The workload is fault-tolerant and can be interrupted or restarted without data loss. You need to minimize the compute costs for this batch job. What is the most cost-effective approach?

options.text: Use standard Compute Engine instances with 3-year committed use discounts.
Use E2 series instances with flexible custom resource allocations and automatic restart disabled.
Use Spot VMs configured with a graceful instance termination handler and automated checkpointing.
Use sole-tenant nodes to ensure dedicated physical hardware for the batch processing tasks.

questions.explanation: Spot VMs are specifically designed for batch computing and fault-tolerant workloads, offering discounts of up to 90%. Since the workload runs only 4 hours a night and is interruptible, Spot VMs maximize cost efficiency compared to reserved or standard instances.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Purchasing a 3-year commitment for an asset that runs only 4 hours a day results in paying for 24 hours of compute daily, making it extremely cost-ineffective.
wrongOptionNotes.B: While E2 instances are economical, they do not provide the massive discounts associated with Spot VMs for batch, fault-tolerant workloads.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Sole-tenant nodes require you to pay for the entire physical server regardless of usage, making them the most expensive option for batch workloads.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your company stores petabytes of log data in Cloud Storage. Regulatory requirements mandate that these logs must be retained for 5 years, but they are rarely accessed after the first 30 days. You need to minimize long-term storage costs. What should you do?

options.text: Export all logs directly to BigQuery long-term storage tables with automatic partitioning.
Implement a Cloud Storage Lifecycle policy to transition objects from Standard to Nearline after 30 days, and then to Archive storage after 365 days.
Create a single Cloud Storage bucket with Standard storage class and configure lifecycle rules to delete objects after 5 years.
Keep all objects in Nearline storage for the entire 5-year duration using a uniform bucket-level policy.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage lifecycle rules automate the transition of data to cheaper storage classes (Nearline, Coldline, Archive) over time. For data accessed less than once a year, Archive storage provides the lowest cost option for long-term compliance retention.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While BigQuery long-term storage discounts apply, raw log storage in Cloud Storage Archive tier is significantly cheaper per gigabyte for simple compliance retention.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Standard storage class has the highest storage cost. Keeping petabytes of rarely accessed data in Standard storage for 5 years is cost-prohibitive.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Nearline storage incurs higher long-term storage costs than Coldline or Archive storage for data retained for several years.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You manage a Google Cloud project with multiple microservices deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Your finance department reports unexpected spikes in cluster resource costs. You need to identify which specific namespaces and workloads are consuming the most resources. What should you do?

options.text: Scale down all non-production GKE namespaces using a custom cron job and monitor the drop in the monthly billing invoice.
Enable Google Cloud Billing export to BigQuery and write a custom query joining billing data with instance labels.
Enable GKE Cost Allocation in the Google Cloud Console and inspect the GKE usage metrics in the Cloud Monitoring dashboard.
Set up a separate GKE cluster for every individual namespace to isolate billing at the project level.

questions.explanation: GKE Cost Allocation enables attribution of cluster resource usage (CPU, memory, persistent disks) to Kubernetes namespaces and pods, allowing organizations to track and optimize microservice spending via BigQuery.

wrongOptionNotes.A: This trial-and-error approach does not provide granular cost attribution and can disrupt development workflows.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Standard billing export only shows cluster-level node costs, not granular pod or namespace usage within a shared cluster.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Running separate clusters for every namespace leads to severe resource fragmentation, idle cluster overhead, and increased infrastructure management costs.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team is running a data warehouse in BigQuery. Queries scanning large partitioned tables are incurring high costs due to full table scans executed by analysts. You need to enforce a cost control mechanism without restricting user access. What should you do?

options.text: Revoke BigQuery Data Viewer permissions from all analysts and require manual approval for every query.
Set up BigQuery custom quotas to limit the maximum bytes billed per user or per project per day.
Disable partitioned tables and force analysts to query raw unpartitioned log dumps.
Convert all BigQuery tables into flat files and store them in Cloud Storage buckets with restricted read access.

questions.explanation: BigQuery allows administrators to set custom billing quotas to limit query costs. By capping the maximum bytes billed per day, teams can prevent accidental high-cost queries from exhausting the monthly budget.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Requiring manual approval for every query introduces severe operational bottlenecks and defeats the purpose of an analytical data warehouse.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Disabling partitioning increases the data scanned per query, which will drastically increase costs rather than control them.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Moving tables to Cloud Storage removes the analytical capabilities, indexing, and partitioning benefits provided by BigQuery.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: An enterprise web application hosted on Compute Engine experiences predictable daily traffic spikes between 9:00 AM and 5:00 PM. Outside these hours, traffic drops by 80%. You want to optimize infrastructure costs while maintaining high availability. What should you configure?

options.text: Use unmanaged instance groups with a cron script that manually executes gcloud compute instances delete outside business hours.
Configure a Managed Instance Group (MIG) with autoscaling based on CPU utilization and scheduled autoscaling policies.
Deploy all instances as Spot VMs and rely on automatic recreation if they are preempted during peak hours.
Provision a static pool of instances sized for peak load and keep them running continuously 24/7.

questions.explanation: Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) support autoscaling based on metrics or schedules. Combining schedule-based scaling for predictable daily patterns with metric-based scaling handles unexpected load changes efficiently and cost-effectively.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Unmanaged instance groups lack auto-healing, load balancing integration, and autoscaling capabilities, making manual shell script management unreliable.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Using Spot VMs for a user-facing production web application during peak hours risks sudden terminations and unacceptable user downtime.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Provisioning for peak load 24/7 results in paying for idle compute capacity 16 hours a day, violating cost optimization principles.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your company is deploying a new containerized application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The application requires consistent compute resources, and your finance team has approved a 1-year financial commitment. How can you achieve the maximum cost reduction for this cluster's nodes?

options.text: Purchase GKE cluster subscription licenses through the Google Cloud Marketplace.
Configure Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscalers with aggressive scale-down parameters.
Purchase Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine resource types (vCPUs and memory) in the target region.
Migrate all workloads to Google App Engine flexible environment to leverage serverless cost models.

questions.explanation: Resource-based Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine apply directly to GKE node instances. Purchasing a 1-year or 3-year commitment for vCPU and memory in a region reduces underlying infrastructure costs significantly.

wrongOptionNotes.A: GKE standard cluster management is charged at a flat hourly rate per cluster, and subscriptions do not discount underlying compute nodes.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling manages pod replicas based on load, but does not provide financial discounts on underlying infrastructure compute.
wrongOptionNotes.D: App Engine flexible environment maintains running instances that can be more expensive for steady-state containerized workloads compared to committed GKE nodes.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are managing a Google Cloud project with multiple Cloud Storage buckets used by various departments. Finance wants visibility into storage costs per department. What is the most effective native method to allocate and track these costs?

options.text: Create separate billing accounts for each department in the Google Cloud Console.
Store each department's files in separate folders within a single centralized bucket and parse access logs.
Apply custom user-defined labels to each Cloud Storage bucket and configure Cloud Billing export to BigQuery to analyze costs by label.
Manually download the monthly CSV invoice and filter line items by project ID.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud labels enable metadata tagging on resources like Cloud Storage buckets. Exporting billing data to BigQuery lets you query costs grouped by these labels for accurate chargeback and showback reporting.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Creating separate billing accounts adds administrative overhead and complicates consolidated invoicing and enterprise discount sharing.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud Billing data is tracked at the bucket level, not the folder or object level. Folders do not allow granular billing attribution.
wrongOptionNotes.D: If multiple departments share a project, project-level billing will not separate their individual costs, and manual CSV parsing does not scale.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your development team frequently spins up temporary test environments on Compute Engine that often remain running over the weekends, causing budget overruns. You need an automated, cost-effective way to shut down non-production instances outside of working hours (6:00 PM to 8:00 AM) across the project.

options.text: Downgrade all test instances to micro instances and leave them running continuously.
Write a custom bash script executed via cron on a separate always-on virtual machine that calls the Compute Engine API.
Configure Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Function that stops instances matching specific labels on a schedule.
Set up a centralized Kubernetes cluster to manage the shutdown states of external Compute Engine instances.

questions.explanation: Cloud Scheduler combined with Cloud Functions provides a serverless, event-driven solution to automate resource lifecycles (like stopping non-production VMs at night and on weekends) without maintaining dedicated servers.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Even micro instances accumulate unnecessary costs when running 24/7 for environments that are only needed 40 hours a week.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Running a separate always-on VM just to execute a script introduces maintenance overhead, potential single points of failure, and unnecessary compute costs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Deploying a Kubernetes cluster purely to handle VM power schedules is overly complex and expensive.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your company runs a database on a Compute Engine instance with a 500GB persistent disk. Due to data cleanup, the actual database size has shrunk to 150GB. However, your monthly storage bill remains based on the 500GB allocation. You need to reduce the storage costs.

options.text: Create a snapshot of the disk, create a new smaller persistent disk from the snapshot, attach it to the instance, and delete the old disk.
Change the persistent disk type from pd-standard to pd-extreme to compress the stored blocks.
Resize the Persistent Disk size downward using the Google Cloud Console or gcloud CLI.
Delete files inside the guest OS until the disk usage drops below 150GB.

questions.explanation: Persistent Disks cannot be shrunk in-place. To reduce storage costs for oversized disks, you must snapshot the current disk, create a smaller persistent disk from that snapshot, attach it to the instance, and delete the original oversized disk.

wrongOptionNotes.B: pd-extreme is designed for high IOPS databases and is significantly more expensive per gigabyte than pd-standard, increasing costs rather than reducing them.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Google Cloud Persistent Disks do not support shrinking disk size directly due to partition table and filesystem risks; you must recreate or resize the filesystem properly.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Deleting files inside the operating system frees up space within the filesystem, but Persistent Disk capacity must be explicitly resized at the Google Cloud API level.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You manage a data processing pipeline that downloads large files from an external source, processes them on a Compute Engine instance, and uploads the results to Cloud Storage. The external source and your Google Cloud project are in different regions, resulting in high inter-region network egress charges. How can you optimize network costs?

options.text: Attach an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer in front of the Compute Engine instance to compress incoming network streams.
Upgrade the Compute Engine network tier from Standard to Premium to get discounted cross-region routing rates.
Migrate the Compute Engine processing instances to the same Google Cloud region where the external data source is hosted, or optimize download caching.
Route all external downloads through a Cloud NAT gateway configured with static IP addresses.

questions.explanation: Network egress charges can form a substantial portion of cloud bills. Placing compute resources in proximity to data sources or optimizing data transfer patterns reduces expensive cross-region and internet egress fees.

wrongOptionNotes.A: An HTTP(S) load balancer is designed for incoming web traffic routing and does not reduce data egress or download costs from external data sources.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Premium Tier uses Google's high-performance global network and is generally more expensive than Standard Tier, which will increase network costs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud NAT provides outbound internet access for instances without external IP addresses, but it does not reduce network data transfer pricing tiers.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your company is planning a 3-year migration project to Google Cloud. Finance wants to lock in the lowest possible rates for Compute Engine instances to stay within a strict budget, knowing the instance footprint will remain stable. What should you purchase?

options.text: Google Cloud Marketplace annual software licenses for operating systems.
3-year Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine resource-based flexibility.
Spot VM capacity reservations for the entire 3-year duration.
Pre-purchased Google Cloud storage buckets with instant tier discounts.

questions.explanation: For stable, long-term workloads spanning years, 3-year resource-based Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) provide the maximum financial savings available on Compute Engine.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Marketplace software licenses apply to third-party software products, not core infrastructure compute compute rates.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Spot VMs cannot be reserved for extended durations and are subject to preemption at any time, making them unsuitable for stable migration baselines.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storage bucket pricing does not discount compute engine instance execution costs.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your development team has deployed numerous debugging snapshots and unmanaged disk images in a Compute Engine project over several months. You need to clean up obsolete resources to reduce monthly storage expenditures. What is the most efficient way to identify and remove unused disk images?

options.text: Delete all snapshots older than 7 days using automated Cloud Storage lifecycle policies.
List all custom images and cross-reference them against currently running or stopped instances to find unattached images, then delete them.
Recreate the entire Google Cloud project to wipe all regional storage artifacts.
Delete all disk images that have names starting with the word 'test' using a shell command.

questions.explanation: Orphaned custom images and snapshots accumulate storage costs over time. Reviewing custom images against current instance inventory ensures safe removal of unused artifacts.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Storage lifecycle policies apply to Cloud Storage buckets, not Compute Engine disk snapshots or custom images.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Recreating a project is a destructive action that destroys all active services, configurations, networks, and data.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Relying on naming conventions is error-prone and can accidentally delete critical production disk images that lack strict naming prefixes.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your application runs on a cluster of Compute Engine instances behind an HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Due to variable user activity, you want to ensure you are only paying for the exact amount of backend compute required without manual intervention, while keeping response times fast. What should you configure?

options.text: A static pool of high-memory instances sized for maximum expected concurrent users.
A Managed Instance Group with autoscaling based on HTTP load balancer request counts or CPU utilization.
