A single oversized instance that vertically scales up by restarting with more CPUs when load increases.
Serverless VPC Access connectors linked directly to unmanaged instance groups.

questions.explanation: Managed Instance Groups with autoscaling provide automatic horizontal scaling of virtual machines, aligning infrastructure costs directly with actual user demand.

wrongOptionNotes.A: A static pool sized for maximum load incurs high idle costs during low-traffic periods.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Vertical resizing requires stopping and restarting the instance, causing service downtime and failing to provide elastic horizontal scaling.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Serverless VPC Access is used for connecting serverless environments to VPC networks, not for autoscaling unmanaged VM groups.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are reviewing monthly Google Cloud billing reports and notice a high charge for inter-zone data transfer within the same region. Your architecture consists of a frontend service in zone `us-central1-a` communicating heavily with a backend database in zone `us-central1-b`. How should you optimize this architecture to eliminate inter-zone data transfer costs?

options.text: Deploy an internal HTTP(S) load balancer between the frontend and backend instances.
Enable Cloud NAT across all subnets in the VPC network.
Migrate both frontend and backend services to reside in the exact same availability zone (`us-central1-a`).
Upgrade your network architecture to use Premium Tier global external IP addresses.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud charges for data transfer between different zones within the same region. Co-locating tightly coupled services in the same zone eliminates these network transfer charges.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While an internal load balancer routes traffic, traffic traversing zones still incurs inter-zone data transfer charges.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud NAT handles outbound internet connectivity for private IPs and does not affect internal zonal data transfer costs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: External IP addresses and Premium Tier routing apply to internet traffic, not intra-project zonal communication.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team is architecting a multi-region deployment of a mission-critical web application across us-central1 and europe-west1 to guarantee high availability and disaster recovery. You need to configure global load balancing with automatic failover if an entire region goes offline. Which combination of Google Cloud services should you deploy?

options.text: Deploy a Cloud VPN gateway between us-central1 and europe-west1 to route traffic through a primary active instance and a standby instance.
Deploy a Global External Application Load Balancer fronting backend services in both regions, backed by regional managed instance groups.
Deploy a Global External Network Load Balancer (TCP proxy) with Network Endpoint Groups pointing to serverless application instances.
Deploy regional external HTTP(S) load balancers in each region with DNS round-robin routing between them.

questions.explanation: A Global External Application Load Balancer provides a single global IP address and uses health checks to monitor backend services across multiple regions, automatically shifting traffic away from unhealthy regions during an outage.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud VPN connects networks, not client-facing web traffic, and does not provide global HTTP load balancing or automated failover for web users.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Global External Network Load Balancers operate at layer 4 and are not designed for application-layer path routing or HTTP(S) web application backends compared to Application Load Balancers.
wrongOptionNotes.D: DNS round-robin does not provide active health checking or automatic failover capabilities required for robust disaster recovery.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your organization requires a disaster recovery strategy for a critical relational database running on Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. The Recovery Point Objective (RPO) must be under 1 minute and Recovery Time Objective (RTO) under 10 minutes across different regions. What is the most effective approach?

options.text: Deploy a separate Cloud SQL instance in the secondary region and write custom application code to dual-write all transactions.
Set up a Cloud SQL cross-region replica in a secondary region with automated failover capabilities.
Configure daily automated backups and point-in-time recovery enabled on a single-zone primary instance.
Take manual snapshots of the persistent disks every hour and copy them to a secondary region bucket.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL cross-region replicas maintain a synchronized copy of your database in another region, enabling fast promotion to primary status to minimize downtime.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Application-level dual writes are complex, prone to consistency bugs, and difficult to maintain compared to native Cloud SQL replication.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Daily backups and PITR cannot achieve an RPO of under 1 minute or an RTO under 10 minutes during a major regional disaster.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Manual snapshots result in high RPO (hours) and slow RTO (hours to restore disks and boot databases), violating requirements.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your company operates an e-commerce platform deployed in a single region (us-central1). Management mandates a multi-region disaster recovery architecture for your Cloud Storage assets that contain critical product images. Data must be replicated continuously to europe-west1 with minimal management overhead. Which storage class configuration should you choose?

options.text: Use Dual-Region storage configured for specific paired regions (e.g., us-central1 and europe-west1 if supported, or matching supported pairs).
Use Multi-Region storage configured for the US multi-region.
Use Coldline storage in us-central1 with Storage Transfer Service jobs scheduled to run daily.
Use Standard Regional storage in us-central1 and write a custom Cloud Function triggered by object uploads to copy every file to a bucket in europe-west1.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage Dual-Region storage provides high availability and geo-redundancy by storing data across two specific geographic regions managed natively by Google Cloud.

wrongOptionNotes.B: US multi-region only replicates across data centers within the United States, failing the requirement to replicate to europe-west1.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Coldline storage is meant for infrequent access, and daily syncs result in a 24-hour RPO, failing disaster recovery requirements.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Custom Cloud Function replication introduces operational overhead, potential race conditions, and lack of atomic consistency guarantees compared to native Cloud Storage replication.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are designing a failover mechanism for stateless backend microservices running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) across us-east1 and us-west1. If us-east1 experiences a complete failure, traffic needs to be routed to us-west1 automatically without manual DNS updates. How should you configure the routing?

options.text: Configure an internal TCP/UDP Load Balancer across the two GKE clusters.
Configure Google Cloud Armor rate limiting rules to drop traffic to the primary region during an incident.
Use a Global External Application Load Balancer with backend services pointing to GKE Ingress controllers in both clusters, utilizing automatic health-check-based traffic shifting.
Create a Cloud DNS managed zone with a low TTL and write a monitoring script that manually updates DNS records when an outage occurs.

questions.explanation: Global load balancing integrated with GKE Ingress and health checks provides seamless, automated multi-region traffic failover.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Internal TCP/UDP Load Balancers are regional and cannot span across distant regions like us-east1 and us-west1.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Google Cloud Armor handles security and DDoS mitigation, not regional failover routing.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Manual script-based DNS updates introduce high RTO and human error risk during a crisis.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your organization is reviewing its disaster recovery posture for stateful workloads running on Compute Engine persistent disks. You need to ensure that disk snapshots taken in us-central1 are available in europe-west1 for rapid VM recovery in case of a regional disaster. What is the correct way to manage these snapshots?

options.text: Configure regional persistent disk snapshots, which automatically replicate across all global regions by default.
Create standard snapshots in us-central1 and use snapshot schedules or manual copy operations to create snapshots in europe-west1.
Manually download the snapshot data to local machines and upload them to a bucket in europe-west1.
Use Cloud Storage buckets with multi-region settings to store the snapshot exports.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine allows you to copy snapshots across regions, enabling you to maintain off-site backups for disaster recovery and cross-region VM recreation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Standard Compute Engine snapshots are stored globally or regionally, but do not automatically replicate to arbitrary distant regions without explicit creation or multi-region policies.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Manual downloading and uploading is inefficient, slow, and operationally burdensome.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Standard disk snapshots are managed via Compute Engine snapshot APIs, not direct Cloud Storage multi-region bucket exports for boot restoration.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your enterprise application uses Memorystore for Redis as an in-memory cache for session data. To ensure resilience against regional failures, you need to implement high availability. Which configuration should you choose?

options.text: Deploy two independent Basic Tier Redis instances in different regions and write application-level synchronization logic.
Attach a persistent disk to the Basic Tier Redis instance to persist data across reboots.
Provision a Standard Tier Redis instance with Read Replicas enabled across multiple zones.
Provision a Basic Tier Redis instance and take manual RDB backups every 4 hours.

questions.explanation: Memorystore Standard Tier provides built-in high availability with primary and replica nodes across different zones, performing automated failover if the primary node fails.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Application-level sync for Redis adds unnecessary complexity and prone to split-brain or consistency issues.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Memorystore for Redis is fully managed and does not support attaching persistent disks directly to nodes.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Basic Tier instances have no automatic failover and data loss or extended downtime occurs if the node fails.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your company runs a critical data pipeline processing files stored in Cloud Storage. The disaster recovery plan dictates that if the primary region (asia-east1) experiences an outage, the application must read from a replicated bucket in asia-northeast1 within 15 minutes. You choose Cloud Storage Dual-Region. How is data consistency handled?

options.text: Dual-Region storage provides eventual consistency for metadata only, requiring manual verification.
Consistency can only be guaranteed if you implement custom object locking mechanisms.
Dual-Region storage replicates data asynchronously with a guaranteed 24-hour delay before consistency is achieved.
Dual-Region storage provides read-after-write consistency for all upload and update operations across both regions.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud Storage provides strong read-after-write consistency for all storage classes, including Dual-Region and Multi-Region, ensuring immediate availability of written data.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Storage provides strong read-after-write consistency globally for all upload and mutation operations.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Object locking is for compliance/retention, not basic read-after-write consistency.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Dual-Region replication is typically completed within milliseconds or seconds, far below a 24-hour window.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your database engineering team is setting up a Disaster Recovery plan for a MySQL database on Compute Engine. They want to minimize RPO during a regional failure. Which replication strategy between a primary VM in us-east1 and a standby VM in us-west1 achieves the lowest RPO?

options.text: Asynchronous replication with binlogs streamed every 6 hours.
Daily database dumps transferred via secure copy (SCP) to the standby VM.
Scheduled snapshot replication using persistent disk snapshot schedules.
Synchronous replication over a dedicated Interconnect with strict quorum enforcement.

questions.explanation: Synchronous replication ensures zero data loss (RPO = 0) by committing transactions across regions before acknowledging writes, though it introduces latency tradeoffs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: 6-hour sync intervals result in a high RPO of up to 6 hours of data loss.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Daily backups result in unacceptable data loss windows for mission-critical databases.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Disk snapshot schedules typically run at hourly or daily intervals, which does not meet low RPO database requirements.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your organization is building a global web service. You want to ensure that if your primary backend in europe-west3 experiences degraded performance or failure, the Global External Application Load Balancer automatically routes incoming user requests to the healthy backup backend in us-central1. How does the load balancer determine when to fail over?

options.text: Based on the total billing cost incurred by each region.
Based on manual operator commands executed via the Google Cloud Console.
Based on periodic HTTP/HTTPS health checks configured on the backend service, which mark regions unhealthy if health check probes fail consecutively.
Based on Round Trip Time (RTT) measurements reported by client web browsers.

questions.explanation: HTTP(S) health checks are the mechanism by which Google Cloud load balancers monitor backend health and automate multi-region traffic failover.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Load balancers route based on traffic, latency, and health check status, never on billing cost metrics.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Failover in a high-availability architecture must be automated via health checks, not manual operator intervention.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Load balancers use server-side health checks and Anycast routing, not browser-reported RTT telemetry.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are managing a multi-region deployment on Compute Engine. Your architecture uses unmanaged instance groups in us-central1 and europe-west1 behind a load balancer. During a disaster simulation, you notice that when the primary region fails, instances in the secondary region do not automatically scale up to handle the increased load. What architectural change is required?

options.text: Upgrade the instances to larger machine types permanently to handle 200% peak load.
Configure Cloud DNS failover routing policies with static IP addresses.
Increase the size of the persistent disks attached to the unmanaged instances in both regions.
Replace unmanaged instance groups with Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) configured with autoscaling and health checks.

questions.explanation: Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) provide automated scaling and healing capabilities necessary to absorb failover traffic loads dynamically.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Over-provisioning permanent capacity in all regions is cost-inefficient; autoscaling MIGs provide elastic capacity during failover.
wrongOptionNotes.B: While DNS failover routes traffic, it does not solve the compute capacity scaling issue for unmanaged instance groups.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Disk size does not affect CPU compute capacity or automated scaling during a failover event.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your company is designing a disaster recovery strategy for a data warehouse running in BigQuery. Datasets are loaded daily from operational databases. Management wants to ensure that data can be recovered if a catastrophic regional failure impacts BigQuery storage in us-central1. What is the recommended best practice for BigQuery disaster recovery?

options.text: Deploy a separate BigQuery dataset in another cloud provider using custom ETL jobs.
Configure BigQuery automatic cross-region streaming replication to AWS S3.
Export all BigQuery tables to Cloud Storage Dual-Region buckets daily.
Manually copy every table to a separate dataset in the same region every hour.

questions.explanation: BigQuery datasets are automatically replicated for high availability, but exporting critical tables to Cloud Storage Dual-Region or multi-region buckets provides an extra layer of disaster recovery protection.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cross-cloud ETL for full data warehouses is complex and unnecessary given Google Cloud's built-in replication and Cloud Storage export options.
wrongOptionNotes.B: BigQuery does not support automatic cross-cloud streaming replication to external cloud providers.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Copying within the same region does not protect against a regional disaster affecting that specific region.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your development team is deploying a containerized microservice on GKE across two regions for disaster recovery. You want to ensure that session data stored in Memorystore for Redis remains intact and accessible if the primary GKE cluster and its local Redis instance fail. How should you design the Redis architecture?

options.text: Deploy a single Memorystore instance in us-central1 and connect the GKE cluster in europe-west1 to it over the public internet.
Configure Memorystore to replicate synchronously across different continents automatically.
Use Cloud Storage to back up Redis keys every second.
Deploy a Memorystore for Redis instance in each region and use application-level fallback logic to the secondary region cache.

questions.explanation: Because Memorystore is a regional service, multi-region disaster recovery requires deploying regional cache instances and implementing application-level failover logic.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cross-region connection over public internet is insecure, introduces high latency, and creates a single point of failure if us-central1 goes down.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Memorystore does not support cross-continent synchronous replication out of the box.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Backing up Redis to Cloud Storage every second is technically unfeasible and defeats the performance purpose of an in-memory cache.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your organization is establishing an RTO (Recovery Time Objective) of less than 1 hour for a virtual appliance running on a Compute Engine instance in us-central1. In the event of a total zonal failure, what is the fastest automated way to restore the compute instance in another zone within the same region?

options.text: Rebuild the instance manually from installation scripts using a startup script.
Take weekly manual disk snapshots and wait for an administrator to provision a new VM when alerted.
Use a Managed Instance Group (MIG) configured across multiple zones with automatic restarting and healing.
Export the VM image to an on-premises data center via VPN.

questions.explanation: Multi-zonal Managed Instance Groups provide automated recovery and instance recreation across zones, minimizing RTO without manual intervention.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Manual rebuilding or relying solely on long startup scripts can exceed RTO targets during a major incident.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual intervention and weekly snapshots result in unacceptable RPO and RTO.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Exporting VM images on-prem during an active cloud outage is slow and defeats cloud disaster recovery best practices.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team is planning a disaster recovery architecture for a custom application running on Compute Engine. Management wants to understand the cost versus RPO/RTO tradeoffs of active-passive versus active-active multi-region designs. Which characteristic best describes an active-passive disaster recovery setup in Google Cloud?

options.text: The secondary region maintains idle or minimal standby compute capacity, resulting in lower compute costs while accepting a higher RTO during failover due to scaling or promotion delays.
Traffic is served simultaneously from both regions with real-time bidirectional data conflict resolution.
Failover happens instantly with zero RTO and zero cost increase compared to single-region deployments.
Data is only stored in memory and never persisted, ensuring zero storage cost.

questions.explanation: Active-passive disaster recovery balances cost efficiency by minimizing standby compute resources in the secondary region while accepting the RTO required to promote databases and scale up compute capacity during an incident.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Simultaneous active serving with bidirectional conflict resolution describes an active-active architecture, not active-passive.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Maintaining standby resources always incurs some baseline infrastructure cost (e.g., storage, database replicas), and promotion adds RTO.
wrongOptionNotes.D: All production DR architectures require durable persistent storage.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are configuring a global web application fronted by a Global External Application Load Balancer. Your primary backend is in us-east1 and your failover backend is in europe-west1. During testing, you find that failover takes up to 3 minutes when you deliberately sever connectivity to us-east1. You need to reduce the failover detection time. What should you adjust?

options.text: Switch from a Global External Application Load Balancer to a TCP Proxy load balancer.
Increase the TTL on your Cloud DNS records to 86400 seconds.
Enable Google Cloud Armor bot management rules.
Decrease the health check interval and timeout settings, and reduce the healthy/unhealthy threshold counts on the backend service health check.

questions.explanation: Adjusting load balancer health check interval, timeout, and threshold settings controls how quickly unhealthy backends are detected and removed from service rotation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Switching load balancer types does not inherently speed up failure detection unless health check parameters are specifically tuned.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Increasing DNS TTL would actually increase propagation delay and slow down failover if DNS-based routing were involved, though global load balancers use Anycast IP rather than DNS changes.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud Armor security policies protect against web attacks, not backend health check timing.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your company uses a single Google Cloud project for development. Developers need the ability to deploy Compute Engine instances and manage Cloud Storage buckets, but security policy strictly forbids them from managing IAM policies or creating service account keys. What is the most secure and appropriate way to grant these permissions?

options.text: Assign the Compute Instance Admin (v1) and Storage Admin predefined roles directly to the developer group.
Assign the Project Editor role to the developers since it grants instance and storage management while excluding billing administration.
Create a custom role with compute.instances.* and storage.buckets.* permissions and assign it to the developers at the project level.
Grant the primitive Owner role to developers and rely on Organizational Policies to block service account key creation.

questions.explanation: When predefined roles are too broad, custom roles provide the principle of least privilege by combining specific permissions required for a workflow while explicitly excluding dangerous operations like IAM modifications or key creation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Storage Admin includes permissions to manage ACLs and IAM policies on buckets, which may exceed the intended scope of developer permissions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: The Project Editor role grants broad permissions including the ability to manage IAM policies and create service account keys, violating security policy.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Relying solely on an Org Policy while using the Owner role is an anti-pattern as it grants excessive privileges and potential bypass vectors.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are managing access to a sensitive Cloud Storage bucket containing PII data. Compliance requires that users can only read specific objects within the bucket and cannot list the contents of the entire bucket. How should you grant this access?

options.text: Use Uniform Bucket-Level Access and generate signed URLs for individual objects that users need to access.
Disable Uniform Bucket-Level Access and apply Fine-Grained Access Control (Access Control Lists) to every individual object.
Grant the Storage Object Viewer role at the bucket level and rely on bucket-level IAM conditions.
Assign the Storage Object Creator role along with the Storage Object Viewer role at the project level.

questions.explanation: Signed URLs provide secure, time-limited access to specific Cloud Storage objects without granting broader list permissions or IAM roles on the bucket itself.

wrongOptionNotes.B: ACLs are legacy mechanisms and Google strongly recommends Uniform Bucket-Level Access. Furthermore, ACLs do not prevent listing when combined with reader roles.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The Storage Object Viewer role includes storage.objects.list permission, which allows users to list all objects in the bucket, violating the requirement.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Project-level roles grant permissions across all buckets, and Object Viewer still grants the list permission for the entire bucket.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are configuring network access for a new Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) private cluster. Worker nodes must not have external IP addresses, but pods need to download container images from public repositories and pull security patches over the internet. What component must you configure?

options.text: A Cloud NAT gateway associated with Cloud Router in the region and network used by the cluster nodes.
A default internet gateway attached directly to the node subnet with an egress firewall rule.
A TCP proxy load balancer configured with internal IP forwarding enabled on all worker node interfaces.
A Dedicated Interconnect connection with a default route pointing to your on-premises proxy servers.

questions.explanation: Cloud NAT provides Network Address Translation for GKE private nodes, allowing them to initiate outbound traffic to the internet while remaining completely inaccessible from external sources.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Nodes without external IPs cannot utilize a standard internet gateway for outbound traffic without a NAT mechanism.
wrongOptionNotes.C: A TCP proxy load balancer is for inbound traffic distribution, not outbound NAT functionality.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While Dedicated Interconnect routes traffic on-prem, it is an over-engineered solution for simple public internet egress and adds unnecessary latency and cost.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are deploying a custom business application on Compute Engine. The application requires access to Google Cloud APIs (such as BigQuery and Cloud Storage) without exposing credentials as static files on disk. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Store user credentials in environment variables within the application startup script.
Configure the default Compute Engine service account and grant it the Project Owner role for universal API access.
Assign a custom Service Account to the Compute Engine instance during creation and grant the service account permissions via IAM.
Create a service account, download its JSON private key, and embed the file path in the application configuration.

questions.explanation: Attaching a dedicated service account to a Compute Engine instance leverages GCP's metadata service to handle token generation and rotation automatically, eliminating the need for static key files.

wrongOptionNotes.A: User credentials should not be hardcoded or passed via environment variables for application authentication; service accounts should be used instead.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Granting the default service account Project Owner violates the principle of least privilege and exposes the entire project to risk.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Embedding JSON private keys on disk is an anti-pattern that creates significant security risks if the instance is compromised.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team needs to provision a new Google Cloud project that will house a cardholder data environment subject to PCI-DSS compliance. You need to ensure that no developer can accidentally create unencrypted Compute Engine disks or public Cloud Storage buckets anywhere in the project. Which feature should you configure?

options.text: A Cloud Monitoring alert policy combined with a Cloud Functions webhook to delete non-compliant resources.
Cloud Billing Budgets and alerts to notify security teams when non-compliant resources are provisioned.
Removing all IAM roles from developers and forcing them to submit tickets for resource provisioning.
Organization Policies enforcing constraints such as 'Disable Public Bucket Access' and 'Require CMEK for Disks'.

questions.explanation: Organization Policy Service allows administrators to set centralized, preventative constraints (like restricting public access or requiring customer-managed encryption keys) that override project-level permissions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Reactive remediation via monitoring and functions introduces a window of vulnerability; preventative policies are required for compliance.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Budgets only monitor spend; they cannot prevent resource creation or enforce configuration compliance.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Removing all roles halts productivity and does not programmatically prevent misconfigurations if permissions are eventually granted.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are configuring a custom Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network with subnets in us-central1 and europe-west1. Instances in us-central1 need to communicate with instances in europe-west1 using internal IP addresses. However, ping tests fail. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Subnets within the same VPC network cannot communicate across different regions by default without a VPN gateway.
Instances across different regions must use external IP addresses even when residing in the same VPC.
Global Dynamic Routing is disabled on the VPC network, preventing cross-region subnet route propagation.
A firewall rule is blocking ICMP traffic or inbound TCP/UDP traffic between the two subnets.

questions.explanation: All subnets within a GCP VPC network can route traffic to each other by default. If traffic fails, check VPC firewall rules, as default rules or explicit denies might block specific protocols (like ICMP for ping).

wrongOptionNotes.A: Subnets in a custom VPC network can communicate across all regions by default without configuring VPN gateways.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Instances within the same VPC can communicate using internal IP addresses regardless of region.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Custom VPC subnets are automatically known to all regions within the VPC; global dynamic routing applies specifically to Cloud Router and VPN/Interconnect routing.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your company is deploying a secure database backend on Compute Engine. Security mandates that database instances must not have public IP addresses and cannot be accessed directly from the public internet, but administrators must still be able to securely connect to them for maintenance via SSH. What is the best practice solution?

options.text: Assign temporary external IP addresses to the database instances only during maintenance windows.
Set up a public bastion host with port forwarding to relay SSH traffic directly to the database instances.
Configure a Cloud VPN tunnel from the administrator's local workstation directly to the VPC network.
Configure IAP (Identity-Aware Proxy) TCP forwarding to tunnel SSH connections through Google's secure proxy.

questions.explanation: Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) enables secure administrative access (SSH/RDP) to Compute Engine instances that do not have external IP addresses, controlling access via IAM policies.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Assigning public IPs exposes instances unnecessarily and violates hardening best practices.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Bastion hosts require managing OS-level SSH keys and maintaining a public-facing instance, whereas IAP removes the need for a bastion host and external IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Setting up a Cloud VPN tunnel for individual remote administrator workstations is overly complex compared to using IAP.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You need to automate the creation of multiple Google Cloud projects across your organization's hierarchy. The projects must be placed under specific folders and linked to a designated billing account. Which tool or service should you use?

options.text: Google Cloud Console Web UI using manual project creation wizards.
Google Cloud Deployment Manager using project resource definitions.
Cloud Storage bucket notifications configured to trigger a Cloud Function whenever a project request file is uploaded.
Google Cloud CLI (gcloud) combined with Resource Manager API and Billing API scripts.

questions.explanation: Resource Manager and Billing APIs provide programmatic control via gcloud or SDKs to automate project provisioning, folder placement, and billing account attachment at scale.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The Console UI is manual and does not scale well for automating the creation of multiple projects.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Deployment Manager is primarily designed for configuring and deploying GCP resources within an existing project, not for creating and organizing projects at the folder/organization level.
wrongOptionNotes.C: This is a convoluted workaround that does not natively manage Google Cloud project hierarchies or billing bindings.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team has configured a new HTTP(S) Load Balancer in front of a Managed Instance Group of backend web servers. Users are reporting intermittent 503 Service Unavailable errors. Upon investigation, you find that the load balancer backend health checks are failing consistently. What is the most likely configuration issue?

options.text: The backend instances are located in a different region than the load balancer frontend.
The web servers are running on port 80, but the health check is configured to check port 443.
Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancers require static external IP addresses assigned directly to each backend instance.
The firewall rules do not allow inbound traffic from the Load Balancer's health check IP ranges (35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22).

questions.explanation: HTTP(S) Load Balancer health checks originate from specific Google IP ranges. VPC firewall rules must allow ingress from these ranges to the backend instances for health checks to succeed.

wrongOptionNotes.A: HTTP(S) Load Balancers are global and can route traffic to backend instances across multiple regions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Port mismatch causes health check failures, but firewall blocks are the most common pitfall when setting up new environments.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Backend instances behind an HTTP(S) Load Balancer do not need external IP addresses; they receive traffic via the load balancer.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are deploying a legacy application on Compute Engine that requires access to a shared relational database. Your security team mandates that all data transferred between the application instance and the database instance must be encrypted in transit using SSL/TLS. How should you configure the Cloud SQL instance to support this?

options.text: Install an SSL certificate directly onto the Compute Engine instance's operating system via OS configuration management.
Enable SSL/TLS enforcement on the Cloud SQL instance and configure the client application with the server CA certificate, client certificate, and client private key.
Rely on Google Cloud's internal fiber network, as all traffic between VPCs is automatically encrypted at the hardware level with SSL/TLS.
Deploy a Cloud VPN tunnel between the application instance and the Cloud SQL instance.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL supports configuring SSL/TLS certificates for encrypted client connections. Enforcing SSL on the instance requires clients to present valid certificates and encrypts all database traffic.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Installing a certificate on the client OS does not configure the database server to enforce or validate SSL connections.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While GCP encrypts traffic at the infrastructure layer, compliance mandates often require application-level or database-enforced SSL/TLS configuration.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud VPN cannot be connected directly to a Cloud SQL instance; Cloud SQL provides native SSL/TLS configuration options.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are managing billing and cost attribution for a Google Cloud project utilized by multiple departments. Finance requests that you track costs associated specifically with a temporary data migration job running across multiple Compute Engine instances and Cloud Storage buckets. What is the most effective mechanism to achieve this?

options.text: Assign separate billing accounts to each temporary resource within the same project.
Create a separate Google Cloud project for every individual job and migrate resources between projects daily.
Rename all resources to include department prefixes so they can be filtered in the Billing report.
Apply consistent resource labels (e.g., department: migration) to all Compute Engine instances and Cloud Storage buckets, and enable label export in Billing.

questions.explanation: Labels are key-value pairs attached to Google Cloud resources. By exporting Cloud Billing data to BigQuery, organizations can query costs filtered by specific resource labels for accurate cost attribution.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Billing accounts are assigned at the project level, not to individual resources within a project.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Creating and migrating projects daily for temporary jobs is operationally inefficient and introduces unnecessary complexity.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Naming conventions are prone to human error and are not a native mechanism for cost allocation.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your development team has built a web application that stores session files. To ensure high availability and scalability across multiple Compute Engine instances in a Managed Instance Group, you need a shared filesystem that supports standard POSIX file locking and can be mounted across all instances simultaneously. Which storage service should you select?

options.text: Cloud Storage with bucket-level versioning enabled.
Filestore Basic or Enterprise tier instance mounted via NFSv3.
Compute Engine persistent disks attached in Read-Write Multi-Attach mode.
Bigtable with HBase client libraries.

questions.explanation: Filestore provides fully managed NFS file storage that allows multiple Compute Engine instances to mount the same filesystem with full POSIX read/write and locking capabilities.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Storage is an object store, not a POSIX-compliant filesystem, and does not support simultaneous file locking required for traditional session files.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Persistent disk multi-attach requires cluster file systems (like GFS2 or OCFS2) to handle file locking; attaching a standard ext4/xfs disk read-write to multiple instances will cause data corruption.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Bigtable is a NoSQL wide-column database, not a shared filesystem.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are troubleshooting a connectivity issue where an application running on a Compute Engine instance cannot reach an external API over the internet. The instance has a valid internal IP address, but no external IP address. You have already verified that a Cloud NAT gateway is configured in the VPC. What else must be configured for outbound internet traffic to succeed?

options.text: Enabling IP forwarding on the Compute Engine instance network interface.
An explicit ingress firewall rule allowing all outbound traffic from the instance IP.
A default route (0.0.0.0/0) pointing to the Default Internet Gateway as the next hop.
A static public IP address assigned directly to the Cloud NAT router instance.

questions.explanation: For instances without external IPs to reach the internet via Cloud NAT, there must be a valid route in the VPC routing table (typically the default 0.0.0.0/0 route pointing to the default internet gateway) to direct the traffic.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IP forwarding is required if the instance acts as a router or gateway for other IPs, not for standard outbound application traffic.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Google Cloud VPC firewall rules are stateful; outbound traffic is allowed by default unless explicitly blocked by an egress rule. Ingress rules do not govern outbound traffic.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud NAT routers do not use Compute Engine instances; they are fully managed regional services that use allocated external IP addresses.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: You are migrating a monolithic application to Google Cloud. The application runs as a single Linux daemon and must automatically restart if the underlying virtual machine crashes or experiences hardware failure. Which Compute Engine feature provides the simplest native mechanism to ensure this recovery?

options.text: Configuring Compute Engine 'Automatic Restart' and 'On Host Maintenance' settings on the instance.
Deploying a preemptible VM instance with a startup script that restarts the daemon.
Writing a custom cron job that checks the daemon status every minute and reboots the OS if it fails.
Managed Instance Groups with autoscaling enabled.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine provides built-in availability controls, including Automatic Restart and live migration during host maintenance, ensuring virtual machines recover automatically from underlying infrastructure faults.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Preemptible VMs can be terminated by GCP at any time with little warning, making them unsuitable for persistent monolithic daemons.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Writing custom cron jobs for hypervisor-level failure recovery is an anti-pattern and does not protect against hardware crashes.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While MIGs support autohealing, they are designed for stateless horizontal scaling rather than managing a single monolithic VM instance daemon.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your organization requires that all database backups stored in Cloud Storage must be automatically transitioned to Coldline Storage after 30 days and deleted entirely after 365 days to optimize costs. What is the most efficient way to enforce this lifecycle requirement?

options.text: Configure Cloud Logging alerts tied to Cloud Functions to intercept object creation and reschedule deletion timers.
Configure Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management rules on the bucket with actions for SetStorageClass and Delete.
Create separate Cloud Storage buckets for each tier and use manual batch copying scripts every month.
Write a custom Python script running on a Compute Engine instance that uses the Cloud Storage API to check object ages and modify storage classes daily.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management allows administrators to define rules json/xml configurations that automatically execute actions (like changing storage classes or deleting objects) based on object age and characteristics.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Intercepting object creations with functions for lifecycle management is a complex workaround for a native Cloud Storage capability.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Manual or scripted bucket-to-bucket copying is inefficient, error-prone, and adds unnecessary data transfer and operational costs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Writing custom scripts to manage object lifecycles introduces unnecessary maintenance overhead and potential failure points when native features exist.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team is investigating an incident where a Compute Engine instance running a production database cannot connect to Cloud SQL. The database instance uses a private IP address. Both instances reside in the same VPC network but in different subnets. You check the firewall rules and find no blocking egress rules. What is the most likely root cause of the connection failure?

options.text: The Cloud SQL proxy must be installed on every subnet for routing internal traffic.
Private Services Access (PSA) connection and VPC Network Peering are not established or incorrectly configured for the Cloud SQL instance.
Cloud SQL uses internal IP addresses that require public IP assignment on the Compute Engine instance to route traffic.
Compute Engine instances cannot communicate with Cloud SQL instances across different subnets without a custom static route.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL instances configured with private IP do not automatically use standard VPC routing. They require a Private Services Access (PSA) allocation and a corresponding VPC Network Peering connection between the consumer VPC and the Google-managed producer VPC.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The Cloud SQL Auth proxy is optional for TCP/IP connections when using private IP and is not a network routing requirement.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Compute Engine instances with internal IP addresses can communicate with private Cloud SQL instances as long as they are in the same VPC or connected via VPC Network Peering, without needing public IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC subnets are regional, but the VPC network itself is global. Instances across different subnets in the same VPC can communicate by default without custom routes.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your company's security team detects that a Compute Engine instance is experiencing high outbound network traffic directed to an unknown external IP. Upon inspection, you find the instance was compromised. Security mandates that you isolate the instance for forensic analysis immediately while retaining its disk state, without shutting down the entire virtual machine or losing RAM contents. What should you do?

options.text: Apply a high-priority ingress and egress firewall rule blocking all traffic to and from the instance's network tags, or move the instance to an isolated VPC network.
Update the network tags on the instance to remove the tag associated with the default allow firewall rules, and apply a strict deny-all egress firewall rule targeting its IP address.
Stop the instance immediately and create a snapshot of the root persistent disk.
Detach the primary persistent disk from the running instance and attach it to a forensic investigation instance.

questions.explanation: To isolate a compromised Compute Engine instance while keeping it powered on to preserve memory forensics, administrators should use VPC firewall rules with high priority targeting the instance's internal or external IP to block all egress and ingress traffic.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Moving instances between VPC networks requires stopping the instance, which discards RAM contents.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Stopping the instance destroys the volatile memory (RAM), which may contain critical forensic artifacts like active network connections and injected binaries.
wrongOptionNotes.D: You cannot detach a root persistent disk from a running Compute Engine instance without stopping it first.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: An application deployed on a Managed Instance Group (MIG) behind an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer is returning HTTP 502 Bad Gateway errors to users. You check the load balancer backend health check status, and all instances are marked as 'UNHEALTHY'. You confirm the application is running successfully on port 8080 locally inside the instances. What is the most likely cause of this health check failure?

options.text: The Managed Instance Group needs to be re-created because rolling updates automatically corrupt health check configurations.
The HTTP(S) Load Balancer requires Cloud Armor to be enabled before backends can pass health checks.
HTTP(S) Load Balancers require backend instances to listen exclusively on port 80 or 443.
Google Cloud health check probes are being blocked by VPC firewall rules that do not allow incoming traffic from the Google Cloud health check IP ranges (`35.191.0.0/16` and `130.211.0.0/22`).

questions.explanation: Load balancer health checks require explicit inbound firewall allowances from Google Cloud's health check probe ranges. If these rules are missing or overridden by higher-priority deny rules, instances will show as unhealthy, causing the load balancer to return 502 Bad Gateway errors.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Rolling updates do not corrupt configurations; health check failures indicate a networking or application configuration issue.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud Armor is a security policy layer and is not required for basic load balancer health checks to function.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Backend services can use custom ports (such as 8080) as long as the backend service and instance configuration match.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team deployed a containerized application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Users report intermittent connection drops and 'Connection Reset by Peer' errors during peak hours. Investigation reveals that CPU throttling is occurring on the Kubernetes worker nodes. How should you resolve this issue permanently?

options.text: Increase the replica count of the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) to scale pods across more nodes.
Increase the liveness and readiness probe failure thresholds in the Kubernetes deployment manifest.
Modify the cluster node pool configuration to use larger machine types with higher vCPU capacity or scale out the node pool size.
Disable Kubernetes network policies to reduce packet inspection overhead on the worker nodes.

questions.explanation: When GKE worker nodes experience CPU throttling, containers on those nodes are starved of CPU cycles, leading to application latency and connection drops. Resizing the node pool or migrating to larger machine types provides the necessary compute headroom.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Scaling pods on overloaded nodes will only exacerbate CPU contention and throttling if the underlying nodes lack capacity.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Adjusting probe thresholds masks the symptom by waiting longer before restarting pods, but it does not fix the underlying resource exhaustion.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Unless explicitly enabled and heavily complex, standard network policies do not cause severe CPU throttling compared to under-provisioned node sizing.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your production application writes critical logs to Cloud Logging. Recently, compliance auditors noticed that a specific subset of security log entries has gone missing over the last week. The log volume is extremely high, and the project is hitting ingestion limits. What is the most robust way to troubleshoot and prevent this log loss?

options.text: Check project-level Cloud Logging quota metrics in the Cloud Monitoring console, and request a quota increase or implement log exclusion filters for non-critical high-volume logs.
Increase the Cloud Logging sink export buffer size to maximum capacity in the IAM policy settings.
Upgrade the Google Cloud project billing tier from Standard to Enterprise to unlock infinite log ingestion capacity.
Manually restart the Cloud Logging agent on all Compute Engine instances to flush pending logs.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud Logging enforces project-level ingestion quotas. When log volume exceeds these quotas, logs are dropped. Administrators should monitor ingestion rates via Cloud Monitoring, request quota adjustments, or filter out noisy, non-critical logs.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Log sinks do not have an adjustable buffer size setting in IAM policies.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Google Cloud does not have a billing tier called 'Enterprise' that provides infinite log ingestion without quota limits.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Log loss due to quota exhaustion happens at the ingestion API level in Google Cloud, not within the local logging agent buffers.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: An engineer deployed a new version of an application on a Compute Engine instance group, but automated health checks are failing because the application fails to start up correctly. The startup script encounters an uncaught exception and exits with a non-zero status. Where should you look first to inspect the exact script error output?

options.text: The VPC flow logs associated with the instance's network interface.
The Google Cloud Billing export dataset in BigQuery.
The Cloud Storage bucket designated for bucket logging.
The instance's serial port output logs in the Google Cloud Console or gcloud.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine streams startup script output directly to the instance serial port (specifically serial port 1). When deployment automation or manual scripts fail, checking the serial port output provides immediate visibility into stderr and exit codes.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC flow logs capture network IP traffic metadata, not operating system startup script execution output.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Billing datasets track costs and usage, not instance startup script logs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Bucket logging records access requests made to Cloud Storage buckets, not Compute Engine startup execution.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your batch processing pipeline running on a group of preemptible Compute Engine instances frequently fails because instances are abruptly terminated before completing their jobs. Management wants to maintain cost savings while minimizing job failures. What is the most appropriate architectural adjustment?

options.text: Migrate all batch workloads to standard non-preemptible instances with committed use discounts.
Configure graceful shutdown and application checkpointing, and leverage Spot VMs with proper signaling (shutdown scripts and metadata monitoring) to save state before termination.
Disable autohealing on the Managed Instance Group to prevent unhealthy instances from being recreated.
Increase the maximum instance limit on the Managed Instance Group autoscaler.

questions.explanation: Spot VMs and preemptible instances offer deep discounts but can be reclaimed at any time with a 30-second warning. To handle this, architectures must implement checkpointing and use shutdown scripts to save state before the instance is stopped.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While standard instances prevent preemption, management may still prefer spot/preemptible pricing if workloads are designed to be fault-tolerant.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Disabling autohealing will prevent failed instances from being replaced, causing the batch pipeline to stall permanently.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Scaling up instances does not prevent preemptible instances from being reclaimed by Google Cloud when capacity is needed.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your team is troubleshooting a persistent timeout issue when an internal application calls an external third-party API over the internet. The application runs on a Compute Engine instance without a public IP address. The instance uses Cloud NAT for outbound internet connectivity. What is the most likely reason for the timeout?

options.text: The instance must have a static external IP address attached directly to its network interface for internet routing through Cloud NAT.
Cloud NAT is running out of allocated source NAT ports due to high concurrent connections from the instance.
The external API server is blocking traffic because Cloud NAT IP addresses are automatically blacklisted by default.
Cloud NAT only supports inbound TCP connections and drops all outbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic.

questions.explanation: Cloud NAT maps private internal IP addresses to public IP addresses and ports. If an instance generates a high number of simultaneous connections, port exhaustion occurs, leading to timeouts. This can be resolved by increasing the number of ports allocated per VM in the Cloud NAT configuration.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Instances using Cloud NAT specifically must *not* have external IP addresses attached to their network interfaces.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Google Cloud NAT IP addresses are dynamic Google-owned IPs and are not automatically blacklisted unless associated with malicious activity.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud NAT is exclusively designed for outbound traffic translation; it does not handle inbound connections.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: An automated CI/CD pipeline running outside of Google Cloud (in GitHub Actions) attempts to deploy artifacts to a Google Cloud Artifact Registry repository using a dedicated service account key. The deployment fails with a `403 Permission Denied` error, even though you verified the service account has the `roles/artifactregistry.writer` role. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: Artifact Registry requires the owner role for any external write operations.
The Artifact Registry API is disabled in the Google Cloud project, or the service account key was generated from a different project than the repository.
GitHub Actions requires all deployment pipelines to use Workload Identity Federation instead of service account keys.
Service accounts cannot authenticate external pipelines without an active Compute Engine instance running as a bastion host.

questions.explanation: A 403 Permission Denied error despite having the correct IAM role usually stems from mismatched project contexts, disabled APIs, or the service account lacking permissions on the specific Artifact Registry resource scope.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The `roles/artifactregistry.writer` role provides sufficient permissions to push images to Artifact Registry.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While Workload Identity Federation is a best practice, service account keys still function if permissions and project contexts are correct; the 403 error is a permissions/scope mismatch.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Service accounts can be used externally via keys or Workload Identity Federation without requiring bastion hosts.

questions.domain: Setting up a Cloud Solution Environment
questions.question: Your organization stores sensitive customer exports in a Cloud Storage bucket. An internal security audit reveals that unauthorized users within the same Google Cloud project were able to read objects in this bucket. You verify that project-level IAM roles are correct. What feature should you investigate and configure to enforce strict object-level access control?

options.text: Configure VPC Service Controls to encrypt all bucket payloads at rest with Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK).
Enable Uniform Bucket-Level Access across the Cloud Storage bucket to disable legacy Access Control Lists (ACLs).
Review and remove overly permissive IAM bindings (such as `allUsers` or `allAuthenticatedUsers`) and audit project-level primitive roles like Editor or Owner assigned to users.
Migrate the bucket to a multi-regional storage class to enforce hierarchical access namespaces.

questions.explanation: Unintended data access in Cloud Storage is commonly caused by overly broad project-level IAM roles (such as Project Editor or Owner) or accidental public access bindings (`allUsers`). Auditing IAM policies and removing primitive roles is critical to securing sensitive buckets.

wrongOptionNotes.A: CMEK encrypts data at rest but does not restrict IAM authorization or determine who can read objects.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Enabling Uniform Bucket-Level Access actually *disables* fine-grained ACLs and relies purely on IAM. If unauthorized users accessed files, IAM roles or public bindings were likely too broad.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storage classes affect availability, durability, and pricing, not authorization security controls.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company is deploying a multi-tenant SaaS application on Google Cloud. You need to enforce an organization policy that restricts the creation of service account keys across the entire organization to prevent credential sprawl and potential leaks, while allowing exemptions for legacy systems in a specific folder. How should you configure this policy?

options.text: Apply the 'constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation' constraint at the organization root with an enforcement of true, and use a policy exception or boolean enforcement override at the target legacy folder.
Remove the Project IAM Admin role from all developers and assign the Service Account Key Admin role globally.
Configure a VPC Service Controls perimeter around the entire organization to block all outbound API requests related to key creation.
Write a custom Cloud Monitoring alert that notifies the security team whenever a service account key is created, and manually delete the key.

questions.explanation: Organization Policy Service allows administrators to set centralized, hierarchical controls over Google Cloud resources. The constraint 'constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation' prevents the creation of service account keys, promoting secure practices like using attached service accounts or Workload Identity.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Assigning Service Account Key Admin globally expands permissions rather than restricting key creation.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC Service Controls protect against data exfiltration by securing API perimeters, but IAM key creation is managed by the IAM service API and requires Organization Policy constraints.
wrongOptionNotes.D: This is a reactive monitoring approach rather than a preventive compliance guardrail.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your security team discovers that several Compute Engine instances in a production project have external IP addresses attached, violating compliance policies. You need to remediate this immediately and ensure developers cannot attach external IPs in the future without violating least-privilege principles.

options.text: Disable the Compute Engine API across all non-production projects.
Delete all VPC firewall rules that allow ingress traffic from the 0.0.0.0/0 IP range.
Enforce the 'constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess' organization policy constraint on the project or folder, and remove existing external IPs from the instances.
Revoke the Compute Instance Admin role from all development engineers and manage all VM creation through a centralized team.

questions.explanation: To prevent unauthorized external IP assignment, Google Cloud provides the organization policy constraint 'constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess'. When enforced, any attempt to create a VM with an external IP or add one to an existing VM is denied.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Disabling the entire API stops all workloads, which is overly destructive and fails to target the production environment where the violation occurred.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Deleting firewall rules affects ingress traffic filtering but does not prevent instances from having external IP addresses assigned or initiating outbound traffic.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While reducing administrative permissions helps, it does not programmatically prevent users from attaching external IPs if they retain the role, nor does it fix existing instances.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are auditing a Google Cloud project containing sensitive patient health records. You need to ensure that all administrative read and write operations on Cloud Storage bucket metadata and object contents are systematically recorded for compliance auditing, and that these audit logs cannot be tampered with by project administrators.

options.text: Write a Cloud Function triggered by Cloud Storage events that logs every file access to a local text file.
Assign the Storage Object Viewer role to the security team on every individual bucket in the project.
Configure Cloud Audit Logs in the project IAM policy to enable both Admin Read and Data Read/Write audit logs for the Cloud Storage service, and store logs in a separate security analytics project.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on all subnetworks within the project's Virtual Private Cloud network.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud Audit Logs include Admin Activity, Data Access, System Event, and Policy Denied logs. Data Access logs (which include Data Read and Data Write) must be explicitly enabled for services like Cloud Storage to track object read and write operations for compliance.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Functions add latency, cost, and complexity, and user-managed text logs can be deleted or modified by project administrators.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Granting viewing permissions allows access to data but does not establish an immutable audit trail of who accessed what and when.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC Flow Logs record network packet metadata (IP addresses and ports), not API calls or Cloud Storage data read/write operations.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company requires that all data stored in BigQuery datasets must be encrypted using a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK) stored in Cloud KMS, rather than Google-managed keys. You need to enforce this requirement across a newly created business unit folder.

options.text: Enforce the 'constraints/bigquery.requireCustomerManagedEncryption' organization policy constraint at the target folder level.
Apply the 'constraints/gcp.resourceLocations' organization policy and configure Cloud KMS key rotation schedules.
Create a custom IAM role that strips the BigQuery Admin role of default key generation capabilities.
Set up a Cloud Monitoring alert policy to detect datasets created without CMEK and automatically delete them.

questions.explanation: Organization policies provide specific service-level constraints, such as 'constraints/bigquery.requireCustomerManagedEncryption', which mandates the use of Cloud KMS keys for BigQuery data protection.

wrongOptionNotes.B: The resourceLocations constraint restricts geographical deployment locations, not encryption key types.
wrongOptionNotes.C: IAM roles control permissions on resources, but they do not automatically mandate CMEK usage upon resource creation.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Reactive deletion of datasets can cause data loss and operational disruption; preventive controls via organization policy are preferred.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your security architecture mandates that developers must not have permissions to assign IAM roles to other users or service accounts, mitigating escalation risks. However, developers still need to deploy and manage application resources within their assigned projects. How should you assign permissions?

options.text: Remove all IAM roles from developers and require them to use the organization administrator account when deployments are needed.
Assign the Project Owner role to a shared group email alias used by the development team.
Assign predefined service-specific roles (e.g., Cloud Run Admin, Compute Admin) directly to developers, while withholding roles like Project IAM Admin and Security Admin.
Assign the Project Editor role to all developers to simplify administration.

questions.explanation: Adhering to least privilege requires separating resource management roles from IAM administration roles (such as Project IAM Admin, Folder IAM Admin, or Owner), ensuring engineers cannot alter permission structures.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Using a shared administrator account violates auditability and least-privilege principles.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Project Owner grants full administrative access over all resources and IAM settings, presenting a severe security risk.
wrongOptionNotes.D: The Project Editor role includes permissions to modify IAM policies and assign roles, violating least-privilege security mandates.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are hardening a production environment on Google Cloud. You need to ensure that compute instances cannot download software packages or communicate with external public repositories over the internet, while still allowing them to securely access Google Cloud APIs and services without traversing the public internet.

options.text: Disable default routes in the VPC and delete the default internet gateway route.
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway with public IP addresses attached to handle all outbound instance traffic.
Configure Private Google Access on the subnet and ensure instances do not have external IP addresses.
Attach external IP addresses to all VMs and configure strict egress firewall rules.

questions.explanation: Private Google Access is a subnet-level setting that enables VMs without external IP addresses to send traffic to Google APIs and services (such as Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and Pub/Sub) via internal IP addresses.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Deleting the default route blocks all internet traffic, but without Private Google Access, it also blocks access to Google APIs and services.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud NAT allows instances without external IPs to reach the public internet, which contradicts the requirement to block internet access.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Attaching external IP addresses exposes instances to the public internet, violating the hardening requirement.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization requires that all Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks created across all projects must be configured in 'Custom subnet mode' rather than 'Automatic subnet mode' to maintain strict IP address allocation control. How can you automate this requirement?

options.text: Enforce the 'constraints/compute.disableGlobalDynamicRouting' organization policy constraint.
Apply the 'constraints/compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation' constraint at the organization level, and use an organization policy constraint or automated vetting for network creation.
Revoke the Compute Network Admin role from all users except the central networking team.
Create a custom shell script that runs nightly, checks for auto-mode networks, and deletes them.

questions.explanation: To prevent the creation of auto-mode VPC networks and ensure proper IP planning, organizations can skip default network creation and enforce infrastructure-as-code validation or policy controls for network creation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Global dynamic routing controls how dynamic routes propagate across regions, not subnet mode creation.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While limiting permissions helps, it does not programmatically enforce that when a network is created, it must be in custom mode.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Nightly scripts are reactive, prone to timing gaps, and can disrupt dependent workloads if networks are abruptly deleted.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An external auditor requests proof that no unauthorized users have been granted primitive roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) on your production Google Cloud project over the past quarter. How should you efficiently verify and report this?

options.text: Run a billing report to identify which user accounts incurred the highest costs during the quarter.
Check the Cloud Asset Inventory to list all current IAM bindings, and query Cloud Audit Logs for historical IAM policy changes.
Review the project dashboard in the Google Cloud Console to see the total number of active users.
Inspect the VPC flow logs for unusual outbound traffic patterns indicating unauthorized access.

questions.explanation: Cloud Asset Inventory enables querying IAM policies across projects and folders, while Cloud Audit Logs (specifically Admin Activity logs) capture every modification made to IAM policies for historical auditing.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Billing reports show cost attribution by project or label, not IAM permissions or role assignments.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The project dashboard shows high-level resource counts and activity, not detailed IAM role assignments or historical changes.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC flow logs monitor network traffic flows, not IAM role grants or authorization changes.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your security team mandates that all Compute Engine instances must use custom service accounts with minimal scopes rather than the default compute service account, which has broad access permissions. How should you enforce this requirement during instance creation?

options.text: Instruct developers to manually deselect the default service account in the Cloud Console or CLI whenever they launch a VM.
Attach a VPC Service Controls perimeter around the Compute Engine API.
Apply an organization policy or use Security Command Center/Deployment Manager templates that restrict or flag VMs using the default service account.
Delete the default compute service account from the IAM permissions page of the project.

questions.explanation: The default compute service account has Project Editor privileges by default. Best practices dictate creating dedicated, least-privilege service accounts for each workload and enforcing their use via automated deployment pipelines and organization governance tools.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Relying purely on manual developer compliance leads to human error and policy drift.
wrongOptionNotes.B: VPC Service Controls protect against data exfiltration across perimeters, but they do not restrict which service accounts are attached to virtual machines.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Deleting the default service account can break existing unmigrated workloads and built-in Google Cloud services that rely on it.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are managing a Google Cloud organization with multiple business units. A security requirement states that confidential data stored in Cloud Storage buckets must never be shared with external domains or public users, regardless of individual project configurations. How can you enforce this centrally?

options.text: Apply a VPC Service Controls perimeter that blocks all traffic originating from outside the corporate network.
Configure a Cloud Monitoring alert that scans bucket IAM policies every hour and sends an email notification.
Enforce the 'constraints/storage.publicAccessPrevention' organization policy constraint set to 'enforced' at the organization root.
Disable the Cloud Storage API across all projects that handle confidential data.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage Public Access Prevention is a security feature available as an organization policy constraint ('constraints/storage.publicAccessPrevention'). When enforced, it prevents users from setting public bindings on buckets, ensuring compliance with data exposure policies.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC Service Controls manage API access perimeters but do not specifically override bucket-level public IAM bindings like Public Access Prevention does.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Alerting is reactive and leaves a window of exposure where data could be publicly accessible.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Disabling the API prevents storing or accessing data entirely, halting legitimate application functionality.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your development team needs to deploy an application on a Compute Engine instance that requires access to Secret Manager to retrieve database credentials. Following Google Cloud security hardening guidelines, how should the application authenticate to Secret Manager?

options.text: Attach a dedicated service account with the 'Secret Manager Secret Accessor' role to the Compute Engine instance.
Store the database password in a plain-text configuration file located in the application's root directory.
Embed a long-lived personal access token generated by the lead developer directly into the application environment variables.
Grant the project Owner role to the default compute service account.

questions.explanation: Applications running on Compute Engine should use attached service accounts with minimal permissions (such as Secret Manager Secret Accessor) to authenticate and retrieve sensitive configuration data from Secret Manager securely.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Storing secrets in plain text files is a major security vulnerability.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Embedding personal access tokens violates credential management best practices and creates auditing and revocation issues.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Granting Project Owner violates the principle of least privilege by exposing all project resources to excessive permissions.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization is subject to strict data sovereignty regulations. You must ensure that no Google Cloud resources (such as Compute Engine instances, Cloud SQL databases, and Cloud Storage buckets) can be provisioned outside of the 'europe-west3' (Frankfurt) region.

options.text: Revoke permissions for all users to deploy resources in regions other than Frankfurt using custom IAM roles.
