wrongOptionNotes.B: If DNS pointed to the wrong IP, clients would experience connection timeouts or resolve errors, not an HTTP 502 generated by the load balancer itself.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Database subnets do not handle incoming HTTP traffic from the external load balancer; the issue lies between the load balancer proxy and the backend web servers.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud Storage logging is unrelated to load balancer runtime routing and proxy failures.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company's nightly data load job fails because a Cloud Dataflow pipeline encounters continuous out-of-memory errors on worker nodes while processing a massive JSON file. You need to reconfigure the pipeline execution parameters without changing the underlying transformation logic. Which parameter should you adjust?

options.text: Specify a larger worker machine type (e.g., n1-standard-8 instead of n1-standard-2) using the --workerMachineType flag.
Increase the maximum number of zone replicas in the Google Cloud VPC firewall rules.
Change the Cloud Storage bucket storage class from Standard to Coldline.
Modify the BigQuery dataset location constraint to match the Dataflow region.

questions.explanation: When Dataflow workers experience out-of-memory errors due to large payloads or complex aggregations, scaling up the worker machine type provides more memory per worker instance to successfully process the data shards.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Firewall rules control network packet filtering and have no impact on worker memory consumption.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Storage classes affect cost and retrieval latency for stored data, not the execution memory of compute jobs reading that data.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Dataset locations prevent cross-region query errors but do not resolve worker-level out-of-memory crashes.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An internal web service deployed on Compute Engine cannot connect to a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance within the same VPC network. The application logs show connection timeout errors. You have confirmed that the Cloud SQL instance is running. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The Compute Engine instance lacks the Cloud SQL Client IAM role assigned to its default service account.
The Cloud SQL instance does not have an external IP address assigned to its public interface.
A firewall rule in the VPC blocks outbound traffic on TCP port 3306, or inbound traffic is blocked on the Cloud SQL instance network.
The database storage auto-resize limit has been reached, causing the database engine to lock all connections.

questions.explanation: Network timeouts connecting from a Compute Engine instance to Cloud SQL are almost always caused by firewall misconfigurations blocking port 3306 (MySQL) or 5432 (PostgreSQL), or routing issues within the VPC network.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IAM roles govern control-plane API access to manage Cloud SQL instances, whereas database network connectivity relies on TCP/IP networking, credentials, and firewall rules.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Resources within the same VPC network communicate securely over private IP addresses and do not require external IP addresses.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storage exhaustion results in specific database error states or write rejections, not connection timeouts at the network layer.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages a web application where users intermittently receive '504 Gateway Time-out' errors during peak hours. The backend application runs on a managed instance group behind an internal TCP Proxy Load Balancer. You want to identify if the backend instances are taking too long to process requests. Where should you look?

options.text: Identity and Access Management policy audit logs for unauthorized permission changes.
Cloud DNS query logs to check for recursive resolver latency.
Cloud Logging for the backend Compute Engine instances to inspect application processing durations and slow request logs.
Cloud Billing reports to verify if budget alerts have throttled CPU allocations.

questions.explanation: A 504 Gateway Time-out from a load balancer indicates that the backend instance failed to return a response within the timeout period. Analyzing application logs on the backend instances helps determine if code execution is bottlenecked.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IAM logs track who did what and when, but provide no visibility into application performance or latency issues.
wrongOptionNotes.B: DNS resolution happens once at the start of a session; it does not cause HTTP gateway timeouts during active request processing.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Billing alerts notify administrators of spending thresholds but do not throttle or slow down active compute instances.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You deployed a new revision of a stateless service on Cloud Run, but immediate user traffic reports show widespread HTTP 500 internal server errors. You need to instantly rollback traffic to the previously stable revision while you investigate the bug. What is the most efficient action to take in the Google Cloud Console?

options.text: Delete the newly deployed revision from the service history so Cloud Run automatically falls back to the old one.
Modify the VPC connector settings to bypass the internal proxy gateway.
Navigate to Cloud Run, select your service, click 'Manage Traffic', and route 100% of traffic back to the previous stable revision.
Restart all active container instances using the gcloud container clusters update command.

questions.explanation: Cloud Run supports immutable revisions. If a new revision introduces bugs causing HTTP 500 errors, administrators can instantly rollback by re-routing 100% of the traffic back to the prior stable revision via the traffic management settings.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Deleting an active revision can lead to errors if requests are still draining; managing traffic splits is the standard, zero-downtime method for rollbacks.
wrongOptionNotes.B: VPC connectors handle private network egress, whereas HTTP 500 errors point to application-level execution failures in the new revision.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud Run is serverless; container lifecycle is fully managed, and gcloud container commands apply to GKE clusters, not Cloud Run services.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your automated build pipeline publishes container images to Artifact Registry, but your Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster fails to pull the images, reporting 'ErrImagePull' and 'ImagePullBackOff' status codes on newly scheduled pods. What is the most likely configuration issue?

options.text: The cluster VPC network has subnet IP exhaustion on secondary IP ranges.
The GKE node service account lacks the 'Artifact Registry Reader' (roles/artifactregistry.reader) permission on the Artifact Registry repository.
The Kubernetes cluster autoscaler is disabled, preventing nodes from scaling up.
The cloud storage bucket storing the container layers has uniform bucket-level access enabled.

questions.explanation: ImagePullBackOff errors in GKE typically stem from incorrect image paths, network egress blocks, or missing IAM permissions granting the GKE node service account read access to the Artifact Registry repository.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Subnet IP exhaustion results in IP allocation failures, not image pull authentication or registry access errors.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Image pull errors occur after a pod is scheduled to a node, meaning node capacity is available; the failure is authentication or network related.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Artifact Registry stores container images internally in managed repositories, not directly inside user-accessible Cloud Storage buckets.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A managed instance group (MIG) configured with autoscaling is failing to scale up during a high-traffic surge. The CPU utilization of existing instances is at 95%, but no new instances are being created. Upon checking the MIG configuration, you notice that the autoscaling policy is set based on an HTTP load balancing utilization metric that is misconfigured. How should you resolve this issue?

options.text: Enable preemptible VM instances on the managed instance group to lower operational costs during traffic peaks.
Increase the maximum number of instances in the instance template to bypass the autoscaling evaluation loop.
Update the autoscaling policy in the MIG configuration to use average CPU utilization as the scaling signal with an appropriate threshold (e.g., 60%).
Delete the health check associated with the backend service to prevent premature instance termination.

questions.explanation: Managed instance group autoscalers rely on specific signals (such as CPU utilization, load balancing capacity, or Cloud Monitoring metrics). If the metric is misconfigured or pointing to an unpopulated signal, the MIG will not scale. Reconfiguring the autoscaler to track CPU utilization fixes the scaling behavior.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Preemptible VMs (or Spot VMs) can be terminated at any time by Google Cloud, which would worsen availability during a traffic spike.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Instance templates define configuration properties like disk images and machine types, not sizing limits; sizing limits are configured on the MIG itself.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Health checks ensure traffic is only routed to responsive instances; removing them risks sending traffic to broken instances.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your production PostgreSQL database hosted on Cloud SQL is experiencing severe performance degradation. Queries that previously executed in milliseconds are now taking minutes. You need to identify the exact queries causing the bottleneck. Which Google Cloud feature should you use?

options.text: Cloud Audit Logs to review administrative changes made to database user passwords and IAM roles.
Cloud Monitoring disk IOPS alerts to verify if the underlying solid-state drives are worn out.
VPC Flow Logs to inspect packet drop rates and TCP retransmissions between the database and application servers.
Cloud SQL Query Insights to analyze query execution plans, load, and identify top resource-consuming queries.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL Query Insights is built specifically for diagnosing database performance problems. It helps identify problematic queries, view execution plans, and pinpoint the source of database CPU and memory spikes.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Audit Logs track management operations and security events, not database query performance or SQL statement execution times.
wrongOptionNotes.B: While high IOPS can indicate bottlenecks, it does not tell you which specific queries or SQL statements are causing the high load.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC Flow Logs provide networking telemetry, but do not provide visibility into internal database query performance or SQL execution plans.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are managing a Google Cloud project with multiple compute instances. Security auditors report that an instance in a public subnet has an active external IP address and is communicating with an unauthorized external endpoint. You need to immediately sever all external network connectivity for this instance without shutting down the running workload. What is the best approach?

options.text: Delete the default VPC network route with the destination 0.0.0.0/0.
Stop the instance using the gcloud compute instances stop command.
Disable the Google Cloud DNS API in the project console.
Remove the external IP address configuration from the Compute Engine instance network interface.

questions.explanation: To isolate a Compute Engine instance from the public internet without shutting down the OS or disrupting internal VPC communications, you can remove its external IP address from the network interface configuration.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Deleting the default route affects all instances in the VPC network, cutting off internet access for the entire subnet rather than isolating the single compromised instance.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Stopping the instance shuts down the workload entirely, which violates the requirement to keep the running workload active while cutting off external access.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Disabling the DNS API stops name resolution but does not terminate active IP connections or prevent direct IP communication.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your development team has deployed a web application to Cloud Run. Users report that file uploads larger than 30 MB consistently fail with a connection reset error. Smaller files upload successfully. What is the most probable cause of this issue?

options.text: The Cloud SQL database connection pool is exhausting its maximum open file descriptor limit.
The project's billing budget has reached its maximum monthly spending threshold.
The Cloud Storage bucket destination has uniform bucket-level access enabled.
The request payload or request timeout limits of Cloud Run are being exceeded during the slow transfer of large files.

questions.explanation: Cloud Run enforces strict limits on request timeouts and memory. When uploading large files, if the transfer time exceeds the configured request timeout or the container memory is exhausted buffering the file, Cloud Run terminates the request.

wrongOptionNotes.A: File uploads are handled by the web application container before reaching the database, so database file descriptors do not cause HTTP upload resets.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Budget alerts send notifications and optionally trigger Pub/Sub topics, but they do not actively terminate or reset TCP connections mid-transfer.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Uniform bucket-level access enforces IAM policies across all objects in a bucket; it does not truncate or reset active HTTP upload streams based on file size.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a multi-tier application where backend worker instances communicate with a shared Cloud Storage bucket. Recently, security alarms triggered because logs showed unauthorized public data downloads from that bucket. You need to immediately prevent public access to all objects in the bucket while retaining internal service access. What should you do?

options.text: Change the bucket storage class from Standard to Archive.
Enable 'Public Access Prevention' on the Cloud Storage bucket.
Rotate the HMAC keys associated with the service account managing the bucket.
Delete all objects in the bucket and recreate the bucket with uniform bucket-level access enabled.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud Storage provides Public Access Prevention, which ensures that data in a bucket cannot be made public by any IAM or access control list (ACL) configuration, providing a definitive safeguard against accidental data leaks.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Storage classes dictate pricing and retrieval latency for long-term storage, not public access permissions.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Rotating HMAC keys invalidates programmatic authentication credentials used for interoperability APIs, but does not fix overly permissive public IAM policies.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While uniform bucket-level access simplifies permissions, it does not automatically block public access if an explicit 'allUsers' binding is present; Public Access Prevention is required.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are troubleshooting a connectivity issue where an application running in a private Google Cloud VPC subnet cannot reach external Google APIs (such as BigQuery or Cloud Storage). The virtual machine instances do not have external IP addresses for security reasons. What is the correct network configuration to fix this issue?

options.text: Configure Private Google Access on the subnet so instances can reach Google APIs using private IP addresses.
Attach a Cloud NAT gateway to the VPC router to provide SNAT for all outbound traffic.
Assign a public static external IP address to every virtual machine interface in the subnet.
Create a Cloud VPN gateway connecting the VPC network to Google's public edge routers.

questions.explanation: Private Google Access is a subnet-level property that enables instances without external IP addresses to communicate with Google APIs and services (like Cloud Storage and BigQuery) securely via internal IP addresses.

wrongOptionNotes.B: While Cloud NAT allows instances without external IPs to reach the public internet, Private Google Access is the native, recommended method specifically for reaching Google APIs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Assigning external IPs violates the security requirement that instances in the private subnet must not have direct public internet connectivity.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud VPN connects a VPC to an on-premises datacenter or another VPC, not to Google's internal API endpoints.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team deployed a containerized application to a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. Users report intermittent 504 Gateway Timeout errors when interacting with the service through an Ingress resource. Upon inspecting the Ingress logs, you find that backend pods are taking longer than the default proxy timeout to process complex database queries. How should you resolve this issue?

options.text: Scale up the number of nodes in the GKE node pool using the gcloud container clusters resize command.
Convert the Ingress resource into a standard TCP Load Balancer using Kubernetes NodePort services.
Modify the cluster's kube-dns deployment replica count to improve domain name resolution speed.
Add a backend-config Custom Resource Definition (CRD) to the Ingress with an increased timeout value and reference it in your service annotation.

questions.explanation: GKE Ingress manages Google Cloud HTTP(S) Load Balancers. When long-running requests exceed default timeouts, administrators can use BackendConfig CRDs to customize parameters such as connection timeouts for the backend services.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Adding nodes increases cluster compute capacity, but does not change the load balancer proxy timeout limit causing the 504 errors.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Switching to NodePort bypasses Layer 7 HTTP load balancing features and does not solve the underlying request processing timeout issue.
wrongOptionNotes.C: DNS resolution speed does not affect connection timeout thresholds during active request processing between the load balancer and backend pods.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your security team mandates that all Compute Engine virtual machine instances deployed across your production Google Cloud project must not have external IP addresses assigned, yet they still need to securely reach internal APIs hosted on Google services. How should you architect this network requirement?

options.text: Configure Private Google Access on the subnet where the instances reside and ensure instances lack external IP addresses.
Attach a secondary IP range to the instances and configure static routes pointing to the default internet gateway.
Set up a TCP proxy load balancer inside the VPC to route internal traffic to Google's public endpoints.
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway attached to the VPC network to proxy traffic destined for Google APIs.

questions.explanation: Private Google Access enables VMs with only internal IP addresses to reach Google APIs and services (such as Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and internal APIs) through Google's internal network path.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Secondary IP ranges are for aliased IPs (like GKE pods), and routing traffic to the default internet gateway requires external IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: A proxy load balancer is unnecessary and introduces extra complexity when Private Google Access natively handles internal communication to Google services.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud NAT is used for outbound internet traffic to external destinations, but Private Google Access is specifically designed for reaching Google APIs internally.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are managing a multi-tier enterprise Google Cloud organization. An auditor discovers that developers have broad permissions to create service accounts with owner-level access across multiple projects. Which IAM best practice should you implement to enforce least privilege?

options.text: Assign the Project Owner role only to group aliases instead of individual developer accounts.
Use Cloud IAM Conditions to automatically expire all user accounts after 90 days.
Apply Organization Policies to restrict the creation of service account keys and disable automatic default service account credential grants.
Configure VPC Service Controls to prevent service accounts from communicating outside the organization boundary.

questions.explanation: Enforcing Organization Policies (such as restricting service account key creation or disabling automatic role grants) prevents users from provisioning overly permissive credentials.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Project Owner is excessively broad; assigning it to groups still leaves a wide attack surface and violates the principle of least privilege.
wrongOptionNotes.B: IAM conditions apply time-based restrictions to bindings, but they do not automatically expire user accounts across the organization.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC Service Controls protect against data exfiltration across perimeters, but they do not restrict IAM role assignments or service account creation permissions.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your compliance team requires that all sensitive database backups stored in a Cloud Storage bucket must be encrypted using a key managed entirely by your security operations team via Cloud KMS, ensuring Google does not manage the root key material. Which storage encryption option should you choose?

options.text: Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK).
Google-managed encryption keys with Cloud HSM verification enabled.
Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) using Cloud KMS.
Application-layer encryption using a local password stored in Secret Manager.

questions.explanation: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) integrate Cloud Storage with Cloud KMS, allowing organizations to maintain control over the key lifecycle while utilizing native service encryption.

wrongOptionNotes.A: CSEK requires you to provide and manage your own raw encryption keys for every API call, which Google does not store; however, CMEK is the standard recommendation for managed KMS control.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Google-managed keys are controlled entirely by Google and do not meet the requirement for enterprise-managed key control via Cloud KMS.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While application-layer encryption provides strong security, it requires manual implementation inside application code rather than leveraging native storage encryption.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your security team needs to restrict access to a production BigQuery dataset so that only analysts physically located within your corporate headquarters' subnet can query the data. How should you implement this guardrail?

options.text: Configure Context-Aware Access and VPC Service Controls to enforce IP-based access boundaries for BigQuery.
Attach a firewall rule to the BigQuery dataset resource blocking all external IP ranges.
Route all BigQuery API calls through an internal HTTP(S) Load Balancer configured with IP whitelisting.
Apply custom IAM roles with conditional statements checking the source IP address of the BigQuery job requester.

questions.explanation: VPC Service Controls create security perimeters around Google Cloud resources like BigQuery, while Context-Aware Access can restrict requests based on origin IP subnets.

wrongOptionNotes.B: VPC firewall rules apply to Compute Engine VM instances, not to serverless managed SaaS services like BigQuery.
wrongOptionNotes.C: BigQuery is accessed via public or private Google API endpoints, not via standard HTTP(S) load balancers.
wrongOptionNotes.D: IAM conditions support expressions based on resource attributes and request time, but they do not natively validate the client's source IP address in API requests.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An external security audit reveals that developers frequently attach broad IAM roles like 'Editor' to service accounts used by Cloud Functions. You need to automate the remediation and prevent future assignments of roles other than 'Cloud Functions Invoker' for these functions. What is the most effective approach?

options.text: Modify the default VPC firewall rules to block IAM administrative API calls from developer workstations.
Use IAM Recommender to identify over-privileged accounts and set up automated remediation using Cloud Asset Inventory feed events with Cloud Functions.
Enable Google Cloud Armor security policies on the Cloud Functions invocation URL.
Rely solely on manual quarterly reviews of the project-level IAM policy page in the Cloud Console.

questions.explanation: Automating security compliance using Cloud Asset Inventory feeds and IAM Recommender allows organizations to proactively detect and remediate excessive permissions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC firewall rules control packet-level network traffic and cannot filter or block IAM API calls.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud Armor protects against web attacks and DDoS at the load balancer layer, not IAM permission assignments.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Manual quarterly reviews do not provide automated prevention or real-time remediation for security compliance.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company operates multiple business units under a single Google Cloud organization. You need to ensure that no developer can create Compute Engine instances with external IP addresses anywhere in the organization. Where and how should you configure this restriction?

options.text: Set an Organization Policy constraint named 'constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess' at the organization root node.
Configure an egress firewall rule at the organization level dropping all traffic to destination IP 0.0.0.0/0.
Write a custom IAM custom role denying 'compute.instances.setExternalIp' and assign it to all developers.
Revoke the Network Admin role from all developers and restrict them to Viewer roles.

questions.explanation: Organization Policies provide centralized control over resource configurations, such as forbidding external IP addresses on Compute Engine instances across the entire hierarchy.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Dropping all egress traffic would break essential internet communication and updates, and firewall rules do not prevent the assignment of external IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: IAM custom roles cannot be deny roles; IAM in Google Cloud is strictly additive. Denials must be handled via Organization Policy Deny rules.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Revoking network roles is too broad and does not specifically prevent instance creation with external IPs if users retain instance creation permissions.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization requires that all audit logs for administrative activities and data access across all projects in your Google Cloud folder must be permanently exported to a secure, immutable storage location for compliance archiving. What is the recommended architecture?

options.text: Stream all logs to a single Compute Engine instance running an open-source syslog server with local disk snapshots.
Configure individual log sinks in every project pointing to local BigQuery datasets with dataset-level access controls.
Rely on the default Cloud Logging retention policy, which retains audit logs indefinitely without manual configuration.
Create a centralized Cloud Logging sink at the folder level configured to export logs to a Cloud Storage bucket with Object Retention Lock enabled.

questions.explanation: Folder-level log sinks aggregate logs across multiple projects, and exporting them to Cloud Storage with Object Retention Lock satisfies strict regulatory immutability requirements.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Maintaining a custom VM-based syslog server introduces operational overhead, single points of failure, and lacks native cloud immutability guarantees.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Managing individual sinks per project is inefficient and does not guarantee centralized compliance archiving or immutability.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Default audit log retention periods in Cloud Logging are fixed (e.g., 400 days for Admin Activity), requiring explicit log exports for long-term compliance.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A junior administrator accidentally exposed a sensitive Cloud Storage bucket containing PII by granting the 'allUsers' principal the Storage Object Viewer role. You need to immediately remediate this security vulnerability and prevent public access to any current or future buckets in the project. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Uniform Bucket-Level Access and update the firewall rules for the project.
Delete the Cloud Storage bucket and recreate it with a new name.
Attach a Cloud Armor security policy to the Cloud Storage bucket endpoint.
Enforce the 'constraints/storage.publicAccessPrevention' organization policy at the project level and remove the 'allUsers' binding.

questions.explanation: Public Access Prevention is a security control that enforces that no bucket in a constrained resource hierarchy can be made public.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Uniform bucket-level access disables fine-grained object ACLs, but it does not automatically block public access if an IAM binding explicitly grants access to 'allUsers'.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Deleting and recreating buckets is disruptive and unnecessary when IAM bindings and Public Access Prevention can be managed directly.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud Armor policies apply to HTTP(S) Load Balancers, not directly to Cloud Storage bucket endpoints.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your security team mandates that communication between microservices running within your Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster must be encrypted in transit using mutual TLS (mTLS) without requiring application code modifications. Which feature should you enable?

options.text: IPsec VPN tunnels established between individual Kubernetes worker nodes.
Google Cloud Armor security policies applied to the GKE ingress controller.
Anthos Service Mesh (or Cloud Service Mesh) with automatic mTLS enabled.
VPC firewall rules enforcing TLS encryption on TCP port 443.

questions.explanation: Cloud Service Mesh (built on Istio) transparently injects sidecar proxies to handle encryption in transit (mTLS) between cluster workloads without code changes.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IPsec tunnels encrypt node-to-node traffic across the network layer, but service mesh provides fine-grained service-level mTLS.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud Armor protects ingress traffic at the edge of the network, not internal pod-to-pod cluster traffic.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC firewall rules operate at layers 3 and 4 (IP and port) and cannot enforce or inspect application-layer TLS encryption.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company is undergoing a PCI-DSS compliance audit. The auditor requests proof that database connections from your application servers to Cloud SQL are encrypted in transit and that unencrypted connections are rejected. How should you configure Cloud SQL?

options.text: Configure Cloud SQL to require SSL/TLS for all connections and enforce client certificate authentication.
Place the Cloud SQL instance inside a private VPC subnet with no public IP address.
Assign a Customer-Managed Encryption Key (CMEK) to the database instance.
Enable automated backups and point-in-time recovery on the Cloud SQL instance.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL allows administrators to configure SSL/TLS enforcement, ensuring that the database server rejects any unencrypted incoming connection attempts.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Using a private IP prevents public internet access, but traffic inside the VPC is still unencrypted unless SSL/TLS is explicitly required by the database configuration.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CMEK encrypts data at rest, whereas PCI-DSS compliance here requires encryption in transit.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Backups and point-in-time recovery protect against data loss, but they do not secure network traffic in transit.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are hardening a Google Cloud project that hosts sensitive internal tools. Security requirements state that human administrators must authenticate using phishing-resistant hardware security keys (FIDO2/WebAuthn), and passwords alone are strictly prohibited. Where should you configure this requirement?

options.text: Configure Google Workspace or Cloud Identity context-aware access and multi-factor authentication (MFA) policies to mandate security keys.
Deploy an Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) backend and configure firewall rules blocking password-based protocols.
Set project-level IAM conditions requiring a security key assertion in every IAM API call.
Apply an Organization Policy constraint restricting login methods to service accounts only.

questions.explanation: Identity providers like Cloud Identity or Google Workspace handle user authentication policies, enabling enforcement of phishing-resistant MFA across Google Cloud users.

wrongOptionNotes.B: IAP controls access to web applications, but user credential policies (such as enforcing hardware keys) are managed at the identity provider level (Cloud Identity).
wrongOptionNotes.C: IAM conditions do not support validating hardware security key assertions for human authentication sessions.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Restricting logins to service accounts would prevent human administrators from logging into the Google Cloud Console.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your development team needs to deploy an internal web application on Compute Engine that can only be accessed by employees connected through your corporate VPN. The application should not have any public exposure. How should you design the network access?

options.text: Configure Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) with public IP addresses on the backend instances.
Attach the instances to a private VPC subnet with no external IP, and connect your corporate VPN via Cloud VPN to the VPC.
Deploy an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer with Cloud Armor rules whitelisting your corporate public IP range.
Assign dynamic external IP addresses to the instances and use VPC firewall rules to block non-VPN traffic.

questions.explanation: Isolating workloads in private subnets with no external IP addresses and routing traffic exclusively through Cloud VPN ensures complete privacy from the public internet.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While IAP secures access, keeping instances completely off the public internet by using private IPs and Cloud VPN is more secure and avoids public exposure.
wrongOptionNotes.C: An external load balancer exposes the application to the public internet, which violates the requirement that the application have no public exposure.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Assigning external IPs exposes instances to potential direct internet attacks, even if firewall rules restrict traffic.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are performing a security review of a Google Cloud project. You discover that a custom service account used by a data processing pipeline has permissions across multiple unrelated projects. Which principle of security design is being violated?

options.text: The principle of high availability, because cross-project service accounts introduce network latency.
The principle of separation of duties, because a single service account is performing data processing.
The principle of defense in depth, because encryption keys are not rotated regularly.
The principle of least privilege, because the service account possesses broader access than necessary for its intended scope.

questions.explanation: The principle of least privilege dictates that accounts (including service accounts) should only be granted the exact permissions needed for their specific task within a defined scope.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IAM permissions do not impact network latency or high availability architectures.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Separation of duties involves dividing critical tasks among multiple users, not restricting service account scopes.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Defense in depth refers to layered security controls, not the scope of IAM role assignments.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your security team requires that all data stored in Cloud Storage buckets across your entire enterprise organization must be encrypted using keys that your company controls via Cloud KMS, and that developers cannot override this policy by creating buckets with Google-managed keys. How should you enforce this?

options.text: Create an IAM custom deny policy preventing users from calling 'storage.buckets.create' without a key parameter.
Set the organization policy constraint 'constraints/storage.requireCustomEncryptionKeys' at the organization root.
Set the organization policy constraint 'constraints/storage.requireCsrk' or configure CMEK enforcement policies at the organization level.
Write a weekly Cloud Monitoring alert that notifies security when a bucket without CMEK is created.

questions.explanation: Organization Policy constraints like 'constraints/storage.requireCustomEncryptionKeys' proactively enforce that all newly created buckets use customer-managed encryption keys.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IAM custom deny policies cannot validate specific bucket creation parameters like encryption keys; organization policies are designed for this.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The correct constraint name for enforcing CMEK on Cloud Storage is constraints/gcp.resourceLocations or specific CMEK enforcement constraints; however, the standard mechanism for forcing CMEK is constraints/storage.requireCustomEncryptionKeys.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Monitoring alerts provide reactive notification rather than proactive prevention of non-compliant resource creation.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You need to grant an external auditor temporary, read-only access to view configuration details of specific Compute Engine instances in a single project without granting them permissions over the entire project or other resources. What is the most secure way to accomplish this?

options.text: Grant the Compute Viewer role (roles/compute.viewer) scoped directly to the specific Compute Engine instance resources using IAM resource-level bindings.
Grant the Project Viewer role at the organization level with an IAM condition expiring in 7 days.
Create a new project, migrate the instances to it, and grant the auditor Project Editor access.
Share your personal Google Cloud console login credentials with the auditor for a limited time.

questions.explanation: Applying IAM roles at the resource level (such as on individual Compute Engine instances) adheres to the principle of least privilege by restricting access scope.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Granting Project Viewer at the organization level provides excessive permissions across all projects, violating least privilege.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Migrating production instances to a new project solely for auditing is highly disruptive and creates unnecessary operational risk.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Sharing credentials violates basic security policies, non-repudiation, and audit logging standards.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a data-processing pipeline on Google Cloud that ingests variable workloads into Compute Engine instances. To minimize costs while meeting a flexible execution window, you want to utilize spare compute capacity with automatic termination notices.

options.text: Provision the instances as Spot VMs with a configured termination notice handler.
Purchase 3-year Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) for flexible compute resources.
Use Preemptible VM instances with a maximum duration flag.
Configure standard Compute Engine instances with sustained use discounts.

questions.explanation: Spot VMs provide deep discounts (up to 91%) on Compute Engine capacity for fault-tolerant workloads that can withstand instance termination when Google reclaims the resources.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Committed Use Discounts are best suited for steady-state predictable workloads, not highly variable workloads with flexible execution windows where capacity might not be needed continuously.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Preemptible VMs are the legacy equivalent of Spot VMs and are largely superseded by Spot VMs, which offer more flexible pricing and availability guarantees.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Sustained use discounts have been replaced by flexible CUDs, and standard instances do not offer the steep cost savings of Spot VMs for variable batch workloads.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages a stateful web application running on Compute Engine instances that experiences steady, predictable traffic year-round. Finance has mandated that you optimize the monthly infrastructure spend as much as possible.

options.text: Migrate all instances to Spot VMs to maximize discount percentages.
Rely entirely on automated sustained use discounts.
Switch all persistent disks from balanced persistent disk to standard persistent disk.
Purchase 1-year or 3-year Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) for compute resources in the target region.

questions.explanation: Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) provide heavily discounted prices in exchange for a commitment to a specific level of resource usage over a 1-year or 3-year term, perfectly matching steady-state production workloads.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Spot VMs can be preempted at any time with a 30-second warning, making them unsuitable for steady-state stateful production web applications.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Google Cloud has largely replaced automatic sustained use discounts for flexible CUDs, and standard CUDs must be purchased explicitly to lock in maximum savings for predictable workloads.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While standard persistent disks are cheaper per GB, they offer significantly lower IOPS and throughput, which will likely degrade the performance of a production web application.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a massive data lake stored in Cloud Storage containing tens of petabytes of historical logs. Most of this data is accessed less than once a year, but compliance requires it to be retained for seven years. You need to minimize storage costs.

options.text: Move all files immediately to Nearline Storage with regional redundancy.
Export all objects to Persistent Disk snapshots associated with an inactive compute instance.
Configure Object Lifecycle Management rules to transition objects directly to the Archive storage class.
Configure Object Lifecycle Management rules to transition objects to Nearline, Coldline, and finally Archive storage class over time.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage Archive is the lowest-cost, highly durable storage service for data archiving, online backup, and disaster recovery, specifically optimized for data accessed less than once a year.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Nearline storage is too expensive for data that is rarely accessed and must be retained for seven years, and regional redundancy does not reduce the base storage tier cost.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Persistent Disk snapshots are significantly more expensive per GB than Cloud Storage Archive and are not designed for unstructured object data archival.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Stepping through Nearline and Coldline adds unnecessary retrieval fees and storage duration charges when the data is destined exclusively for long-term archival.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company is deploying a new containerized API on Cloud Run. The API experiences unpredictable traffic spikes ranging from zero requests to thousands of requests per second. You need to ensure cost efficiency while preventing cold-start latency during unexpected bursts.

options.text: Provision a fixed pool of 50 Always On container instances to absorb any potential traffic spike.
Set a small number of minimum instances (e.g., 1) and configure CPU allocation to be allocated only when processing requests.
Set the minimum number of container instances to zero and configure CPU allocation to be always allocated.
Deploy the service on a dedicated GKE cluster with node auto-scaling.

questions.explanation: Cloud Run allows you to balance cost and performance by scaling down to zero when idle, but setting a minimal warm instance count prevents cold starts while keeping baseline costs low.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Provisioning a large fixed pool of instances defeats the scale-to-zero and pay-per-use cost benefits of Cloud Run, resulting in excessive idle costs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Keeping CPU allocated only during request processing reduces costs, but setting minimum instances to zero guarantees cold starts when traffic spikes from zero.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Managing a GKE cluster for an unpredictable API introduces unnecessary management overhead and baseline infrastructure costs compared to serverless Cloud Run.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team is running a batch processing job on Compute Engine that completes in 4 hours every night. Currently, the job uses n2-standard-8 instances, but resource utilization monitoring shows that CPU utilization never exceeds 30% and memory utilization is below 25%. You need to optimize costs.

options.text: Switch the machine family from N2 to E2 and keep the same vCPU and memory count.
Downsize the instance machine type to a smaller n2-standard-2 configuration.
Upgrade the instances to c2-standard-8 compute-optimized instances for faster execution.
Attach additional local SSDs to improve the I/O throughput of the batch job.

questions.explanation: Right-sizing over-provisioned virtual machine instances based on historical utilization metrics is one of the most effective ways to eliminate waste and optimize cloud spend.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While E2 instances are cost-effective, simply switching families without changing size might not optimize the resource footprint as effectively as downsizing an over-provisioned machine type.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Compute-optimized instances are more expensive per hour and are unnecessary for jobs that are not bottlenecked by CPU performance.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Local SSDs add extra monthly cost and are unnecessary unless the batch job is heavily bottlenecked by disk I/O, which is not indicated.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your development team has set up a shared BigQuery dataset for ad-hoc SQL queries across 50 analysts. Due to poorly optimized queries scanning entire multi-terabyte tables daily, your monthly BigQuery billing has spiked unexpectedly. You need to enforce cost containment without restricting table access.

options.text: Enable query caching and instruct users to manually clear their local browser caches.
Revoke BigQuery data viewer permissions from all analysts and route queries through a single service account.
Set up BigQuery reservation pricing with a fixed slot commitment.
Disable on-demand query pricing entirely across the entire Google Cloud organization using an organization policy constraint.

questions.explanation: BigQuery slot reservations (flat-rate pricing) allow companies with predictable or high-volume analytical workloads to cap their costs by purchasing fixed compute capacity instead of paying per terabyte scanned.

wrongOptionNotes.A: BigQuery automatically caches query results for 24 hours, but ad-hoc analytical queries with slight parameter variations bypass the cache, failing to solve large-scale table scans.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Routing all queries through a single service account breaks auditability, user accountability, and granular access controls.
wrongOptionNotes.D: There is no organization policy constraint that outright disables on-demand pricing without moving to reservations or modifying project configurations.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company operates an application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that handles variable workloads. During off-peak hours at night, cluster resource utilization drops significantly, but you are still paying for the underlying provisioned node capacity.

options.text: Deploy all workloads inside App Engine standard environment instead of GKE.
Manually delete half of the cluster nodes every evening and recreate them every morning using a Cloud Scheduler script.
Configure GKE Autopilot mode for the cluster.
Enable Cluster Autoscaler and configure horizontal pod autoscaling (HPA) along with node auto-provisioning.

questions.explanation: The GKE Cluster Autoscaler automatically adjusts the size of your cluster's node pools based on resource demands, scaling down nodes when traffic decreases to save costs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Rewriting and migrating containerized GKE applications to App Engine is operationally heavy and fails to address the Kubernetes cost optimization requirement.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual or scripted node deletion is brittle, prone to scheduling failures, and risks application downtime.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While Autopilot manages node provisioning, migrating an existing standard cluster just for off-peak scaling is disruptive; Node Auto-provisioning or cluster autoscaler is the direct solution.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your database administrator has provisioned a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance for a development environment. The instance is currently sized as db-n1-standard-4 with 100 GB of SSD storage and automated backups enabled. Developers only access the database during business hours (8 hours a day, 5 days a week). How can you optimize costs for this non-production database?

options.text: Downgrade the instance storage type from SSD to HDD storage.
Enable automated storage increases and reduce the initial provisioned storage to 10 GB.
Configure Cloud SQL to use High Availability (regional) deployment to reduce idle resource consumption.
Stop the Cloud SQL instance outside of business hours using a custom script or automation.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL allows storage auto-increase, enabling administrators to provision smaller initial disk sizes for non-production databases and let storage scale automatically as data grows, avoiding upfront over-provisioning.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud SQL for MySQL does not support HDD storage; it uses SSD persistent disks exclusively.
wrongOptionNotes.C: High Availability provisions a failover replica in a secondary zone, which doubles the compute and storage costs and is unnecessary for a development environment.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud SQL instances cannot be 'stopped' to pause billing; compute charges accrue unless the instance is deleted, though backups and storage still incur baseline costs.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization stores terabytes of reporting exports in a Cloud Storage bucket. These reports are generated weekly and must be kept available for immediate access whenever requested by business stakeholders, but they are rarely read after the first month. You want to minimize ongoing storage costs without incurring retrieval fees.

options.text: Store the reports in Nearline Storage indefinitely.
Transition the objects immediately to Archive Storage upon creation.
Compress the bucket using standard multi-regional bucket compression policies.
Transition the objects to Coldline Storage after 30 days.

questions.explanation: Coldline Storage offers lower cost per GB than Standard or Nearline storage for data accessed less than once a month, backed by a 30-day minimum storage duration.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Nearline storage has a higher per-GB storage cost than Coldline, making it sub-optimal for data retained long-term with low access frequency.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Archive storage has a 365-day minimum storage duration requirement and retrieval fees, which makes it less suitable if reports are accessed moderately during their first month.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud Storage does not provide automatic bucket-level compression; compression must be handled by the application prior to upload.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a containerized service on a Managed Instance Group (MIG) of Compute Engine instances behind an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Traffic follows a predictable pattern: heavy load during daytime business hours and near zero at night. You want to minimize compute expenses during the night.

options.text: Migrate the MIG instances to Spot VMs without changing the autoscaling parameters.
Use a Cloud Scheduler cron job to manually resize the MIG instance group size to zero every night.
Replace the MIG with a single oversized n2-instance to handle peak load without scaling.
Configure autoscaling on the MIG based on CPU utilization with a lower minimum number of instances for nighttime.

questions.explanation: MIG autoscaling dynamically adjusts the number of VM instances in the group based on load metrics (such as CPU utilization), ensuring you only pay for necessary compute capacity.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While Spot VMs save money, using them for a web application without handling preemption gracefully can cause availability issues, and autoscaling still controls the instance count.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Resizing an autoscaled MIG manually will conflict with the autoscaler configuration, and setting instances to zero causes complete service outage unless traffic is truly nonexistent.
wrongOptionNotes.C: A single instance eliminates high availability, offers no cost scaling, and creates a single point of failure.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your development team has deployed a high-throughput messaging architecture using Pub/Sub. The pipeline ingests logs from thousands of IoT devices. Finance is concerned about the high data ingestion costs. How can you optimize Pub/Sub messaging costs?

options.text: Increase the acknowledgement deadline to allow messages to batch longer on the server side.
Configure Pub/Sub message retention duration to 0 days to avoid storage billing.
Switch the Pub/Sub topic storage location from multi-region to regional to save on replication fees.
Enable message compression on the client side before publishing messages to Pub/Sub topics.

questions.explanation: Pub/Sub pricing is primarily driven by the volume of data ingested and delivered. Reducing the payload size through client-side compression directly decreases billing.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The acknowledgement deadline only controls how long a subscriber has to acknowledge a message before redelivery; it does not affect ingestion billing or server-side batching.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Pub/Sub stores unacknowledged messages for up to 7 days, but acknowledged messages are deleted immediately. Message storage is typically a minor fraction of total Pub/Sub cost compared to data volume.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Pub/Sub topics do not incur multi-regional storage replication fees in the same way Cloud Storage does; Pub/Sub pricing is based on data volume throughput.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages a legacy application running on Compute Engine. The application requires a shared file system accessible by multiple virtual machine instances simultaneously across different zones. You need to provision this storage while balancing cost and performance.

options.text: Provision a Filastore Enterprise tier file share.
Provision a Filastore Basic tier file share.
Attach a Regional Persistent Disk in read-write mode to all instances simultaneously.
Create a Cloud Storage bucket and mount it as a local directory on all instances using Cloud Storage FUSE.

questions.explanation: Filastore Basic tier provides cost-effective, fully managed NFS storage that can be mounted across multiple Compute Engine instances concurrently.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Filastore Enterprise tier is designed for high-availability mission-critical workloads with multi-zone replication, carrying a significantly higher price tag than Basic tier.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Regional Persistent Disks can only be attached in read-write mode to a single instance at a time (multi-writer is limited to specific cluster filesystems and limitations), making them unsuitable for general multi-instance file sharing.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While Cloud Storage FUSE allows mounting buckets, object storage does not support POSIX file locking semantics required by many legacy shared file system applications.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company is running a data warehouse query workload in BigQuery. Certain complex queries scan petabytes of data repeatedly by different business units. You want to reduce query costs without limiting user access.

options.text: Export all BigQuery tables to Cloud Storage and query them using external tables.
Enable BigQuery BI Engine to accelerate SQL queries with in-memory analysis.
Convert all BigQuery datasets to legacy SQL syntax.
Partition all destination tables by ingest time and cluster by primary key.

questions.explanation: BigQuery BI Engine is an in-memory analysis service that accelerates SQL queries and reduces data scanning costs for analytical workloads.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Querying external data sources in Cloud Storage can be slower and does not inherently bypass BigQuery query scanning costs or performance bottlenecks.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Standard SQL is recommended for BigQuery; legacy SQL does not reduce query costs or improve performance optimization.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While partitioning and clustering reduce data scan costs for future queries, they require altering existing tables and query structures, whereas BI Engine directly optimizes repeated analytical queries.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization operates a mission-critical web application hosted on Compute Engine. To ensure high availability, you deployed instances across two regions behind a Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer. However, cross-region traffic and inter-zone data transfer costs are higher than budgeted. How can you optimize network egress costs?

options.text: Replace the Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer with a Regional Internal TCP/UDP Load Balancer.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on all subnets to inspect packet headers.
Route all internet egress traffic through a single NAT gateway in us-central1.
Configure load balancing traffic distribution to prefer backend instances in the same region as the client using backend bucket locality settings.

questions.explanation: Minimizing cross-region and cross-zone traffic by aligning client requests with local regional backend resources significantly reduces Google Cloud network egress charges.

wrongOptionNotes.A: An internal load balancer is not accessible to external internet clients, breaking the public web application architecture.
wrongOptionNotes.B: VPC Flow Logs record network flow metadata for monitoring and auditing, but they do not alter routing behavior or reduce data transfer costs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Routing all global traffic through a single region's NAT gateway increases cross-region transit costs and creates a massive bandwidth bottleneck and single point of failure.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages a large fleet of Compute Engine instances across multiple Google Cloud projects. Many stopped or unattached persistent disks have been left behind, accumulating unnecessary storage charges. You need to identify and clean up unattached disks efficiently.

options.text: Set up a Cloud Monitoring alert based on CPU utilization metrics for disk resources.
Use Cloud Asset Inventory to query for persistent disks where the users field is empty or unattached.
Review the serial port logs of every running virtual machine instance.
Inspect VPC Flow Logs for IP address assignments on disk block devices.

questions.explanation: Cloud Asset Inventory provides a centralized repository of Google Cloud resource metadata, enabling administrators to discover unattached disks, idle instances, and other cost optimization targets across projects.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Persistent disks do not emit CPU utilization metrics; monitoring CPU applies to virtual machine instances.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Serial port logs contain boot and OS operational messages for specific virtual machines, not metadata about unattached persistent disks.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Persistent disks are block storage devices operating at the hypervisor level and do not have IP addresses or generate VPC flow logs.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company operates a critical transactional database hosted on Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in the us-central1 region. As part of your disaster recovery (DR) strategy, you need to configure a cross-region replica in us-east1 to meet a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) of under 1 minute and a Recovery Time Objective (RTO) of under 15 minutes. What is the most operationally resilient approach to achieve this?

options.text: Deploy a Compute Engine instance running PostgreSQL in us-east1 and configure native database streaming replication from the Cloud SQL instance.
Create a read-only replica in the same zone (us-central1-a) to ensure high availability and point-to-point data synchronization.
Set up a standard database dump using pg_dump every hour, upload the backup to a multi-region Cloud Storage bucket, and restore it in us-east1 upon failure.

Configure a Cloud SQL cross-region replica in us-east1 and monitor replication lag using Cloud Monitoring, preparing a runbook to promote the replica manually or via automated scripts if us-central1 experiences an outage.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL cross-region replicas allow you to replicate data asynchronously to another region. In the event of a regional failure, promoting the replica makes it the new primary database, ensuring business continuity with minimal data loss (RPO) and quick recovery (RTO).

wrongOptionNotes.A: While technically possible, managing a self-managed replica on Compute Engine increases operational overhead and requires manual failover plumbing compared to managed Cloud SQL replicas.
wrongOptionNotes.B: A same-region or same-zone replica does not protect against a disaster affecting the entire us-central1 region.
wrongOptionNotes.C: This approach results in an RPO of up to 1 hour and an RTO of several hours due to backup restoration time, failing both requirements.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are designing a multi-region disaster recovery architecture for a stateless web application deployed across Compute Engine instances in us-central1 and europe-west1. You need to implement global load balancing with automatic failover in case an entire region goes offline. Which Google Cloud service combination should you choose?

options.text: Cloud DNS with a Round Robin routing policy and no health checking mechanisms.
Regional External Application Load Balancer in us-central1 with a DNS entry pointing secondary traffic to europe-west1 using manual TTL updates.
Cloud VPN tunnels connecting us-central1 and europe-west1 with BGP routing enabled for automatic path failover.
Global External Application Load Balancer with backend services in both us-central1 and europe-west1, configured with health checks and weighted or failover routing policies.

questions.explanation: The Global External Application Load Balancer is designed for multi-region architectures. It uses Anycast IP addresses to route user requests to the closest healthy backend, ensuring automatic failover when regional health checks fail.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Round Robin without health checks will continue sending client traffic to dead endpoints during an outage, causing widespread application errors.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Regional load balancers cannot route traffic across regions, and manual DNS TTL updates provide slow failover times that violate modern DR standards.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud VPN connects networks, not end-user web traffic to application backends.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization runs a financial analytics workload on Compute Engine instances within a custom VPC in us-central1. You are planning a high-availability DR strategy that requires replicating virtual machine disk states and configurations to us-east1. What is the best method to protect against regional zone or infrastructure failures for persistent workloads?

options.text: Mount a single multi-region standard Persistent Disk across instances running in both us-central1 and us-east1 simultaneously.
Take daily local snapshots and store them exclusively in a regional Cloud Storage bucket in us-central1.

Use regional Persistent Disks to automatically replicate data synchronously across two zones within the same region, and maintain an automated snapshot schedule with cross-region snapshot copies to us-east1.
Rely entirely on live migration of Compute Engine instances to automatically shift virtual machines to another region during a failure.

questions.explanation: Regional Persistent Disks offer high availability by replicating data across two zones in a region. For disaster recovery across regions, leveraging automated snapshot schedules combined with cross-region snapshot copies ensures that disk states are available in a secondary region.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Persistent Disks can only be attached in read-write mode to instances within the same zone (or multi-writer mode within the same zone for specific cluster file systems), not across different regions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Storing snapshots in the same region does not protect against a catastrophic regional disaster.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Live migration is designed for infrastructure maintenance events within the same zone and cannot migrate running instances across geographic regions.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages a microservices-based application deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters in both asia-east1 and us-west1. You need to ensure that if the primary cluster in asia-east1 experiences a complete service disruption, client traffic is seamlessly redirected to the us-west1 cluster. How should you configure global routing and health checking?

options.text: Configure a regional internal HTTP(S) load balancer in asia-east1 and peer it with the us-west1 VPC network.
Deploy a Global External Application Load Balancer with Network Endpoint Groups (NEGs) from both GKE clusters as backends, utilizing HTTP(S) health checks.
Rely on Kubernetes Cluster Federation to automatically migrate pods across regions without any load balancing layer.
Use a TCP Proxy Load Balancer with internal IP addresses pointing to Kubernetes pod IPs across the WAN.

questions.explanation: Container-native load balancing using Network Endpoint Groups (NEGs) enables GKE clusters to integrate directly with Google Cloud load balancers. By registering NEGs from multiple regions to a Global External Application Load Balancer, you achieve seamless multi-region failover.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Regional internal load balancers cannot handle cross-region external client traffic or provide global failover capabilities.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Kubernetes alone cannot direct external public traffic from clients across regions without a global ingress or load balancing mechanism.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Pod IPs are ephemeral and internal to the cluster; routing global external traffic directly to cross-region pod IPs across the internet is unsupported and insecure.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company is designing a multi-region disaster recovery plan for a batch processing system that reads input files from Cloud Storage, processes them via Compute Engine, and writes outputs back to Cloud Storage. You want to ensure data availability even if an entire multi-region location suffers an outage. Which Cloud Storage storage class should you choose for the data buckets?

options.text: Multi-region storage class, providing geo-redundancy with data stored redundantly across at least two geographic macro-locations separated by at least 100 miles.
Coldline storage class in a regional bucket with a 90-day minimum storage duration.
Nearline storage class configured for a single zone to minimize storage costs.
Standard regional storage class deployed in us-central1.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage multi-region buckets automatically replicate data across multiple geographic regions. This ensures high durability and availability, protecting your pipeline inputs and outputs against regional disasters.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Coldline is optimized for data accessed less than once a year and is restricted to regional availability, providing poor DR characteristics.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Single-zone Nearline storage lacks geo-redundancy and has minimum retention/retrieval fee overheads unsuited for active multi-region processing pipelines.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Regional storage stores data within a single specific region, offering no protection against a broad regional outage.

questions.domain: Planning and Implementing a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization requires an active-passive disaster recovery setup for a legacy application running on Compute Engine. The primary environment is in us-central1, and the passive standby environment is in us-east1. To minimize costs, you want the standby environment to maintain stopped virtual machine instances while keeping disk storage and configurations intact, ensuring rapid startup during a disaster. What is the most effective configuration?

options.text: Run the standby instances at full capacity 24/7 in us-east1 to ensure zero startup delay.
Configure preemptible VM instances in us-east1 to act as the standby cluster.
Delete all instances and disks in us-east1 entirely, relying on manual console creation steps when an alert triggers.

Provision the standby instances in us-east1 in a stopped state, configure regional or replicated Persistent Disks, and use automated startup scripts or Deployment Manager/Terraform templates to launch instances during a failover event.

questions.explanation: An active-passive DR strategy balancing cost and RTO often maintains compute resources in a stopped state or utilizes infrastructure-as-code scripts with replicated disks. This eliminates idle compute hourly charges while ensuring the environment can be powered on quickly.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Running identical production capacity continuously in a passive standby region doubles compute costs, defeating the requirement to minimize standby costs.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Preemptible VMs can be terminated by Google Cloud at any time, making them completely unreliable for a disaster recovery standby environment.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Manual recreation during an incident severely increases RTO and introduces human error risks during high-stress outages.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages a web application running on a regional Managed Instance Group (MIG) behind an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Users report that during peak traffic hours, new instances created by autoscaling take too long to start serving traffic, causing intermittent 502 errors. The application takes several minutes to initialize caches upon boot. How should you resolve this issue while minimizing operational overhead?

options.text: Switch the load balancer to a TCP Proxy load balancer and handle SSL termination directly on the backend instances.
Configure a health check-based readiness delay or use application-based health checks with a properly tuned initialDelaySec and set up a MIG instance template initialization timeout.
Increase the maximum number of instances in the MIG autoscaling policy to absorb the slower boot times through sheer volume.
Pre-scale the MIG manually every morning to its absolute peak capacity before business hours begin.

questions.explanation: When instances require significant initialization time before serving traffic, standard auto-healing or load balancer health checks might mark them as healthy too early. Configuring appropriate initial delay settings and robust application health checks ensures traffic is only sent when the service is fully ready.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Changing load balancer types does not resolve instance initialization delays and breaks HTTP(S) specific routing features.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Throwing more instances at the problem does not fix the root cause of routing traffic to uninitialized instances and wastes resources.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Manual scaling defeats the purpose of an autoscaling MIG and leads to excessive compute costs during unpredictable workloads.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a high-throughput data processing pipeline on Google Cloud. Log entries from dozens of Compute Engine instances are ingested into Cloud Logging. Due to strict cost constraints and data retention policies, you need to prevent specific verbose debug log messages from being ingested and stored, while keeping all other logs intact. What is the most efficient way to achieve this?

options.text: Create a logging exclusion filter in Cloud Logging to drop logs matching the specific debug criteria before they are stored.
Write a custom cron job on each Compute Engine instance to continuously truncate local log files on disk.
Modify the application source code to suppress standard output writing entirely when running in production mode.
Downgrade the log sink destination to a standard file storage bucket and manually delete files daily using a script.

questions.explanation: Cloud Logging exclusions provide a native mechanism to filter out unwanted log entries at ingestion time, preventing them from consuming billable log storage quota.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud Logging ingests logs sent to standard streams, not just local files. Local truncation does not prevent logs from being ingested.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Modifying application code is an anti-pattern when infrastructure-level log management tools like Cloud Logging exclusions are available.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Sinks export logs; they do not filter out log ingestion charges within Cloud Logging unless exclusions are applied.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are managing a Google Cloud project with multiple microservices. You notice that billing alerts are not triggering promptly, and finance teams report a delay of up to a day in seeing granular cost breakdowns. You need to verify and establish near-real-time visibility into resource consumption patterns by team and environment. What should you configure?

options.text: Export Cloud Billing data to a BigQuery dataset and set up scheduled queries or dashboard views for continuous tracking.
Attach a budget alert notification to an email distribution list with a lowered threshold percentage.
Write a custom bash script running on a Compute Engine instance to scrape the metadata server every minute for pricing information.
Rely entirely on the Google Cloud Console Billing overview page which updates every hour automatically.

questions.explanation: Exporting Cloud Billing data directly to BigQuery is the recommended approach for deep, flexible, and timely analysis of cost patterns across complex multi-service projects.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Budget alerts notify when spending crosses thresholds, but they do not provide granular cost breakdowns or accelerated data reporting.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The metadata server provides instance attributes and pricing tokens, but scraping it does not track overall project-wide multi-service billing data.
wrongOptionNotes.D: The Cloud Console billing page has limited granularity and does not provide customizable near-real-time streaming analytics like BigQuery.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a containerized service on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). During deployment updates, users intermittently experience connection drops because traffic is routed to pods that are in the process of shutting down. The application code handles graceful shutdown signals, but Kubernetes terminates the container too quickly. How should you fix this issue?

options.text: Switch the Kubernetes service type from ClusterIP to NodePort across all cluster nodes.
Increase the terminationGracePeriodSeconds in the Pod specification to allow ongoing requests to complete before the container is killed.
Reduce the replica count in the Deployment specification to zero before applying any new updates.
Enable horizontal pod autoscaling with a minimum target CPU utilization of 90 percent.

questions.explanation: Configuring `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` ensures that when pods receive a SIGTERM signal, they have adequate time to finish inflight requests before receiving a SIGKILL.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Changing service types alters network exposure methods but does not resolve pod lifecycle termination timing issues.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Reducing replicas to zero causes total downtime during deployments, defeating the purpose of rolling updates.
wrongOptionNotes.D: HPA manages replica scaling based on resource usage, not pod shutdown behavior or graceful termination windows.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a mission-critical PostgreSQL database on Cloud SQL. You receive alerts indicating that the primary instance has run out of disk space, causing the database to become unresponsive.
