You need to recover immediately and prevent recurrence without manually expanding disk storage every time growth occurs.

options.text: Restart the Cloud SQL instance via the Google Cloud Console to clear temporary swap space files.
Delete all automated backups stored in the Cloud SQL instance to instantly free up disk space.
Migrate the database to a smaller machine type with less memory to conserve underlying physical hypervisor resources.
Enable Cloud SQL storage auto-increase and immediately increase the current disk size if necessary to restore operations.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL provides a storage auto-increase feature that automatically scales storage capacity when the instance detects low free space, avoiding unexpected outages.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Restarting a disk-full database instance will typically fail or result in immediate crash-loop behavior because the database engine cannot write critical logs.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Automated backups are stored and managed by Google Cloud outside the instance data disk; deleting them manually is not directly supported or effective.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Lowering machine type specs does not resolve disk capacity exhaustion and will likely degrade database query performance.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your engineering team needs to troubleshoot a performance degradation issue on a Linux Compute Engine instance. You suspect that a memory leak in a custom daemon is causing the system to swap heavily. Which combination of built-in Google Cloud and native Linux tools should you use to confirm memory and swap utilization metrics?

options.text: Review the project's Cloud Audit Logs for any unauthorized IAM permission changes made during the last 24 hours.
Run a static code analysis check on the Google Cloud Deployment Manager configuration templates.
Examine the VPC Flow Logs for the network interface attached to the virtual machine instance.
Install the Cloud Monitoring agent (Ops Agent) to track memory metrics, and SSH into the instance to inspect 'free -m' and 'vmstat'.

questions.explanation: To diagnose OS-level resource exhaustion like swapping and memory leaks, combining historical platform monitoring via the Ops Agent with active local inspection tools is essential.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Audit Logs track administrative actions and security events, not internal operating system memory or swap performance.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Deployment Manager templates define infrastructure setup, not running OS runtime memory performance.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC Flow Logs record IP traffic flowing to and from instance interfaces, providing no insight into local OS memory consumption.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a batch processing system running on a Compute Engine instance that reads large binary datasets from a Google Cloud Storage bucket. Recently, jobs have slowed down drastically, and logs show frequent 'Rate Exceeded' (HTTP 429 / 503) errors when calling Cloud Storage APIs. What is the underlying architectural cause and remedy?

options.text: The bucket storage class is set to Archive, which restricts read throughput and forces 429 rate-limiting errors.
The Compute Engine instance has run out of local SSD capacity, forcing Cloud Storage to throttle incoming data streams.
The object naming structure causes request hot-spotting on a single partition; you should adopt randomized naming prefixes to distribute load across multiple partitions.
You must upgrade the instance to a Compute Engine type with a higher core count to bypass Google Cloud API rate limits.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage achieves high read/write scalability by partitioning keys. Sequential naming patterns cause hot-spotting, which can be mitigated by introducing randomized character prefixes.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Archive storage class affects retrieval pricing and minimum storage durations, not API request rate limits or hot-spotting.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud Storage throttling is governed by request rates and naming prefixes, not local SSD storage capacity on client virtual machines.
wrongOptionNotes.D: API rate limits are tied to project and bucket request patterns (specifically naming prefixes), not client instance core counts.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company enforces strict compliance policies stating that all production Compute Engine virtual machine instances must not have external public IP addresses assigned. However, instances occasionally need to download software packages and security patches from the public internet. What is the recommended, secure Google Cloud architecture to enable outbound-only internet connectivity?

options.text: Set up a public HTTP proxy server on a shared development instance and route all production traffic through it unencrypted.
Attach a secondary network interface (nic1) to each instance and connect it directly to an external public subnet.
Configure a firewall rule allowing all egress traffic to destination IP 0.0.0.0/0 on port 80 and 443.
Configure Cloud NAT associated with a Cloud Router in the VPC region where the private instances reside.

questions.explanation: Cloud NAT allows instances without external IP addresses to send outbound packets to the internet and receive corresponding responses, maintaining security isolation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Routing production traffic through an unmanaged proxy introduces single points of failure and security vulnerabilities.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Attaching public interfaces directly violates the compliance policy by giving instances external public IP addresses.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Firewall rules alone cannot perform Network Address Translation; instances without external IPs cannot reach the public internet even with open egress rules.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a web application running in a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. You want to ensure that if a node crashes or becomes unhealthy, pods running critical workloads are automatically rescheduled onto healthy nodes without manual intervention. Which Kubernetes resource or configuration should you verify?

options.text: Configure each pod with hostNetwork: true to bypass the Kubernetes container networking overlay layer.
Ensure workloads are managed by Deployments or StatefulSets, and nodes are part of a managed node pool with node auto-repair enabled.
Run all workloads as static pods configured manually via configuration files placed directly on the root disk of each virtual machine.
Set the replica count for each pod to exactly one and disable horizontal pod autoscaling across the cluster namespaces.

questions.explanation: GKE managed node pools with auto-repair combined with standard Kubernetes controllers (Deployments) ensure high availability and self-healing cluster infrastructure.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Using hostNetwork exposes host network namespaces directly to containers, presenting a major security risk without solving node resilience.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Static pods are managed directly by the kubelet on a specific node and are not rescheduled by the control plane if the node fails entirely.
wrongOptionNotes.D: A replica count of one guarantees downtime if that single pod or its underlying node experiences an unrecoverable failure.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are reviewing access controls across multiple Google Cloud projects in your organization. A security audit flags that an IAM role granted to a service account is overly permissive (Project Editor). You need to remediate this following the principle of least privilege while ensuring the service account can still read and write objects in a specific Cloud Storage bucket.

options.text: Revoke the Project Editor role from the service account and grant the 'Storage Object Admin' role specifically on the target Cloud Storage bucket.
Leave the Project Editor role assigned but add a deny policy on all other services except Cloud Storage.
Delete the service account entirely and recreate it with default Compute Engine service account credentials.
Downgrade the service account role from Project Editor to Project Viewer across the entire organization folder.

questions.explanation: The principle of least privilege requires scoping IAM roles to the minimum required resource level (e.g., binding storage roles directly to the bucket rather than granting project-wide editor access).

wrongOptionNotes.B: While IAM deny policies exist, the standard and cleaner remediation for over-permissioned service accounts is to scope down roles to the necessary resource level.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Default service accounts often carry broad permissions and deleting them can break running applications depending on those keys.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Project Viewer grants read access across all project resources, which remains overly permissive and lacks write access to the bucket.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages a stateful web application running on Compute Engine instances with persistent disks. During a routine disk resize operation on a running instance, the filesystem size does not reflect the newly allocated disk capacity. What step did the engineer likely miss?

options.text: Creating a snapshot of the persistent disk before executing the Google Cloud CLI resize command.
Running the OS-level filesystem expansion command (e.g., 'sudo resize2fs' or 'sudo xfs_growfs') to resize the partition and filesystem.
Restarting the Google Cloud Operations Suite agent inside the guest operating system via systemctl.
Re-attaching the persistent disk to a different virtual machine instance in read-only mode.

questions.explanation: When expanding a persistent disk in GCP, the disk capacity increases at the hypervisor layer, but the guest OS filesystem must be manually or automatically resized using tools like `resize2fs` (ext4) or `xfs_growfs` (XFS).

wrongOptionNotes.A: Taking snapshots is a best practice for backup, but it does not expand the active filesystem on the running disk.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Restarting monitoring agents refreshes metrics collection, but it does not alter block storage filesystems or partition tables.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Re-attaching disks in read-only mode prevents writing changes and does not resize underlying filesystems.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization requires that all custom machine images (Compute Engine images) created by development teams must be stored securely and only accessible within specific organizational boundaries. Where should these images be stored and how should permissions be managed?

options.text: Upload all custom disk images as public raw tarballs to a publicly accessible Cloud Storage bucket.
Store them in a centralized Google Cloud project and use IAM policies at the project or folder level to restrict access.
Store the images exclusively on the local scratch disks of ephemeral Compute Engine instances.
Keep all custom images inside the individual developer's personal Google Cloud free-tier sandbox account.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine custom images are project-level resources. Centralizing them in a dedicated host project and managing access via IAM provides secure, auditable image sharing.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Storing sensitive custom images in a public Cloud Storage bucket exposes proprietary software and violates security compliance.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Local scratch disks are ephemeral and lose all data when instances are stopped or terminated.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Sandbox accounts lack enterprise controls, governance, and centralized security oversight.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a web application deployed behind an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Users are intermittently reporting 504 Gateway Timeout errors when submitting large file uploads. Backend instances are healthy and have adequate CPU. What is the most likely configuration issue causing this symptom?

options.text: The Cloud SQL database max_connections limit has been reached.
The VPC firewall rules are blocking incoming TCP port 80 traffic entirely.
The SSL certificate attached to the load balancer frontend has expired.
The load balancer backend service timeout is set too low for the duration required to upload large files over slower client connections.

questions.explanation: HTTP(S) Load Balancer backend timeouts dictate how long the load balancer waits for a backend response. If slow uploads exceed this window, the load balancer terminates the connection with a 504 error.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Reaching database connection limits typically causes 500 internal server errors or database connection refused exceptions, not load balancer 504 timeouts.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Blocking port 80 completely would cause 100% connection failures rather than intermittent timeouts during specific file upload operations.
wrongOptionNotes.C: An expired SSL certificate results in browser security warnings and connection handshaking failures, not intermittent 504 gateway timeouts during uploads.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a multi-tier application on Google Cloud. You need to design an automated backup strategy for persistent disks attached to production database instances. The strategy must meet a recovery point objective (RPO) of 24 hours and a recovery time objective (RTO) of 2 hours, while retaining backups for 30 days. What is the most native and efficient way to implement this?

options.text: Export all database tables into CSV files and email them to the engineering distribution list daily.
Write a custom Python script running on an external server to download disk contents via SCP every night.
Manually stop the database instances every evening, take a disk snapshot via the Console, and restart them manually.
Create a Cloud Backup and DR policy or Compute Engine Snapshot Schedule (Snapshot Policy) attached to the persistent disks set to run daily.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine automated snapshot policies provide native, policy-driven lifecycle management for disk backups, ensuring compliance with RPO and retention goals without custom tooling.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Emailing database exports is insecure, fails to meet enterprise recovery standards, and does not provide proper database state restoration.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Writing custom scripts for block-level disk backups introduces unnecessary maintenance overhead and security risks compared to managed GCP services.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Manual backups are prone to human error, do not provide reliable automation, and cause unnecessary scheduled downtime.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are troubleshooting a networking issue in a Google Cloud VPC. Two Compute Engine instances in the same subnet and VPC cannot communicate with each other over internal IP addresses. You have verified that both instances are running and healthy. What should you check first as a potential root cause?

options.text: Verify that Cloud NAT is enabled on the subnetwork to facilitate internal instance routing.
Inspect the active VPC firewall rules to ensure there are no overriding deny rules or missing allow rules for internal traffic.
Check if the external HTTP(S) Load Balancer frontend IP address is configured correctly.
Review the Cloud Billing export configuration in BigQuery for cost anomaly detection.

questions.explanation: Intra-VPC communication is enabled by default, but custom firewall rules with improper priorities or explicit deny rules can block traffic between virtual machine instances.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud NAT is exclusively used for outbound internet connectivity for private instances, not for intra-VPC instance-to-instance communication.
wrongOptionNotes.C: External load balancers route traffic from the internet to backends; they are not involved in direct instance-to-instance internal subnet communication.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Billing exports track financial data and have no impact on packet routing or firewall behavior within a VPC.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your production application running on Compute Engine experiences intermittent connection drops to a backend Cloud SQL instance. You suspect network latency or firewall rule misconfigurations. Which tool should you use first to analyze packet paths and identify where network drops might be occurring within your VPC?

options.text: Run traceroute from your local workstation to the private IP of the Cloud SQL instance.
Modify the default VPC firewall rules to allow all egress traffic globally.
Enable Cloud Audit Logs on the Compute Engine instances to trace TCP handshake failures.
Use VPC Flow Logs combined with Cloud Logging to inspect sampled packet metadata and analyze traffic patterns.

questions.explanation: VPC Flow Logs record network flows sent to and from VM instances, providing crucial telemetry for diagnosing connectivity issues, latency, and packet drops within a Google Cloud VPC.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud SQL internal IP addresses are not directly reachable from outside the VPC without a proxy or VPN, making external traceroute ineffective.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Opening all egress traffic is a severe security risk and does not troubleshoot the underlying connectivity path.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud Audit Logs record administrative actions and API calls, not layer-4 packet transmission or TCP handshakes.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A managed instance group (MIG) behind an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer is failing its health checks, causing instances to be repeatedly recreated in a continuous loop. Where should you look first to determine why the health checks are failing?

options.text: Modify the firewall rules to block all traffic from the load balancer health check IP ranges.
Increase the maximum size of the Managed Instance Group to absorb the failing instances.
Check the HTTP(S) Load Balancer backend service health check status and review application error logs in Cloud Logging.
Delete the instance template and create a new project from scratch.

questions.explanation: When instances in a MIG fail health checks and undergo recreation loops, inspecting the load balancer's backend health check status alongside Cloud Logging application logs quickly identifies path or service failures.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Blocking health check IP ranges will guarantee that health checks fail permanently.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Scaling up the MIG will only generate more failing instances without addressing the root cause of the health check failure.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Recreating the project is an extreme and unnecessary step for troubleshooting a localized health check configuration or application crash.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster is experiencing a cluster-wide memory exhaustion issue on several worker nodes, causing pods to be evicted unexpectedly. Which tool should you use to diagnose which pods are consuming excessive memory?

options.text: Inspect the Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) flow logs for high packet counts.
Examine the project billing export tables in BigQuery to find high-cost containers.
Review Cloud IAM policy bindings for unauthorized user access.
Use Cloud Monitoring dashboard and Kubernetes metrics explorer to analyze pod memory utilization over time.

questions.explanation: Cloud Monitoring and Kubernetes metrics are designed to track resource metrics such as CPU and memory utilization at the node, pod, and container levels.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC flow logs record network traffic volume, not container memory allocation or usage.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Billing data tracks financial costs, not real-time pod memory consumption or eviction events.
wrongOptionNotes.C: IAM policies manage permissions and access control, not runtime memory consumption.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An internal application running on a Compute Engine instance cannot resolve the DNS name of a Cloud SQL database instance. What is the most appropriate first step to troubleshoot this name resolution failure?

options.text: Upgrade the machine type of the Compute Engine instance to a higher tier.
Verify that Cloud DNS is properly configured and that Private Services Access is established within the VPC network.
Delete the Cloud SQL instance and restore it from a backup in a different region.
Restart the Compute Engine instance operating system to clear its ARP cache.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL instances with private IPs require proper Private Services Access setup and VPC peering configurations so that internal DNS queries can correctly resolve the database endpoints.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Scaling up compute resources has no impact on DNS resolution failures.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Recreating the database instance is destructive and unnecessary when troubleshooting a VPC networking or DNS issue.
wrongOptionNotes.D: An OS restart does not fix underlying VPC routing or Private Services Access misconfigurations for Cloud SQL.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team receives an alert that a critical Cloud Storage bucket containing customer exports is publicly accessible. You need to immediately remediate this security vulnerability while ensuring legitimate internal service accounts retain access. What is the best approach?

options.text: Delete the entire Cloud Storage bucket and recreate it with a randomized name.
Disable all Cloud IAM permissions across the entire Google Cloud project.
Change the storage class of the bucket from Multi-Regional to Standard.
Enforce Public Access Prevention on the bucket and review IAM policies to ensure valid internal service accounts retain necessary access.

questions.explanation: Enforcing Public Access Prevention on Cloud Storage buckets provides a definitive guardrail against public exposure without requiring complex audits of individual object ACLs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Deleting the bucket destroys production data and is an unnecessarily disruptive remediation action.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling all IAM permissions blocks all workloads and administrative access across the project, causing a total outage.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Storage classes affect availability and pricing tiers, not public exposure or access control settings.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A production microservice deployed on Cloud Run is returning HTTP 503 Service Unavailable errors intermittently under load. You need to identify whether the container instances are crashing due to out-of-memory errors or failing to start in time. Where should you investigate?

options.text: Check the Google Cloud billing console for budget threshold alerts.
Review the VPC firewall rules to ensure HTTP traffic is permitted.
Check Cloud Logging for container startup failures, SIGKILL events, or memory limit exceeded messages.
Inspect the Cloud Storage audit logs for permission denied errors.

questions.explanation: Cloud Run writes container logs directly to Cloud Logging, where operators can inspect crash logs, SIGKILL signals, and startup latency to troubleshoot 503 errors.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Billing alerts indicate financial thresholds, not container-level runtime errors or crashes.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud Run manages its own ingress routing; VPC firewall rules do not govern direct Cloud Run service endpoints unless connected via VPC connector.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud Storage audit logs track bucket access and are unrelated to Cloud Run container compute execution.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization's security team reports that an unencrypted persistent disk attached to a production Compute Engine instance violates compliance policy. You need to migrate the existing unencrypted disk to use a Customer-Managed Encryption Key (CMEK) with Cloud KMS. What is the correct procedure?

options.text: Create a snapshot of the unencrypted disk, create a new disk from that snapshot while specifying the CMEK key, and attach the new encrypted disk to the instance.
Detach the disk, export it to an external local server, encrypt it locally, and upload it back to Google Cloud.
Run the gcloud compute disks update command and pass the Cloud KMS key flag directly to encrypt the active disk in place.
Format the disk using an operating system filesystem utility with AES-256 encryption flags.

questions.explanation: Persistent disks cannot be encrypted in-place with CMEK. The correct pattern is to take a snapshot, create a new disk from the snapshot using the CMEK key, and swap the disks.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Exporting production disks off-platform introduces security risks and violates standard migration workflows.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Google Cloud does not support encrypting an existing unencrypted persistent disk in place with a CMEK via an update command.
wrongOptionNotes.D: OS-level encryption does not satisfy Google Cloud persistent disk encryption requirements managed via Cloud KMS.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A scheduled batch job running on a Compute Engine instance fails intermittently because it cannot authenticate against a BigQuery dataset. The instance uses the default compute service account. What is the most secure and recommended way to resolve this access issue?

options.text: Hardcode a personal user account's password into the batch script configuration file.
Disable Identity and Access Management (IAM) checks for the BigQuery dataset.
Assign the Project Editor role to the default compute service account to ensure full access to all services.
Grant the specific IAM role (e.g., BigQuery Data Viewer) to the instance's service account on the target dataset or project.

questions.explanation: To allow instances to access Google Cloud services securely, assign granular IAM roles directly to the instance's service account following the principle of least privilege.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Hardcoding credentials or using personal user accounts for automated workloads is a major security violation.
wrongOptionNotes.B: IAM checks cannot be disabled on BigQuery datasets; access control is strictly enforced.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Assigning Project Editor is overly permissive and violates security best practices.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a containerized workload on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Users report that a specific application endpoint is returning HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout errors. You check the ingress controller logs and confirm requests are timing out before reaching the backend pods. What should you check next?

options.text: Delete all VPC subnets and recreate the cluster control plane.
Switch the GKE cluster from a regional cluster to a zonal cluster.
Check the Google Cloud billing console to verify that the credit card is active.
Inspect the Kubernetes Deployment readiness and liveness probes to ensure pods are ready to accept traffic and not stuck in a restart loop.

questions.explanation: HTTP 504 Gateway Timeouts often occur when an ingress controller cannot route traffic to healthy backend pods because readiness probes are failing or pods are overwhelmed.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Recreating subnets and control planes is highly disruptive and unnecessary for diagnosing timeout issues.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Changing cluster topology does not resolve application-level timeouts caused by failing probes or overloaded pods.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Billing status affects project suspension, not intermittent HTTP 504 gateway timeouts on active clusters.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a mission-critical Cloud SQL PostgreSQL database. During peak traffic hours, CPU utilization reaches 100%, and application response times degrade severely. Which tool should you use to identify the specific inefficient SQL queries causing the performance spike?

options.text: Check the IAM policy simulator to verify user permissions on the database.
Examine the Cloud Storage bucket logs where database backups are stored.
Review the VPC flow logs for unusual external IP scanning activity.
Enable and review Cloud SQL Query Insights to analyze query performance, execution time, and CPU consumption.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL Query Insights is built specifically to help developers and database administrators identify and troubleshoot slow-running queries and high CPU consumers.

wrongOptionNotes.A: IAM policy simulator tests authorization permissions, not database query performance or CPU bottlenecks.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Backup logs only show backup job completion status, not live query execution performance.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC flow logs track network traffic packets, not database query efficiency or SQL execution plans.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your development team deployed a new version of an application to a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster using a Deployment resource. Shortly after, users report errors. You need to quickly roll back the deployment to the previous stable version. What is the most efficient command to execute?

options.text: Manually SSH into every container and uninstall the application binary.
Run kubectl rollout undo deployment/[DEPLOYMENT_NAME] to revert to the previous revision.
Delete the entire GKE cluster and restore a snapshot of the cluster configuration using Cloud Backup.
Modify the Dockerfile locally and rebuild the base operating system image for all nodes.

questions.explanation: Kubernetes native rolling updates maintain revision history, allowing operators to execute a quick rollback using `kubectl rollout undo` during a faulty deployment.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Manual SSH into containers is anti-pattern in Kubernetes and often restricted or impossible depending on the container base image.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Recreating the cluster is extremely disruptive and takes far longer than a standard Kubernetes rollout undo.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Rebuilding node base images does not address the application deployment revision running inside the Kubernetes pods.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A production Compute Engine instance running a vital processing script has run out of disk space on its root persistent disk, causing the application to crash. You need to resolve the immediate outage and prevent recurrence. What is the best combination of actions?

options.text: Delete the virtual machine instance and create a new instance with a smaller machine type.
Change the VPC firewall rules to allow larger packet payloads.
Resize the persistent disk in the Google Cloud Console or via gcloud, then use filesystem resizing commands (e.g., resize2fs) inside the OS.
Stop the instance, detach the root disk, attach it as a secondary disk to another project, and delete half of the system binaries.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud persistent disks can be resized dynamically while attached to a running instance. Once resized in the cloud console, the underlying OS filesystem must be expanded to use the extra space.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Recreating the VM without resizing the disk does not solve the underlying root disk capacity exhaustion.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Firewall rules govern network packet filtering, not disk storage capacity.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Deleting system binaries will corrupt the operating system installation.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team needs to audit administrative changes made across multiple Google Cloud projects within your organization over the past 90 days. Where should you look to retrieve these historical administrative logs?

options.text: Check the Google Cloud billing export to see which users initiated API calls.
Query the centralized Cloud Logging sink exported to BigQuery or use the Logs Explorer filtered by Admin Activity log type.
Review the VPC flow logs for connection setup timestamps.
Inspect the local /var/log/syslog files on each Compute Engine instance in the project.

questions.explanation: Admin Activity logs capture administrative operations against resource configurations and are accessible via Cloud Logging or BigQuery log sinks for long-term auditing.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Billing export tracks resource consumption costs, not individual administrative audit events or API calls.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC flow logs record network packet metadata, not IAM changes or cloud administration actions.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Local instance syslog files only contain local OS logs, not centralized Google Cloud project-level administrative API actions.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a web application served behind an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Users report intermittent 502 Bad Gateway errors. You verify that the backend instances are running, but the load balancer logs show connection failures to the backends. What should you check first?

options.text: Increase the disk size of the load balancer frontend configuration.
Disable SSL/TLS termination on the load balancer and force HTTP-only traffic.
Change the project billing account ID.
Verify that backend instance firewall rules allow ingress traffic from the HTTP(S) load balancer health check and proxy IP ranges.

questions.explanation: External HTTP(S) Load Balancers require appropriate firewall rules allowing incoming connections from Google Cloud load balancer proxy and health check ranges. Without these rules, proxies cannot reach backends, resulting in 502 errors.

wrongOptionNotes.A: External HTTP(S) load balancers are managed Google services and do not have user-adjustable disk sizes.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling TLS compromises security and does not address backend connection failures caused by missing firewall rules.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Billing account changes do not impact backend routing or proxy connectivity.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company requires all virtual machine instances to synchronize time using a reliable NTP service to prevent authentication failures across distributed services. How should you verify or configure time synchronization on Google Cloud Compute Engine Linux instances?

options.text: Ensure that the internal metadata NTP server (metadata.google.internal) is configured in the guest operating system's time synchronization settings.
Route all NTP traffic through an external public NTP server over the public internet.
Manually set the system clock using the date command every morning via a cron job.
Disable NTP entirely and rely on local hardware crystal clocks.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine provides time synchronization through the metadata server (metadata.google.internal), ensuring instances maintain accurate clocks without needing external internet access.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Using public NTP over the public internet introduces unnecessary latency and security risks compared to Google's internal metadata NTP.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Manual clock setting via cron is inaccurate, prone to drift, and fails to maintain sub-millisecond synchronization.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Hardware clocks drift significantly over time, leading to severe authentication and distributed transaction failures.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your production Node.js application running on a Compute Engine instance suddenly becomes completely unresponsive. Checking the serial port output reveals repetitive Out of Memory (OOM) killer invocations by the Linux kernel terminating the Node process. You need to investigate the exact memory usage patterns leading up to the crashes over the last 24 hours.

options.text: Inspect the boot disk filesystem using another temporary instance to read local application core dump files.
Navigate to Cloud Monitoring metrics explorer, select the VM instance resource, and view the memory/utilization metric alongside log entries filtered for kernel OOM messages.
Check the Cloud Billing console to see if the instance exceeded its allocated monthly budget limit.
Run gcloud compute instances get-serial-port-output and parse the text file for real-time memory consumption percentages.

questions.explanation: Troubleshooting memory exhaustion on Compute Engine requires correlating system metrics (CPU/Memory utilization via Cloud Monitoring) with operating system logs (Cloud Logging capturing kernel syslog and OOM killer terminations).

wrongOptionNotes.A: While core dumps can help debug application code, detaching disks and inspecting them is inefficient and unnecessary for diagnosing standard system-level OOM events.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Budget limits do not restrict instance memory or trigger OOM killer events; they only send financial notifications.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Serial port output displays historical text logs emitted to the console but does not provide real-time or historical numerical percentage metrics for memory consumption.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An external HTTP(S) Load Balancer distributing traffic to a Managed Instance Group (MIG) starts returning HTTP 502 errors for all incoming requests. You need to quickly isolate whether the load balancer can reach the backend instances.

options.text: Examine the Cloud Storage bucket logs where access logs for the project are stored.
Increase the maximum number of instances in the Managed Instance Group autoscaler configuration.
Review the VPC flow logs for the subnet containing the database servers.
Inspect the load balancer's backend health check status in the Google Cloud console or via gcloud to see if instances are passing health checks.

questions.explanation: HTTP 502 errors on an HTTP(S) Load Balancer point directly to communication failures between the load proxy and the backend instances, making health check statuses the primary diagnostic target.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Access logs in Cloud Storage record request metrics after the fact, but checking active backend health statuses provides immediate isolation for connectivity issues.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Scaling up instances will not resolve HTTP 502 errors if existing instances are failing health checks or crashing due to application errors.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The issue involves traffic between the load balancer and the MIG web servers, not necessarily the database tier.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team is alerted that a production Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster is reporting Pod creation failures with 'FailedCreatePodSandBox' errors across multiple worker nodes. You need to determine the root cause.

options.text: Update the external DNS records managed by Cloud DNS.
Check the Kubernetes cluster events and node container runtime logs for resource exhaustion or storage driver failures affecting the node sandbox creation.
Verify the Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions assigned to the Cloud SQL database instance.
Examine the billing export dataset in BigQuery to ensure your project has sufficient funds.

questions.explanation: FailedCreatePodSandBox is a kubelet-level error. Investigating node events, disk pressure, and container runtime health in GKE cluster logs is the correct troubleshooting path.

wrongOptionNotes.A: DNS records control name resolution, whereas Pod sandbox creation is a local node-level operation managed by kubelet.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud SQL IAM permissions do not impact Kubernetes Pod sandbox creation.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Billing states do not cause specific sandbox creation failures inside active worker nodes.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a data processing pipeline where Compute Engine instances write output files to a Cloud Storage bucket. Recently, jobs have started failing with HTTP 403 Forbidden errors when attempting to write objects, although they ran successfully last week.

options.text: Increase the persistent disk size attached to the processing instances.
Review the Cloud Billing console to confirm that the project's credit card is valid.
Check if the VPC firewall rules blocking egress traffic on TCP port 443 were recently added.
Inspect the service account attached to the Compute Engine instances to verify if its IAM roles on the Cloud Storage bucket were recently modified or revoked.

questions.explanation: HTTP 403 is strictly an authentication/authorization error. The most common cause in GCP is a modification to the service account IAM permissions granting access to Cloud Storage.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Disk size limits result in write errors due to lack of space, not HTTP 403 permission errors.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Billing issues result in project suspension or service disablement, not specific HTTP 403 errors from Cloud Storage APIs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC firewall rules block network packets entirely, resulting in connection timeouts or resets, not HTTP 403 authorization responses.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A critical Python application deployed as a serverless service on Cloud Run is throwing uncaught runtime exceptions during startup due to a missing environment variable. You need to quickly locate the exact stack trace and error message.

options.text: Inspect the VPC flow logs for packets dropped destined for the Cloud Run regional endpoint.
Open Cloud Logging, filter by the Cloud Run service resource and severity level ERROR, and inspect the container startup logs.
Access the serial port output of the Cloud Run service via the Google Cloud console.
SSH directly into the underlying container instance using the gcloud compute ssh command.

questions.explanation: Cloud Run logs all container stdout/stderr directly to Cloud Logging, making it the central repository for debugging container startup failures and runtime exceptions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC flow logs capture network metadata, not application-level runtime exceptions or stack traces.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Serial port output is a Compute Engine feature and is not available for Cloud Run services.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless platform; you cannot SSH into the underlying container instances.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your database administrator reports that a production Cloud SQL PostgreSQL instance is experiencing high lock contention and slow query execution. You need to identify which specific SQL queries are currently running and holding locks.

options.text: Restart the Cloud SQL instance immediately via the Google Cloud console.
Export the Cloud SQL audit logs to BigQuery and write a SQL query over the audit logs.
Connect to the Cloud SQL database using the psql client or query the pg_stat_activity system view.
Review the Google Cloud Operations Suite uptime checks configured for the database instance.

questions.explanation: Diagnosing database-level performance issues like lock contention requires querying native database inspection views (e.g., pg_stat_activity) rather than relying solely on cloud infrastructure monitoring.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Restarting the instance forces a failover or drop of connections but does not identify the root cause or problematic queries.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud SQL audit logs track administrative actions and user connections, but not real-time internal query execution states or locks.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Uptime checks only verify basic TCP connectivity and HTTP/HTTPS responses; they cannot inspect internal database queries or locks.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A production Compute Engine instance in your VPC cannot communicate with an internal API server running in another subnet within the same VPC network. You suspect a firewall rule is blocking the traffic. How should you verify if a specific firewall rule is dropping the packets?

options.text: Run the gcloud compute firewall-rules diagnose command to test real-time packet delivery.
Enable firewall rules logging on the applicable firewall rules and inspect the resulting log entries in Cloud Logging.
Inspect the serial console output of the API server instance for firewall drop messages.
Check the project's Billing export to ensure network egress traffic is not rate-limited.

questions.explanation: VPC firewall rules logging is specifically designed to capture connection decisions (allow/drop) made by firewall rules, assisting in network troubleshooting.

wrongOptionNotes.A: There is no gcloud compute firewall-rules diagnose command; the correct tool for active path analysis is Network Intelligence Center Connectivity Tests.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Firewall drops occur at the Google Cloud SDN layer before packets ever reach the guest OS serial console.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Billing data does not reflect real-time firewall packet drops or network connectivity failures.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team receives an alert that a Pub/Sub subscription's unacked message count is rising rapidly, indicating that the subscriber application is failing to process messages. You need to investigate the behavior of the subscriber worker instances.

options.text: Delete the Pub/Sub subscription and recreate it with a larger retention duration.
Modify the IAM policy on the Pub/Sub topic to grant public access.
Review Cloud Monitoring metrics for the subscriber Compute Engine instances (CPU utilization, network traffic) and check application error logs in Cloud Logging.
Increase the Pub/Sub topic message retention period to maximum capacity.

questions.explanation: When Pub/Sub backlog grows, the issue lies in consumer throughput or errors. Checking subscriber CPU, memory, and application error logs is the standard diagnostic path.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Deleting and recreating a subscription results in message loss or disruption without fixing the underlying subscriber processing failure.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Public access does not resolve subscriber processing failures and introduces severe security vulnerabilities.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Extending retention stores messages longer but does not help consumers process the backlog or resolve application errors.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a Google Cloud Storage bucket configured with Object Lifecycle Management rules intended to transition old objects to Nearline storage. You notice that objects older than 30 days are still residing in the Standard storage class, increasing costs. How should you troubleshoot this?

options.text: Verify the exact JSON structure of the lifecycle configuration rules, paying close attention to object age conditions, storage class targets, and matching prefixes.
Check the VPC subnet routing tables to ensure lifecycle requests can reach Google's internal APIs.
Increase the IAM permissions of the user account that originally created the bucket.
Restart the Cloud Storage backend service using the gcloud storage command-line tool.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage lifecycle rules run asynchronously. If rules fail to apply, verifying the syntax, age filters, and matching conditions in the bucket's lifecycle JSON configuration is the correct troubleshooting step.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud Storage lifecycle evaluation is a server-side automated process that does not rely on customer VPC routing tables.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Lifecycle rules are evaluated automatically by the storage service based on bucket configuration, independent of user session permissions.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud Storage is a fully managed multi-tenant Google service; users cannot restart backend storage services.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An application running on a Compute Engine instance attempts to connect to a Cloud SQL instance via its private IP address, but the connection times out. You have verified that both instances are in the same VPC network. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The Cloud SQL instance has automated backups disabled in the maintenance settings.
The local NTP daemon on the Compute Engine instance is unconfigured.
Private Services Access (PSA) peering connection is not established, or VPC firewall rules are blocking traffic on TCP port 3306 or 5432.
The Compute Engine instance lacks a public external IP address assigned to its network interface.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL private IP connectivity relies on Private Services Access (VPC peering) and correct VPC firewall rules. Connection timeouts indicate routing or peering misconfigurations.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Automated backups protect against data loss; they have no impact on network connectivity or routing to private IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Time synchronization issues can cause authentication token drift but do not cause TCP connection timeouts to database private IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Private IP connectivity between resources within the same VPC network does not require public external IP addresses.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team receives an alert that a critical Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster has node disk pressure. Several pods have been evicted. You need to identify which pods or containers are consuming excessive ephemeral storage on the worker nodes.

options.text: Run the gcloud container clusters resize command to increase the cluster node count.
Check the BigQuery audit logs dataset for unauthorized data access queries.
Inspect node conditions using kubectl describe nodes and review metrics in Cloud Monitoring for container ephemeral storage usage.
Reboot the GKE control plane cluster via the Google Cloud console.

questions.explanation: Node disk pressure in GKE requires inspecting node status and using Cloud Monitoring to identify which containers are writing excessive ephemeral data (e.g., logs, temp files).

wrongOptionNotes.A: While scaling out nodes adds capacity, failing to identify what consumed the disk will lead to the same disk pressure on new nodes if rogue workloads persist.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Audit logs track access security, not local container disk utilization.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Rebooting the control plane does not free ephemeral storage consumed by local workloads on worker node disks.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: A batch job running on a Compute Engine instance fails to start because it cannot authenticate against Google Cloud APIs using its attached service account. You need to verify if the instance's metadata server is reachable and if the service account is correctly configured.

options.text: Check the project-wide IAM policy to ensure the project owner has active billing permissions.
Review the VPC flow logs for dropped packets on TCP port 80.
Increase the maximum size of the instance's boot disk to allow metadata caching.
SSH into the instance and run a curl command against the metadata server endpoint (metadata.google.internal) to verify token generation.

questions.explanation: Testing the local metadata server endpoint (metadata.google.internal) via curl is the standard troubleshooting step when a Compute Engine instance fails to authenticate against Google Cloud APIs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Instance metadata and service account tokens are local instance operations and do not depend on project owner billing status.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Metadata requests use special internal routing and do not traverse standard VPC data paths logged by VPC flow logs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Metadata is served via a special-purpose local IP address (169.254.169.254) and does not rely on boot disk capacity.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company's security operations team reports that a specific user account performed unauthorized modifications to production IAM policies. You need to identify the exact timestamp, user email, and changes made.

options.text: Query the Cloud Audit Logs (specifically Admin Activity logs) in Cloud Logging or BigQuery to review IAM policy change events.
Review the VPC flow logs for unusual packet volumes destined for the IAM API endpoint.
Inspect the serial port output of the project's primary Compute Engine virtual machine instance.
Check the Cloud Billing export to see if cost allocation tags were altered.

questions.explanation: Cloud Audit Logs (Admin Activity) track all administrative actions, such as IAM policy modifications, providing full accountability for security investigations.

wrongOptionNotes.B: VPC flow logs record IP traffic metadata, not the content or identity of administrative API calls.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Serial port output contains OS boot messages and console logs for single VMs, not organization-wide IAM policy updates.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Billing exports track cost data, not IAM administrative audit records.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An application deployed on a Managed Instance Group (MIG) behind an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer is failing health checks. Instances are continually being deleted and recreated in a thrashing loop. You need to stabilize the environment to investigate.

options.text: Disable the VPC firewall rules that allow health check probes from Google Cloud load balancers.
Temporarily suspend the autohealing policy on the Managed Instance Group to prevent unhealthy instances from being automatically deleted.
Delete the external HTTP(S) load balancer frontend configuration to stop incoming traffic.
Increase the maximum number of instances in the MIG autoscaler configuration.

questions.explanation: When instances thrash due to autohealing, suspending the MIG autohealing policy is the essential first step to preserve broken instances for debugging.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Disabling health check probe rules will cause all instances to immediately fail health checks, accelerating instance destruction.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Deleting the load balancer disrupts all traffic and does not stop the MIG from thrashing instances if the underlying application health checks continue to fail.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Adding more instances will only cause more instances to fail health checks and enter the recreation loop, worsening thrashing.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a mission-critical web application running on Compute Engine instances behind a regional Managed Instance Group. Users report intermittent connection resets. Upon checking Cloud Monitoring, you notice high CPU utilization on the backend instances during traffic peaks. What is the most effective architectural troubleshooting step?

options.text: Review the Managed Instance Group autoscaling configuration and target CPU utilization thresholds to ensure new instances spin up quickly enough under load.
Downgrade the instance machine types to smaller sizes to reduce compute costs.
Change the project's billing account to a higher tier plan.
Convert all attached persistent disks from standard persistent disks to regional persistent disks.

questions.explanation: High CPU utilization leading to connection drops during traffic peaks points to lagging autoscaling. Reviewing and tuning the MIG autoscaling policies ensures prompt capacity expansion.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Downgrading machine types during peak loads will worsen CPU exhaustion and increase connection failures.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Billing plans do not alter CPU performance limits of individual virtual machine instances.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Regional persistent disks provide synchronous replication across zones for high availability, but they do not solve CPU performance bottlenecks.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company is deploying a secure internal web application on a Compute Engine instance. The application needs to read configuration files from a private Cloud Storage bucket. To adhere strictly to security best practices, how should you grant the instance permission to access the bucket without hardcoding or managing long-lived user credentials?

options.text: Make the Cloud Storage bucket publicly readable so the unauthenticated application can fetch configuration files via standard HTTP GET requests.
Generate a user-managed HMAC key for your personal account, store it in the instance's metadata, and have the application use those keys to authenticate.
Attach a custom service account to the instance with the Storage Object Viewer role on the target bucket, and ensure the instance uses this service account.
Assign the Primitive Editor role at the project level to the default Compute Engine service account.

questions.explanation: Security best practices in Google Cloud dictate using dedicated service accounts with granular, least-privilege IAM roles attached directly to resources like Compute Engine instances rather than embedding credentials or using over-permissioned default accounts.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Making configuration buckets publicly accessible exposes sensitive internal configuration data to the public internet.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Using personal user credentials or HMAC keys tied to user accounts violates security compliance and introduces severe security risks if the keys are leaked.
wrongOptionNotes.D: The project Editor role grants overly broad permissions across all services in the project, violating the principle of least privilege.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization requires that no Compute Engine instances in your production VPC are ever assigned public IP addresses, yet instances must be able to securely download OS updates and packages from public repositories. What is the recommended architectural setup to satisfy this compliance requirement?

options.text: Attach a second network interface (NIC) connected to a public subnet to every private instance.
Disable external IP addresses on the instances and configure Cloud NAT on the VPC router to handle outbound traffic securely.
Configure a bastion host with IP forwarding enabled and route all instance internet traffic through it manually.
Use the Serial Console to stream updates directly to the internal instances.

questions.explanation: Cloud NAT provides managed Network Address Translation for VMs without external IP addresses, allowing secure outbound communication while maintaining strict perimeter security by blocking unsolicited inbound traffic.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Attaching a public NIC exposes the instance directly to the internet with a public IP, violating the requirement.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While a bastion host or NAT instance can work, it requires manual maintenance, high availability configuration, and is prone to bottlenecks compared to managed Cloud NAT.
wrongOptionNotes.D: The serial console is for interactive troubleshooting and text logging, not for routing software package updates.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An external security audit reveals that several Google Cloud IAM custom roles created across your projects contain excessive permissions that exceed the actual needs of the roles. You need to remediate this finding by restricting permissions to adhere to the principle of least privilege. What is the most effective approach?

options.text: Convert all custom roles into primitive roles at the organization level.
Disable the Identity and Access Management API across all projects.
Delete all custom roles entirely and assign all affected users the project Owner role.
Edit the custom roles to remove unused or overly broad permissions, ensuring that each role only contains permissions strictly required for its function.

questions.explanation: Custom IAM roles allow fine-grained permission control. Regular auditing and pruning of unused permissions ensure compliance with least-privilege security postures.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Primitive roles (Viewer, Editor, Owner) are broad and violate least-privilege principles.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling the IAM API breaks all authentication and authorization mechanisms for the project.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Assigning the project Owner role grants absolute control and vastly increases security risk, which is the opposite of the remediation goal.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your security team mandates that all data written to a newly created Cloud Storage bucket must be encrypted using a custom encryption key managed by your team, rather than a Google-managed encryption key. Which feature should you implement?

options.text: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) using Cloud KMS to create and control the encryption key.
Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK) where your application provides the raw AES-256 key on every API request and Google never stores the key.
Enable Google Cloud default account password rotation in the IAM console.
Apply a VPC Service Controls perimeter around the storage bucket.

questions.explanation: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) integrate Cloud Storage with Cloud KMS, letting organizations retain administrative control over the lifecycle, rotation, and usage of encryption keys.

wrongOptionNotes.B: While CSEK gives you complete control, it places the full burden of key management and loss prevention on the client application, whereas CMEK managed via Cloud KMS is the standard enterprise practice for bucket-level compliance.
wrongOptionNotes.C: IAM password rotation applies to user accounts, not Cloud Storage bucket data encryption.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC Service Controls provides perimeter security against data exfiltration, but it does not handle encryption key management.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your development team needs to deploy a new application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Security policy dictates that application pods must not run with root privileges and must drop all Linux capabilities by default. How should you configure the Kubernetes workload?

options.text: Enable Google Cloud Shielded VMs on the underlying node pool.
Grant the default service account cluster-admin permissions before deploying the pod.
Enable Binary Authorization on the GKE cluster.
Configure the Pod security context to set runAsNonRoot: true and drop all capabilities in capabilities.drop.

questions.explanation: Kubernetes security contexts allow administrators to enforce security settings such as running containers as non-root users and dropping dangerous Linux capabilities.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Shielded VMs protect the integrity of the node's bootloader and kernel, but they do not enforce container-level runtime security contexts.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Giving cluster-admin permissions to the service account increases cluster vulnerability and does not restrict container runtime root execution.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Binary Authorization ensures only trusted container images are deployed based on cryptographic signatures, but it does not configure runtime container user privileges.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are configuring a secure Bastion Host (jump box) in your Google Cloud VPC to allow administrators to securely SSH into internal backend instances. Which combination of practices provides the highest security posture?

options.text: Attach a service account with project Owner permissions to the bastion host.
Assign a public static IP address to the bastion host and open TCP port 22 in the firewall to 0.0.0.0/0.
Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) TCP forwarding, remove public IP addresses from the bastion host, and restrict firewall rules to allow SSH only from the IAP netblock.
Configure a VPN tunnel to your corporate office and disable all firewall rules in the VPC.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) secures administrative access by authenticating and authorizing connection attempts before establishing TCP tunnels, eliminating the requirement for public SSH exposure.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Attaching overly permissive service accounts to entry points like bastion hosts increases the blast radius if the bastion is compromised.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Exposing port 22 to the entire internet makes the bastion host extremely vulnerable to brute-force attacks and unauthorized access.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Disabling firewall rules removes internal segmentation, violating security best practices.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company's compliance department requires that all external API calls made by services running inside your VPC are logged and monitored, and that unauthorized data exfiltration attempts are blocked. Which Google Cloud service combination should you deploy?

options.text: VPC Service Controls to create secure perimeters around sensitive data resources, combined with VPC Flow Logs for network traffic auditing.
Enabling project-wide primitive viewer roles for all security auditors.
Cloud NAT logging combined with local firewall rules on every instance.
Cloud Armor security policies applied directly to internal VPC subnets.

questions.explanation: VPC Service Controls helps mitigate the risk of data exfiltration from Google Cloud services, and VPC Flow Logs provide comprehensive network monitoring for compliance audits.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Assigning viewer roles addresses authorization for viewing resources, not data exfiltration prevention or network monitoring.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While Cloud NAT logs outbound traffic, it does not prevent data exfiltration across Google Cloud APIs or enforce perimeter boundaries like VPC Service Controls.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud Armor protects applications behind external HTTP(S) load balancers against web attacks and DDoS, not internal VPC subnets directly.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a Google Cloud project containing sensitive financial data. Security policy states that service accounts must not have long-lived keys downloaded as JSON files. How can developers authenticate applications running outside Google Cloud (such as on-premises servers) to access Google Cloud resources securely?

options.text: Hardcode the administrator password and username directly into the application connection string.
Configure Workload Identity Federation to allow external identity providers to authenticate directly and impersonate a Google Cloud service account.
Generate a master project JSON key, encrypt it with a password, and store it in an unencrypted shared network folder.
Create individual IAM user accounts for every external server and assign them project Owner roles.

questions.explanation: Workload Identity Federation enables secure authentication from external environments to Google Cloud without requiring static, long-lived service account keys.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Hardcoding credentials is an insecure practice that leads to credential leakage.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Storing static service account keys on shared network folders violates security standards and risks credential exposure.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Creating user accounts for automated servers violates compliance and bypasses proper service account management.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your security operations center (SOC) alerts you that an unusual volume of administrative modifications has occurred across multiple projects within your Google Cloud organization. You need to investigate who made the changes and which resources were affected. Where should you look first?

options.text: The serial console output of the primary database instance.
The VPC Flow Logs of the default network.
The Kubernetes cluster pod error logs.
The Organization-level Cloud Audit Logs (Admin Activity and Data Access logs) exported to a centralized BigQuery dataset or Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.explanation: Cloud Audit Logs maintain an immutable record of administrative actions and resource modifications, making them the primary source for security investigations.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Serial console output captures boot and kernel messages for a single instance, not cross-project administrative IAM or resource changes.
wrongOptionNotes.B: VPC Flow Logs record network packet metadata, not IAM changes or administrative resource modifications.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Pod logs record application-level or container runtime logs within a specific cluster, not organization-wide administrative actions.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An application running on a Compute Engine instance needs to read secrets (such as database credentials and API tokens). To comply with organizational security guidelines, these secrets must be encrypted at rest, centrally managed, and automatically versioned. Which Google Cloud service should you use?

options.text: Compute Engine instance metadata server as plain text.
Cloud Storage buckets with public read access enabled.
A plain text text file stored in the root directory of the application boot disk.
Secret Manager

questions.explanation: Secret Manager provides a secure, centralized storage solution for sensitive data with versioning, rotation capabilities, and audit logging.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Storing secrets in instance metadata without encryption or management controls is insecure as anyone with root access on the instance or metadata query capability can read them.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Storing secrets in public buckets exposes them immediately to the internet.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Plain text files on disk lack encryption, versioning, access auditing, and centralized management.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your security team discovers that a Cloud Storage bucket containing sensitive customer Personally Identifiable Information (PII) has public access enabled, violating company policy. You need to immediately remediate the issue and ensure that public access can never be inadvertently enabled on any bucket in the project again. What should you do?

options.text: Disable the Cloud Storage API across the project.
Remove public access from the specific bucket and enforce Public Access Prevention at the project or bucket level.
Change the storage class from Standard to Coldline.
Delete the Cloud Storage bucket and all contained objects permanently.

questions.explanation: Public Access Prevention is a robust compliance guardrail that ensures data stored in Cloud Storage cannot be exposed to the public internet.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Disabling the API breaks all applications relying on Cloud Storage, which is overly disruptive.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Storage classes relate to data retention and cost optimization for access frequency, not access control or security posture.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Deleting the bucket destroys production data, whereas enforcing Public Access Prevention remediates the security risk while preserving the data.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization wants to ensure that all virtual machine disks attached to Compute Engine instances in a specific project are encrypted using keys that your company controls via Cloud KMS, and that developers cannot provision instances with unencrypted or default Google-managed disks. Which feature should you configure?

options.text: Enabling VPC Flow Logs on all subnets.
Granting all developers the project Owner role so they can manually encrypt disks.
An organization policy constraint that requires the use of Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) for Compute Engine disk creation.
A custom bash script running via cron on every instance to check disk encryption status.

questions.explanation: Organization Policy Service allows administrators to set declarative constraints (such as requiring CMEK) to enforce security and compliance standards automatically across Google Cloud resources.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC Flow Logs audit network traffic, not disk encryption compliance.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Project Owner roles grant excessive permissions and do not enforce automated policy constraints.
wrongOptionNotes.D: A cron script is reactive and cannot prevent a developer from initially provisioning an unencrypted disk.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are managing a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. Your security team mandates that communication between pods across different namespaces must be restricted by default, allowing only explicitly authorized traffic. Which Kubernetes feature should you implement?

options.text: Google Cloud VPC firewall rules applied to individual pod IP addresses.
Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) configured for the GKE master endpoint.
Cloud Armor security policies deployed as sidecar containers.
Kubernetes Network Policies

questions.explanation: Kubernetes Network Policies provide internal pod-level security controls, allowing administrators to enforce least-privilege networking between microservices.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC firewall rules operate at the node subnet level, not at the individual container or pod namespace level within a GKE cluster.
wrongOptionNotes.B: IAP secures access to the Kubernetes control plane/API server, not pod-to-pod traffic within the cluster.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud Armor is an HTTP(S) load balancer security policy service, not a Kubernetes pod-level networking control.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An external penetration test report indicates that your Google Cloud environment is vulnerable because service accounts have been assigned overly broad, primitive roles (Owner and Editor) across multiple projects. As the cloud architect, what is the best practice recommendation to remediate this finding?

options.text: Upgrade all service accounts to have project Owner status to ensure no permissions errors occur.
Enable Billing Export to BigQuery to track the cost of service accounts.
Audit the exact permissions needed by each service account and replace primitive roles with predefined or custom IAM roles tailored to specific tasks.
Delete all service accounts and run all applications using user account credentials.

questions.explanation: Primitive roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) grant broad permissions and should be avoided for service accounts in favor of predefined or custom roles tailored to specific service requirements.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Upgrading service accounts to Owner increases security risk and exacerbates the vulnerability identified in the audit.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Billing export helps with cost management, not IAM security hardening.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Using user credentials for automated applications is an insecure anti-pattern and violates operational best practices.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company stores sensitive compliance logs in a Cloud Storage bucket. To satisfy regulatory requirements, the data must be rendered permanently immutable and unmodifiable by any user—including project owners and administrators—for a period of 5 years. Which feature should you configure?

options.text: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) with key rotation enabled.
Cloud Storage Bucket Lock using Object Retention Policy in Governance or Compliance mode.
Enabling IAM conditions to restrict access based on the time of day.
Standard Object Lifecycle Management rules configured to delete files after 5 years.

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage Bucket Lock (Object Retention Policy) enforces WORM (Write Once, Read Many) storage capabilities to meet strict regulatory compliance requirements.

wrongOptionNotes.A: CMEK protects data confidentiality via encryption, but it does not prevent object deletion or enforce WORM (Write Once, Read Many) compliance.
wrongOptionNotes.C: IAM conditions restrict when roles apply, but they do not make stored data immutable or prevent deletion by users with administrative rights.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Lifecycle rules manage automated deletion or class transitions, but they do not prevent premature deletion or tampering by administrators.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages a web application running on a fleet of production Compute Engine instances behind an HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Traffic spikes unpredictably, and you need to optimize monthly infrastructure costs while maintaining fault tolerance and meeting latency SLOs. Which configuration provides the most cost-effective scaling approach for this stateless workload?

options.text: Use a Managed Instance Group with autoscaling based on HTTP load balancer request rates, utilizing standard instances with appropriate minimum and maximum size boundaries, combined with committed use discounts.
Use a Managed Instance Group with autoscaling based on CPU utilization, backed by preemptible instances for baseline load and standard instances for overflow.
Migrate all instances to e2-micro machine types with horizontal autoscaling to maximize instance count and minimize per-instance hourly costs.
Provision a fixed number of oversized n2-standard-32 instances to comfortably handle peak traffic without needing autoscaling or load balancing features.

questions.explanation: For stateless web applications behind an HTTP(S) Load Balancer, Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) with request-based or CPU-based autoscaling offer elasticity. To optimize costs without sacrificing stability, organizations should utilize standard persistent instances matched with Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) for predictable capacity, avoiding unreliable preemptible or spot instances for critical baseline workloads.
