wrongOptionNotes.B: Preemptible instances can be terminated at any time with a 30-second warning, making them unsuitable for baseline load in production web applications due to potential availability disruptions.
wrongOptionNotes.C: e2-micro instances have heavily throttled CPU performance and low memory caps, which will fail under high-throughput production web traffic and violate latency SLOs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Over-provisioning a fixed number of large instances causes severe waste during off-peak hours and fails to provide horizontal elasticity or redundancy.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a high-volume data ingestion pipeline where tens of terabytes of log files are uploaded daily to a regional Cloud Storage bucket. These files are accessed frequently for the first 30 days by an analytics engine, and then accessed rarely for archival purposes over the next year. You need to implement a cost-optimized storage strategy.

options.text: Manually script a daily cron job that downloads objects at day 30, changes their metadata, and re-uploads them to Archive Storage.
Transition objects immediately from Standard Storage to Archive Storage upon upload, and retrieve them whenever the analytics engine needs them.
Configure an Object Lifecycle Management rule to transition objects from Standard Storage to Nearline Storage after 30 days, and then to Coldline Storage after 90 days.
Keep all objects in Standard Storage indefinitely, and query them using BigQuery external tables to avoid copying data.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management allows you to automatically transition objects to lower-cost storage classes (Nearline, Coldline, Archive) based on the age of the object. This ensures you pay for Standard storage only when access is frequent, drastically cutting costs for long-term data retention.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Manual scripts or data movement incur network egress fees, compute overhead, and maintenance burden, whereas Cloud Storage Lifecycle rules handle this natively and free of charge.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Archive Storage has a minimum storage duration of 365 days and retrieval fees. Using it for data that is accessed frequently during the first 30 days will increase overall costs due to high retrieval operations.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storing tens of terabytes in Standard Storage long-term results in unnecessarily high monthly storage costs when archival tiers are significantly cheaper.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a data processing application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The workloads consist of batch jobs that run for a few hours every night. Your finance department has mandated that you cut the infrastructure compute costs for these non-urgent batch jobs by at least 50% without rewriting the application architecture.

options.text: Scale up the existing primary GKE node pool by adding more general-purpose n2-standard-8 instances and rely on horizontal pod autoscaling.
Migrate the batch jobs from GKE to Google App Engine standard environment.
Provision a dedicated GKE node pool configured with Spot VMs, and use Kubernetes node selectors or tolerations to schedule the batch jobs onto these nodes.
Purchase 3-year committed use contracts for Compute Engine memory-optimized instances to handle the nightly batch jobs.

questions.explanation: Spot VMs (and formerly preemptible VMs) provide heavily discounted compute capacity on Compute Engine and GKE. For batch processing jobs that are fault-tolerant or can be restarted, utilizing Spot VM node pools in GKE is the most effective way to drastically reduce operational compute expenditure.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Adding general-purpose on-demand instances will increase infrastructure costs proportionally, failing to meet the mandate for cost reduction.
wrongOptionNotes.B: App Engine standard is designed for web applications and microservices with strict request timeout limits, making it unsuitable for long-running nightly batch jobs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Memory-optimized instances are extremely expensive and typically unnecessary for standard batch jobs, and 3-year commitments lack the flexibility needed if the batch processing requirements change.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your development team has deployed a microservices-based application on Google Cloud Run. The service experiences spiky, unpredictable traffic throughout the day. To prevent cold starts while controlling costs during idle nighttime hours, how should you configure the Cloud Run service settings?

options.text: Set the minimum number of container instances to zero (or a small baseline like 1 during peak business hours) and configure CPU allocation to only be allocated during request processing.
Set the minimum number of container instances to zero, but implement CPU allocation to be always allocated even when not processing requests.
Set the minimum number of container instances to zero and the maximum to zero.
Set the minimum number of container instances to a high fixed number like 20 to ensure zero cold starts 24/7.

questions.explanation: Cloud Run bills you only for the exact resources consumed down to the 100-millisecond. By configuring CPU allocation to occur 'only during request processing' and utilizing scale-to-zero capabilities during idle hours, you eliminate charges for idle container capacity.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Keeping CPU always allocated while min instances is zero is contradictory and still incurs unnecessary charges if instances scale to zero.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Setting the maximum instances to zero means the service cannot accept any requests at all.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Maintaining 20 instances running 24/7 incurs continuous billing for idle resources, violating cost optimization goals during low-traffic periods.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization operates a large data warehouse using BigQuery. Monthly queries scan petabytes of unstructured CSV files stored in Google Cloud Storage, resulting in extremely high query costs. Data analysts run ad-hoc queries frequently against the raw files. What is the most cost-effective architectural change to reduce BigQuery scan costs?

options.text: Migrate all data from Cloud Storage into traditional persistent disk storage attached to a fleet of Compute Engine MySQL database servers.
Upgrade the BigQuery reservation to use flat-rate slot pricing instead of on-demand pricing.
Convert the raw CSV files stored in Cloud Storage into partitioned and clustered Parquet or ORC columnar formats.
Increase the BigQuery cache retention period to 48 hours.

questions.explanation: BigQuery charges for on-demand queries based on the number of bytes read. Storing data in columnar formats like Parquet or ORC, and organizing tables using partitioning and clustering, allows BigQuery to prune unnecessary data blocks, drastically lowering query scan volumes and costs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Moving petabytes of data to relational databases on persistent disks would incur massive storage and operational overhead, and would not scale for analytical queries.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Flat-rate slot pricing is only cost-effective for very large, highly predictable, continuous workloads (typically exceeding 100 slots). For ad-hoc queries scanning variable data, on-demand query pricing or optimized file formats are better starting points.
wrongOptionNotes.D: BigQuery caches query results for approximately 24 hours automatically if the query is identical and underlying data hasn't changed. Ad-hoc exploratory queries rarely hit the exact same cached result set.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a database workload on Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL that has maintained a stable, predictable resource usage pattern for the past six months. Management wants to reduce the ongoing monthly spend for this database instance without reducing performance or availability.

options.text: Convert the Cloud SQL instance to a Development/Testing instance tier to disable automated backups and high availability.
Purchase a 1-year or 3-year Committed Use Discount (CUD) for Cloud SQL database resources.
Migrate the database tables to standard text files stored in a Cloud Storage bucket and query them via custom scripts.
Downsize the instance memory and vCPU specifications during peak business hours to save on hourly rates.

questions.explanation: When workloads are steady and predictable, leveraging Google Cloud's Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) for Cloud SQL provides an effortless way to reduce costs by committing to a baseline level of vCPUs and memory for a 1 or 3-year term.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Disabling high availability and backups on a production database violates operational best practices and introduces unacceptable risk of data loss or extended downtime.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Moving a transactional database to flat files removes ACID compliance, indexing, and transactional integrity, breaking the application.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Resizing a Cloud SQL instance requires a restart, which causes downtime and connection drops, making it entirely inappropriate for fluctuating peak business hours.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a data transfer pipeline that ingests hundreds of gigabytes of logs daily from an on-premises data center into Google Cloud. Currently, data is being transferred over the public internet, resulting in high bandwidth costs and inconsistent throughput. You need a cost-effective and reliable connectivity option for ongoing high-volume data transfer.

options.text: Set up a Dedicated Interconnect or Partner Interconnect connection.
Purchase high-tier enterprise broadband internet from multiple commercial Internet Service Providers.
Compress the logs into password-protected zip files and email them to a Google Cloud service account inbox daily.
Deploy a fleet of Compute Engine proxy instances with external IP addresses to act as load balancers for the incoming logs.

questions.explanation: For high-volume, continuous data transfer between on-premises environments and Google Cloud, Google Cloud Interconnect (Dedicated or Partner) provides lower egress costs and predictable, high-speed performance compared to public internet routes.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Commercial internet still relies on public routing, subject to unpredictable public peering, variable latency, and standard internet egress pricing.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Email is entirely unsuited for hundreds of gigabytes of automated industrial data transfer, failing both reliability and security standards.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Proxy instances on public IPs do not resolve public internet bandwidth pricing tiers and introduce single points of failure and operational complexity.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your engineering team has deployed several exploratory sandbox Compute Engine instances in a development project. Developers frequently forget to shut down these instances over the weekend, resulting in wasted budget. You need an automated, cost-effective way to ensure these instances are only running during standard working hours.

options.text: Hire a night-shift system administrator to manually log into the Google Cloud Console and shut down all instances every evening.
Configure a Managed Instance Group autoscaling policy with a minimum size of zero and zero cooldown period.
Implement Cloud Scheduler combined with Cloud Functions (or Workflows) to automatically issue stop commands to the development instances every evening and start commands every morning.
Delete the Compute Engine instances completely at 5 PM every day and recreate them from custom instance templates every morning using startup scripts.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine charges for stopped instances only for the persistent disk storage; vCPU and memory charges stop immediately when an instance enters the TERMINATED state. Automated scheduling using Cloud Scheduler and Cloud Functions is the optimal serverless pattern for stopping non-production instances during non-working hours.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Manual labor is expensive, error-prone, and inefficient for routine cloud resource management tasks.
wrongOptionNotes.B: MIG autoscalers cannot scale down stateful or standard development VMs to absolute zero based strictly on a time-of-day clock unless specifically tied to custom metrics.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Recreating instances daily introduces overhead with disk provisioning, IP re-assignment, and potential state loss, whereas simply stopping and starting instances preserves persistent disks without incurring compute charges.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company stores millions of customer invoice PDF documents in a Google Cloud Storage bucket. These invoices must be retained for 7 years for compliance, but are rarely accessed after the first 30 days. To minimize storage costs, you need to select the most economical storage class for this long-term retention.

options.text: Standard Storage
Nearline Storage
Coldline Storage
Archive Storage

questions.explanation: Cloud Storage Archive is the lowest-cost, highly durable storage service for data archiving, online backup, and disaster recovery. For data retained for years with minimal access, Archive Storage provides maximum cost savings.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Standard Storage is optimized for active data that is accessed frequently, making it the most expensive tier for 7-year retention.
wrongOptionNotes.B: While Nearline is cheaper than Standard, it is intended for data accessed roughly once a month. Archive Storage offers significantly lower monthly storage costs for 7-year archival compliance.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Coldline Storage is designed for data accessed at most once a year, but its price point is higher than Archive Storage, which is specifically tailored for multi-year compliance retention.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your data engineering team is running heavy Spark and Hadoop batch analytics jobs on Google Cloud. The jobs process massive datasets and run on Datroc cluster instances. Because these jobs are fault-tolerant and can be restarted if interrupted, you want to minimize the compute expenditure of the Dataproc worker nodes.

options.text: Configure the Dataproc cluster to use a primary worker pool consisting of standard on-demand instances and a secondary worker pool consisting of Spot VMs.
Reduce the network bandwidth tier of the Dataproc instances to the lowest possible setting.
Disable the Dataproc cluster when not in use and recreate the entire cluster manually via the command line for every single batch run.
Configure all master and worker nodes in the Dataproc cluster to run exclusively on sole-tenant nodes.

questions.explanation: Dataproc allows you to leverage Spot VMs in secondary worker pools. Because analytical batch frameworks like Hadoop and Spark can tolerate worker node loss, utilizing Spot VMs for secondary workers cuts processing compute costs dramatically.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Hadoop and Spark distributed data processing frameworks require high-throughput inter-node network communication; throttling network bandwidth will cause shuffle bottlenecks and job failures.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While cluster deletion saves storage/compute, rebuilding clusters from scratch every time adds unnecessary pipeline latency and complexity compared to native scaling and Spot worker pools.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Sole-tenant nodes dedicate physical hardware servers exclusively to your project, which is much more expensive and defeats cost optimization.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company operates an application on a managed instance group of Compute Engine instances. Analysis of Cloud Monitoring metrics reveals that the instances are consistently running at less than 15% CPU utilization during both peak and off-peak hours, yet they were provisioned using large n2-standard-16 machine types. What is the most appropriate action to optimize costs?

options.text: Attach additional Persistent Disk SSD volumes to each instance to improve IOPS performance.
Right-size the instances by modifying the instance template to use a smaller machine type (such as n2-standard-4 or e2-standard-4) and rolling out the update to the managed instance group.
Enable preemptible instances across the entire managed instance group without changing the machine type.
Increase the maximum number of instances in the managed instance group autoscaler.

questions.explanation: Right-sizing is a fundamental cost-optimization practice. When monitoring reveals low resource utilization (low CPU, memory, or network usage), downsizing to a smaller machine type or custom instance configuration eliminates wasted spend.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Adding storage disks does nothing to fix over-provisioned CPU and memory and will only increase storage costs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While preemptibles reduce cost, keeping instances oversized (n2-standard-16) means you are still paying for excessive vCPUs and memory that the application does not need.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Increasing maximum instances when existing instances are underutilized will only add more idle capacity, increasing costs.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages a web application that stores session files and user uploads in a Cloud Storage bucket. Over time, millions of temporary thumbnail files accumulate in the bucket and are never cleaned up, consuming significant storage capacity and increasing costs. How can you automate the deletion of these temporary files efficiently?

options.text: Create an Object Lifecycle Management configuration with a rule that matches objects with a specific prefix or age (e.g., older than 7 days) and specifies the 'Delete' action.
Manually navigate the Cloud Storage browser in the Google Cloud Console each week and select files by hand.
Write a custom Python script that runs locally on your workstation every morning, lists all objects in the bucket, filters by prefix, and deletes them one by one via API calls.
Delete the entire Cloud Storage bucket every week and recreate it from scratch using a deployment script.

questions.explanation: Object Lifecycle Management allows you to define rules that automatically delete or transition objects based on age, prefix, or custom time parameters. This native feature eliminates the need for external cron scripts or manual maintenance.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual deletion is impractical, tedious, and error-prone for millions of files.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Running scripts locally is inefficient, depends on a local machine being online, incurs network transit overhead, and is prone to script interruption.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Deleting the entire bucket would destroy permanent user uploads and session data alongside temporary thumbnails, causing catastrophic data loss.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization is reviewing network egress charges across your Google Cloud projects. You notice that a high volume of data is being transferred between Compute Engine instances located in different zones within the same region, resulting in unexpected networking costs. How can you mitigate regional cross-zone traffic costs?

options.text: Move all Compute Engine instances into a single global VPC subnet spanning multiple continents.
Disable internal DNS resolution across the Virtual Private Cloud.
Configure all instances to use external IP addresses instead of internal IP addresses for inter-service communication.
Redesign the application architecture so that tightly coupled services communicate within the same availability zone where possible, or evaluate pricing rules for intra-regional traffic.

questions.explanation: Understanding Google Cloud networking pricing is crucial for cost optimization. Data transfer between zones within the same region incurs standard cross-zone data transfer fees. Co-locating tightly coupled services in the same zone avoids these charges.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Subnets in Google Cloud are regional, not global, and cross-continent traffic incurs significantly higher inter-region and cross-continent egress charges.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling internal DNS breaks application service discovery without altering network routing paths or reducing traffic volume.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Using external IP addresses for internal traffic routes data through external paths and incurs higher external internet egress charges, worsening costs.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a database cluster on Compute Engine. Due to compliance mandates, you must maintain incremental daily backups and full weekly backups of the primary persistent disks. However, retaining these snapshots indefinitely has caused backup storage costs to skyrocket. What is the most cost-effective solution?

options.text: Upgrade the persistent disks from standard persistent disk (pd-standard) to extreme persistent disk (pd-extreme).
Configure a Snapshot Schedule (Resource Policies) with an automatic retention policy (e.g., delete snapshots older than 30 days).
Manually export all snapshots as raw virtual disk files into Standard Cloud Storage buckets every day.
Disable all disk snapshots entirely to avoid incurring any snapshot storage charges.

questions.explanation: Compute Engine persistent disk snapshots are incremental, but storing them indefinitely leads to high costs. Using Compute Engine Resource Policies to define automated snapshot schedules with retention policies ensures old snapshots are pruned automatically.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Extreme persistent disks are designed for extremely high IOPS database requirements and carry a massive cost premium, which does not address snapshot storage accumulation.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Manual exports add operational complexity and incur conversion and storage overhead that is far more expensive than native incremental snapshots with lifecycle management.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Disabling backups violates compliance mandates and puts the organization at high risk of data loss during a failure.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your engineering team needs to run a high-performance computing (HPC) simulation that requires thousands of CPU cores simultaneously for a 48-hour period. After 48 hours, the job completes and the infrastructure is no longer needed. To minimize costs, what is the best strategy for provisioning the compute instances?

options.text: Provision the required instances using a Managed Instance Group backed by Spot VMs for the duration of the batch run, leveraging flexible batch tooling.
Provision the required thousands of cores using standard on-demand Compute Engine instances with standard persistent disks.
Purchase 3-year Committed Use Discounts for compute-optimized instance families.
Deploy the simulation across multiple regional Google Kubernetes Engine clusters using only standard e2-medium nodes.

questions.explanation: For short-term, large-scale, fault-tolerant batch or HPC workloads, Spot VMs offer the maximum discount available on Google Cloud, allowing you to spin up thousands of cores for a fraction of the on-demand cost.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Running thousands of on-demand cores for a short, intensive HPC job without discounts or spot pricing leads to unnecessarily high peak expenditure.
wrongOptionNotes.C: A 3-year commitment for a workload that runs for only 48 hours results in paying for nearly three years of unused compute capacity.
wrongOptionNotes.D: e2-medium nodes lack the massive CPU and memory density required for heavy HPC simulations and would severely bottleneck the compute job.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company operates a global web application fronted by an External HTTP(S) Load Balancer, backed by Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) in both us-central1 and europe-west1. To implement an active-passive disaster recovery strategy, you need to configure traffic routing so that users are automatically failed over to europe-west1 only if the primary us-central1 backend becomes completely unhealthy. How should you configure the load balancing components?

options.text: Create two backend services, add them to a backend bucket, and configure weighted round-robin routing.
Use a URL map with path matchers to send all traffic to us-central1 by default, and use HTTP redirection rules for failover.
Configure a single global backend service with both regional MIGs, add the us-central1 backend with maximum capacity, and add the europe-west1 backend configured with a failover mode setting.
Configure a global backend service with both MIGs, set the capacity scaler for europe-west1 to 0%, and rely on automatic failover policies in the backend service configuration.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud External HTTP(S) Load Balancers support configuring backend services with primary and failover backends. When the primary regional backend instances fail health checks beyond the configured threshold, traffic is automatically routed to the designated failover backend region.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Backend buckets are for serving static content from Cloud Storage, not for managing Compute Engine instance group backends.
wrongOptionNotes.B: URL maps with HTTP redirection do not perform dynamic health checking or seamless transport-layer failover for backend infrastructure.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Setting the capacity scaler to 0% prevents traffic from going to the region entirely, but it does not act as a failover target because zero capacity means the region cannot accept failover traffic dynamically.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your production PostgreSQL database runs on Cloud SQL in the us-east1 region. To prepare for regional disasters, you have established a cross-region read replica in us-west1. An unexpected major outage impacts us-east1, and you need to promote the us-west1 replica to become the standalone primary database. What is the correct procedure to achieve this with minimal data loss?

options.text: Execute a failover operation using the gcloud sql instances failover command targeting the read replica.
Delete the primary instance in us-east1, then run the gcloud sql instances promote-replica command on the us-west1 replica.
Create a new Cloud SQL instance in us-west1, restore the latest automated backup from us-east1 to it, and reconfigure applications to point to the new instance.
Update the connection string in your applications to point to the read replica's IP address and keep it in read-only mode.

questions.explanation: To recover from a regional outage using a cross-region read replica, you must promote the read replica to a primary standalone instance using the promote-replica action. This detaches it from the replication stream and enables read-write operations.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The failover command is exclusively used for high-availability (HA) instances with a standby in the same region, not for promoting cross-region read replicas.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While this works, restoring from a backup is much slower and risks higher RPO than promoting an existing live cross-region replica.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Read replicas cannot accept write traffic. Applications require a fully promoted writable primary database.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages a multi-region deployment across us-central1 and europe-west1. Persistent disks containing critical application state must be replicated across these regions. Because standard Persistent Disks are zonal, what is the recommended approach to achieve near-zero RPO and low RTO for block storage across regions?

options.text: Attach a single Persistent Disk simultaneously to instances in both us-central1 and europe-west1 in multi-writer mode.
Use Local SSDs with built-in cross-region mirroring enabled via gcloud.
Configure standard Persistent Disks to replicate synchronously across us-central1 and europe-west1.

Use regional Persistent Disks replicated synchronously across two zones within the same region, and implement an application-level or storage-level asynchronous replication mechanism to the remote region.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud Persistent Disks provide regional replication across zones within the same region, but do not natively replicate synchronously across different regions. Cross-region disaster recovery requires asynchronous database replication, snapshot scheduling, or application-level syncing.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Multi-writer mode is restricted to multiple VMs within the same zone and does not span across regions or even different zones.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Local SSDs are ephemeral, physically attached to the host machine, and do not support mirroring or cross-region replication.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Zonal and regional persistent disks can replicate across zones in a single region, but cross-region synchronous replication is not supported by Google Cloud block storage.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a stateless API service deployed across two Managed Instance Groups in asia-east1 and us-west1, fronted by a global external HTTP(S) Load Balancer. During a regional network partition affecting asia-east1, health checks fail, and traffic is successfully rerouted to us-west1. However, users experience elevated error rates because the us-west1 MIG is not provisioned with enough instances to handle the sudden doubling of global traffic. What architectural adjustment should you implement to resolve this resilience issue?

options.text: Double the static size of the us-west1 MIG so it always runs at 50% capacity during normal operations.
Enable autoscaling on both MIGs based on CPU utilization and configure appropriate minimum and maximum instance limits with headrooms to handle regional loss scenarios.
Switch the load balancer from global external HTTP(S) load balancing to regional external HTTP(S) load balancing.
Configure the load balancer to drop excess traffic instead of forwarding it when a region fails.

questions.explanation: When designing multi-region architectures for failover, capacity planning must account for the loss of a region. If one region goes down, surviving regions must have sufficient maximum autoscaling limits and compute headroom to handle the transferred load.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Running instances at half capacity permanently doubles baseline compute costs, which is inefficient compared to using dynamic autoscaling.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Regional load balancers cannot fail over across regions, which would eliminate cross-region resilience entirely.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Dropping traffic defeats the purpose of multi-region resilience and high availability.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization requires that a critical stateful application maintain an RPO (Recovery Point Objective) of under 1 hour and an RTO (Recovery Time Objective) of under 15 minutes in the event of a regional disaster. The application runs on Compute Engine instances with Cloud SQL. Which backup and replication configuration aligns best with these requirements?

options.text: Configure single-zone zonal persistent disks with no snapshots, relying on local log shipping.
Configure automated daily Cloud SQL backups and take a weekly snapshot of persistent disks.
Deploy a cross-region Cloud SQL read replica for rapid promotion, and use Cloud Storage multi-regional buckets for application state alongside automated hourly disk snapshots.
Rely entirely on manual backups taken once a month by an operations engineer.

questions.explanation: To achieve strict RPO (<1 hour) and RTO (<15 minutes), architectures must utilize continuous asynchronous replication (such as Cloud SQL cross-region replicas) and frequent automated snapshot policies or multi-regional storage.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Zonal disks with no backups or replication offer zero protection against regional disasters.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Daily backups yield an RPO of up to 24 hours, failing the requirement of an RPO under 1 hour.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Manual monthly backups result in an unacceptable RPO of 30 days and high manual RTO.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a disaster recovery environment in europe-west3 for a primary production environment in us-central1. Compute Engine instances in europe-west3 are kept powered off to reduce costs, but their attached persistent disks must be kept synchronized with the primary environment. What is the most cost-effective and operationally resilient way to maintain synchronized disk data in the DR region?

options.text: Use Cloud Storage Transfer Service to mirror persistent disks directly.

Configure Cloud Backup and DR Service or automated Cloud Storage snapshot schedules to replicate disk snapshots asynchronously to the target region, and use them to provision instances only when failover is triggered.
Keep the DR instances running 24/7 so they can continuously rsync files over internal IP addresses.
Configure Cloud Storage backup schedules to export disk images manually every hour.

questions.explanation: For warm or cold disaster recovery environments, maintaining running compute instances is costly. Instead, using automated snapshot schedules or Google Cloud Backup and DR Service ensures block storage data is synchronized to the DR region while compute costs remain zero until failover.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Storage Transfer Service transfers objects to and from Cloud Storage, not block-level persistent disks.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Running compute instances 24/7 just for file synchronization defeats the cost-saving intent of a cold or warm standby DR strategy.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Manual exports are prone to failure and do not provide continuous synchronization.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are testing a multi-region failover scenario for a web application. Your external HTTP(S) Load Balancer has backends in us-central1 and europe-west1. During your drill, you simulate a failure in us-central1 by blocking its health check probes, but traffic fails to switch over to europe-west1, and users continue to see connection errors. What should you check first in the load balancer configuration?

options.text: Verify that the SSL certificate attached to the target HTTPS proxy is globally valid.
Verify that the backend service health check firewall rules are properly configured to allow traffic from Google Cloud health check IP ranges.
Ensure that Cloud DNS has the correct A records pointing to the backend instances.
Check if Cloud Logging is enabled on the load balancer.

questions.explanation: When troubleshooting load balancer failover issues, verifying health check configuration and firewall rules is critical. Google Cloud health checker probes must be permitted through firewall rules (ranges 35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22) for the load balancer to accurately assess backend health.

wrongOptionNotes.A: An invalid SSL certificate causes handshake or trust errors, not a failure in regional backend routing or failover.
wrongOptionNotes.C: External HTTP(S) Load Balancers use anycast IPs managed by Google's frontend network, not direct Cloud DNS records pointing to backend instance IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud Logging records traffic logs but does not impact health check evaluations or traffic routing decisions.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team is designing a disaster recovery plan for a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) application. The application stores persistent state in a PostgreSQL database and static assets in Cloud Storage. If the primary GKE cluster in asia-northeast1 suffers an unrecoverable outage, you need to spin up a new GKE cluster in asia-southeast1 and restore operations. Which component requires the most careful synchronization planning to ensure a minimal RPO?

options.text: The persistent database data managed by Cloud SQL or cross-cluster database replication streams.
The Kubernetes Service accounts and IAM role bindings.
The GKE cluster control plane node version and Kubernetes YAML manifests.
The container image tags stored in Artifact Registry.

questions.explanation: In containerized architectures on GKE, stateless workloads and cluster configurations are easily redeployed via GitOps or CI/CD. The primary challenge in disaster recovery is ensuring transactional data (databases) and persistent storage are synchronized to meet the RPO target.

wrongOptionNotes.B: IAM and service accounts are project-level resources, not regional, so they do not need to be replicated per cluster.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Kubernetes manifests and control plane configurations can be easily reapplied via CI/CD pipelines (GitOps) and do not determine data RPO.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Artifact Registry is globally accessible across regions within a project, so container images are already available anywhere without regional replication overhead.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your application runs on Compute Engine instances behind a regional Managed Instance Group (MIG) in us-central1. You want to ensure high availability against zone failures within the region. How should you configure the MIG?

options.text: Configure a zonal MIG and manually copy instance templates across three different zones.
Configure a regional MIG that distributes instances across multiple zones within us-central1.
Deploy three separate zonal MIGs and attach them to three independent load balancers.
Set up a global MIG spanning us-central1 and europe-west1.

questions.explanation: Regional Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) distribute virtual machine instances across multiple zones within a single region. If a zone fails, the regional MIG automatically recreates instances in the remaining healthy zones within the region, ensuring high availability.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Zonal MIGs operate within a single zone and do not provide automated multi-zone failover or balancing.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Managing three separate MIGs and load balancers adds unnecessary complexity compared to using a single regional MIG.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Managed Instance Groups are regional or zonal; 'global MIGs' do not exist in Google Cloud terminology.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company operates a critical web service that must withstand a complete Google Cloud region outage. You deploy identical infrastructure in us-east4 and us-west1, fronted by a global external HTTP(S) Load Balancer. You want to ensure that if us-east4 experiences an outage, client sessions stored in the application instances are not abruptly terminated or lost. What is the best architecture to handle user session state during regional failover?

options.text: Store sessions in local SSDs attached to the primary Compute Engine instances.
Rely on sticky sessions configured on the global external HTTP(S) Load Balancer.

Store user session data in an external, highly available distributed data store such as Memorystore for Redis or Cloud Spanner, rather than locally on individual Compute Engine instance disks or memory.
Configure local file-based session replication via rsync every minute between us-east4 and us-west1 instances.

questions.explanation: For multi-region architectures to be truly resilient, application tiers must be stateless. Storing session data in centralized, highly available, and replicated data stores like Memorystore for Redis or Cloud Spanner prevents session loss during regional failovers.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Local SSDs are ephemeral and tied to a specific host and zone, making them useless for cross-region failover.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Sticky sessions tie a user to a specific backend instance or region; when that region fails, sticky sessions break and sessions are lost.
wrongOptionNotes.D: File-based sync between running instances across regions is slow, fragile, and prone to race conditions under heavy load.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are reviewing the disaster recovery posture for a critical batch data processing pipeline that runs daily on Compute Engine. The pipeline reads from Cloud Storage and writes results to BigQuery. The business requires that if a regional disaster occurs, the processing pipeline can be re-initiated in a secondary region within 2 hours. Which resource configuration is most critical to ensure this RTO?

options.text: Copying all BigQuery datasets to an on-premises data center every hour.
Configuring Cloud NAT with static IP addresses in both regions.
Keeping 100 Compute Engine instances running idle 24/7 in the secondary region.
Pre-scripting and testing the infrastructure deployment using Terraform or Deployment Manager in the secondary region so that compute resources can be spun up on demand.

questions.explanation: For workloads that do not require instant active-active failover, an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) approach using Terraform enables rapid, automated deployment of compute resources in a secondary region during a disaster, balancing cost efficiency with an acceptable RTO.

wrongOptionNotes.A: BigQuery data is already stored durably across multiple zones/regions; copying it off-cloud is redundant and expensive.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Cloud NAT assists with outbound internet connectivity, but it does not address compute infrastructure provisioning speed for disaster recovery.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Running idle compute instances continuously for a batch workload that runs once a day wastes significant budget.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your production application uses Cloud SQL for MySQL with High Availability (HA) enabled in us-central1. An underlying hardware failure occurs in the primary zone, triggering an automatic failover to the secondary zone. How does this failover affect your application's connection to the database?

options.text: Applications must be restarted to update their hardcoded IP addresses to the new standby instance.
All active transactions are preserved and seamlessly migrated without any connection interruption.
The Cloud SQL instance IP address remains the same, but active connections are dropped, requiring application-level connection pooling and retry logic to reconnect seamlessly.
The database becomes entirely read-only until manual administrative intervention occurs.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL High Availability manages regional failover automatically by switching the service IP to the standby instance. Although the IP address remains constant, active TCP connections drop during the transition, requiring application-level connection retry logic.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud SQL High Availability uses automatic IP failover, meaning application IP configurations do not need manual updates.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Failover involves a brief interruption where active uncommitted transactions are rolled back and connections are reset.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud SQL HA failover is fully automated and promotes the standby to primary with read-write capabilities automatically.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your engineering team is implementing a backup strategy for persistent disks attached to production databases. Company policy mandates that backups must be protected against accidental deletion or malicious tampering by rogue administrators. How should you configure your Cloud Storage or Compute Engine disk snapshots to meet this requirement?

options.text: Store all snapshots in a public Cloud Storage bucket with uniform bucket-level access enabled.
Apply CMEK (Customer-Managed Encryption Keys) using Cloud KMS with a strict IAM policy.
Enable Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management rules with retention locks.
Utilize snapshot retention policies with resource-level locks (e.g., Cloud Storage bucket retention or Compute Engine snapshot policies with secure access controls).

questions.explanation: Protecting backups against malicious deletion requires a combination of least-privilege IAM access controls (restricting snapshot deletion permissions) and utilizing snapshot policies or retention locks where supported across Google Cloud storage services.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Making backup buckets public is a severe security violation that exposes sensitive backup data to the public internet.
wrongOptionNotes.B: CMEK protects data confidentiality via encryption keys, but it does not prevent a snapshot resource itself from being deleted unless combined with specific retention policies.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Object lifecycle management and retention locks apply to objects in Cloud Storage buckets, not directly to Compute Engine disk snapshots.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a mission-critical web application running on Compute Engine instances behind a global external HTTP(S) Load Balancer. During a major traffic surge, you notice that latency spikes and some backend instances become unresponsive due to CPU exhaustion. To improve system resilience and prevent cascading failures without adding more hardware, what load balancing feature should you configure?

options.text: Switch from HTTPS to HTTP to reduce CPU overhead from SSL handshakes.
Disable health checks so the load balancer stops probing busy instances.
Configure backend capacity limits and connection draining alongside autoscaling.
Increase the load balancer timeout setting to 600 seconds.

questions.explanation: Configuring backend capacity limits on your load balancer backends ensures that the load balancer stops sending requests to overloaded instance groups, protecting them from cascading failure and allowing traffic to be routed elsewhere.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Downgrading production traffic to unencrypted HTTP is a severe security violation and does not solve backend capacity issues.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling health checks prevents the load balancer from detecting unhealthy instances, leading to increased user errors.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Increasing timeouts keeps failing connections open longer, exacerbating resource exhaustion and worsening latency.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization requires that all data stored in Cloud Storage for disaster recovery purposes must be stored redundantly across multiple geographic locations separated by at least hundreds of kilometers, while remaining accessible for reads even if an entire region fails. Which storage class should you select?

options.text: Standard Storage configured in a single region.
Nearline Storage in a dual-region configuration.
Coldline Storage in a single zone.
Multi-Regional Storage (Multi-Region bucket configuration).

questions.explanation: Google Cloud Multi-Region and Dual-Region storage classes store data redundantly across multiple geographic regions, ensuring that if a catastrophic disaster strikes one region, data remains accessible in the secondary region with minimal RPO and RTO.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Regional storage stores data within a single Google Cloud region, offering no protection against a complete regional disaster.
wrongOptionNotes.B: While dual-region storage provides multi-location redundancy, Nearline is optimized for data accessed less than once a month, whereas Multi-Region or Standard Dual-Region is better suited for high-frequency active disaster recovery reads.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Coldline and single-zone configurations do not provide cross-region redundancy.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a containerized service deployed on Google Cloud. You need to configure a log-based metric in Cloud Logging to track the frequency of application error logs containing a specific exception string. You created the metric using gcloud, but when you query it in Metrics Explorer, you notice that no data points are appearing despite active traffic throwing those errors. What is the most likely cause of this issue?

options.text: Log-based metrics must be explicitly enabled inside the Cloud Run or GKE container configuration environment variables before they can capture stdout streams.
Log-based metrics require a corresponding log sink to be configured to export logs to BigQuery before Metrics Explorer can index them.
The metric query used an invalid advanced log filter syntax, causing Cloud Logging to silently drop the metric definition.
Log-based metrics only evaluate logs ingested after the metric was created and do not parse historical log entries retroactively.

questions.explanation: Cloud Logging log-based metrics process incoming log entries in real-time as they are written to the logging API. They do not evaluate historical logs that were ingested before the metric resource was provisioned.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Logging automatically captures stdout/stderr streams from container platforms without requiring container environment modifications.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Log-based metrics operate directly on the Cloud Logging stream and do not depend on log sinks or BigQuery exports to function.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Invalid filters generally return validation errors during creation rather than silently failing to accumulate data without error output.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a web application running on a regional Managed Instance Group (MIG) of Compute Engine instances. You recently updated the instance template to include a new version of your application code and performed a rolling update on the MIG. Users are now reporting intermittent 502 Bad Gateway errors. Upon investigation, you discover that the instances are passing their load balancer health checks immediately upon boot, but the application server takes up to 60 seconds to fully initialize and bind to port 80. How should you resolve this issue?

options.text: Increase the maximum number of instances in the Managed Instance Group to absorb the slow boot times.
Configure a load balancer-based health check with an appropriate response timeout value.
Modify the startup script to sleep for 60 seconds before executing any application commands.
Implement application-based health checks in the MIG configuration and set an appropriate initial delay.

questions.explanation: To prevent instances from receiving production traffic before their application stacks are fully operational, you must use application-based health checks within your Managed Instance Group configuration to coordinate readiness during rolling updates.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Adding more instances will not solve the underlying race condition where newly booted instances accept traffic before the application is ready.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Load balancer health checks test connectivity and response codes, but they do not account for application startup delay if the port is already listening prematurely.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Using a sleep command in a startup script blocks the instance startup agent and is an anti-pattern that delays deployment without providing true application readiness feedback to the MIG.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages a Compute Engine instance running a crucial batch processing script. The instance frequently runs out of memory during peak execution, causing the Linux kernel's Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer to terminate the primary process. You need to capture a snapshot of the system state, including memory and disk usage metrics, specifically during these failure events for root cause analysis. What is the best way to achieve this using native Google Cloud operations tools?

options.text: Create a Cloud Monitoring uptime check targeting the local loopback interface of the virtual machine.
Configure an autoscaling policy on the single instance to add a secondary Compute Engine instance when memory utilization is high.
Set up a Cloud Logging alert policy combined with a notification channel to email the team whenever memory usage crosses 90%.
Install the Cloud Monitoring agent and configure it to collect custom OS metrics and system logs, then monitor the syslog for OOM killer events.

questions.explanation: The Google Cloud Operations suite relies on the Operations agent installed on Compute Engine instances to gather detailed OS telemetry, log system events like the Linux OOM killer, and send them to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging for analysis.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Uptime checks are designed to monitor external IP addresses or load balancer endpoints via HTTP/TCP, not internal OS kernel states.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Compute Engine autoscaling only applies to Managed Instance Groups, not standalone single instances.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Standard Cloud Logging and Monitoring alert policies capture resource metrics at 1-minute or 60-second intervals, which frequently miss rapid OOM spikes that occur instantly.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company runs a database cluster on Google Cloud. You have set up Cloud Monitoring alerts to notify your on-call engineers via SMS when CPU utilization exceeds 85% for more than 5 consecutive minutes. Recently, a brief 30-second traffic spike triggered multiple alerts, waking up engineers unnecessarily, even though the database recovered automatically. How should you adjust the alert policy configuration to prevent these false positives while retaining reliability?

options.text: Modify the alert policy condition duration to require that the condition persists for a longer continuous window before firing.
Switch the notification channel from SMS to an email distribution list so engineers are less disturbed.
Adjust the alignment period and reduce the aggregation window to capture 10-second metric granularities.
Disable the alert policy entirely and rely on daily Cloud Monitoring dashboard reviews.

questions.explanation: To eliminate noise from transient traffic spikes, you should configure the condition duration of the Cloud Monitoring alert policy so that it only triggers when a metric threshold is breached continuously over a sustained timeframe.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Changing the notification channel masks the underlying misconfiguration of the alert trigger condition rather than fixing it.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Increasing granularity makes the system more sensitive to transient spikes, worsening the false positive issue.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Disabling alerts removes proactive monitoring and violates basic operational availability practices.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You manage a web application deployed on a Managed Instance Group behind an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Users complain that they intermittently experience connection timeouts when uploading large files (>100MB). Standard HTTP requests work without issue. What is the most likely configuration issue causing this behavior?

options.text: The firewall rules attached to the instances are blocking TCP window scaling extensions.
The backend service timeout setting on the HTTP(S) Load Balancer is set too low, causing the connection to drop before large file transfers complete.
The Cloud CDN cache configuration is rejecting files larger than 10MB.
The Managed Instance Group autoscaler is scaling down instances too quickly during uploads.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud HTTP(S) Load Balancers have a configurable backend service timeout (defaulting to 30 seconds). For applications handling large uploads or long-lived requests, this timeout must be explicitly increased to prevent premature connection termination.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Google Cloud VPC firewalls permit standard TCP option headers like window scaling by default.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Uploads (HTTP POST/PUT requests) are not cached by Cloud CDN, so CDN configuration limits do not impact upload flows.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Autoscaling is driven by CPU utilization or load balancing capacity, which typically remains elevated during large file uploads.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your organization operates a mission-critical workload on Compute Engine. Due to a recent audit finding, you need to ensure that all administrative activity, data access, and system calls on your Linux instances are securely captured and retained in an immutable log bucket that cannot be modified even by project administrators. Which Google Cloud service combination should you implement?

options.text: Write a custom cron job on each virtual machine to copy /var/log/auth.log to a standard Cloud Storage bucket every hour.
Install a third-party SIEM agent on each instance and export text logs to local ephemeral disks.
Configure Cloud Audit Logs with Data Access logging enabled, and stream the logs into a Cloud Storage bucket protected by a Bucket Lock (Retention Policy).
Enable Google Cloud VPC Flow Logs and set up an alert policy when unauthorized IP addresses connect to the instances.

questions.explanation: To meet strict compliance and immutability mandates, organizations use Cloud Audit Logs combined with Cloud Storage Bucket Locks (Object Retention Policies) to ensure logs cannot be altered or deleted prematurely.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Custom cron scripts are prone to tampering, single points of failure, and do not provide cryptographically secure immutability guarantees.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Ephemeral disks lose data upon instance termination and do not satisfy compliance requirements for centralized immutable retention.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC Flow Logs capture network flow metadata, not administrative activity or application-level system calls.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: You are troubleshooting a performance issue on a Linux Compute Engine instance running a heavy analytical workload. You suspect the instance is experiencing CPU throttling due to reaching its allocated core limits or credit exhaustion (if using E2/N1/N2 types). Where can you look in Google Cloud to verify if CPU throttling or resource contention is occurring at the hypervisor level?

options.text: Review the Cloud Billing reports to check if the instance type was recently downsized.
Examine the instance's serial port output logs for kernel panic warnings.
Check Cloud Monitoring metrics for the instance, specifically looking at 'CPU steal time' or 'CPU utilization' over time.
Inspect the VPC flow logs for packet drop counters associated with the instance's network interface.

questions.explanation: Cloud Monitoring automatically collects hypervisor-level metrics for Compute Engine instances. Metrics such as CPU utilization and CPU steal time reveal whether an instance is constrained by underlying hardware capacity.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Billing tracks costs and committed use discounts, but it does not provide operational telemetry regarding CPU contention.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Serial port output displays system boot and kernel initialization text, not real-time hypervisor CPU stealing metrics.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC flow logs track network traffic metadata, not CPU allocation or hypervisor performance metrics.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your team manages an application deployed across multiple Google Cloud regions. You need to create a Cloud Monitoring dashboard that displays CPU utilization across all instances in all regions grouped by project. When you build the dashboard widget using the Metrics Explorer, you notice that the data is fragmented and difficult to read because instance names are random and dynamic due to Managed Instance Groups. How should you structure the query to make the dashboard readable?

options.text: Export all raw metrics to a local text file using gsutil and render them using an external web server.
Use metric filters with regular expressions and apply group-by aggregations based on instance labels or zone metadata.
Hardcode every individual virtual machine IP address into a separate chart widget on the dashboard.
Disable Managed Instance Groups and manage all virtual machines as static standalone instances.

questions.explanation: In dynamic cloud environments with Managed Instance Groups, using metric labels and group-by aggregations in Cloud Monitoring ensures that dashboards remain clean and scalable without relying on static naming conventions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Exporting raw logs manually bypasses native Cloud Monitoring visualization tools and requires unnecessary custom infrastructure maintenance.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Hardcoding IP addresses in auto-scaled environments is an anti-pattern because instances frequently change IPs upon recreation.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Disabling MIGs sacrifices high availability, automated healing, and autoscaling capabilities just for dashboard simplicity.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: An application running on Compute Engine instances is writing large volumes of structured log data to standard output (stdout). Your finance team reports that log ingestion costs in Cloud Logging have doubled over the last month. You need to reduce log ingestion expenses immediately without breaking your ability to debug critical errors. What is the most effective native configuration change to implement?

options.text: Delete the default _Default log bucket entirely to stop all log storage across the Google Cloud project.
Create a log exclusion filter in Cloud Logging to drop verbose debug and info logs while retaining warning and error severities.
Modify the application code to write logs to local disk files instead of stdout.
Lower the logging quota limits in the IAM & Admin console to restrict how many bytes the project can write.

questions.explanation: Log exclusion filters in Cloud Logging enable administrators to selectively drop specific high-volume log streams (like DEBUG level logs) during ingestion, effectively lowering monitoring costs without sacrificing critical error visibility.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Deleting the default log bucket breaks logging infrastructure and prevents capturing any audit or error logs.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Writing to local disk files without the Operations agent capturing them results in log data loss when instances terminate, defeating centralized monitoring.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Quotas restrict maximum capacity, but hitting them results in dropped logs unpredictably rather than targeted cost reduction of verbose logs.

questions.domain: Ensuring Successful Operation of a Cloud Solution
questions.question: Your company operates an e-commerce platform hosted on Google Cloud. During a flash sale, traffic spikes dramatically, and you notice that your backend application instances are becoming unresponsive. Upon checking Cloud Monitoring, you see that the CPU utilization across all instances in the MIG is at 100%, but the autoscaler has not added new instances quickly enough. What configuration setting should you review and adjust on the Managed Instance Group to improve response time during future traffic surges?

options.text: Disable health checks on the load balancer so traffic hits the instances instantly regardless of readiness.
Increase the cool-down period on the autoscaler to 30 minutes to prevent rapid instance flapping.
Switch the backend from a regional Managed Instance Group to a single large Compute Engine instance with 96 vCPUs.
Review and lower the target CPU utilization threshold, and ensure the autoscaling stabilization (cooldown) period is appropriately sized.

questions.explanation: To ensure rapid response to sudden traffic surges, autoscaler target thresholds (such as CPU utilization) should be set low enough so that scaling is triggered before instances become overloaded and unresponsive.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Disabling health checks causes the load balancer to route traffic to failed or uninitialized instances, leading to application errors.
wrongOptionNotes.B: A longer cool-down period would actually slow down scaling actions further, worsening response times during traffic surges.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Vertical scaling introduces a single point of failure and violates high availability architecture best practices.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A team of developers reports that they cannot access a newly created Cloud SQL instance from their Compute Engine application instances, despite both residing in the same Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network. The application logs indicate a connection timeout. How should you troubleshoot and resolve this issue?

options.text: Verify that authorized networks on the Cloud SQL instance include the internal IP address or CIDR range of the client Compute Engine instances or that Private Services Access is properly configured.
Modify the Compute Engine default service account to include the database-client role.
Attach a public IP address to the Cloud SQL instance and update the application connection string to use the public endpoint.
Grant the developers the Cloud SQL Admin role on the project IAM policy.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL internal connectivity requires proper VPC networking configuration, specifically Private Services Access for instances using internal IP addresses, alongside standard firewall rules.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Service accounts control authentication and authorization to APIs, not network routing or TCP connectivity to Cloud SQL.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Enabling public IP addresses violates security best practices and is unnecessary for instances within the same VPC network.
wrongOptionNotes.D: IAM roles control management and control-plane access, not network connectivity or database communication ports.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your production application running on Compute Engine fails to write data to a Cloud Storage bucket, throwing a 403 Forbidden error. The instance was recently redeployed using a new service account. What is the most likely root cause and correct resolution?

options.text: The instance needs to be restarted to generate a new OAuth2 token for Cloud Storage.
The new service account lacks the Storage Object Creator or Storage Object Admin IAM role on the target Cloud Storage bucket.
The Cloud Storage bucket has uniform bucket-level access disabled, causing authentication clashes.
The Compute Engine instance lacks a public IP address, preventing it from reaching the Cloud Storage API endpoint.

questions.explanation: Applications running on Compute Engine inherit permissions from their attached service account. When permissions change or instances are redeployed with different service accounts, corresponding IAM bindings on resources like Cloud Storage buckets must be updated.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Restarting the instance does not resolve missing IAM permissions assigned to the service account.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Disabling uniform bucket-level access allows finer-grained ACLs, but a missing IAM role will still result in access denial regardless of this setting.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Compute Engine instances without public IPs can access Google APIs and services using Private Google Access or VPC Service Controls.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An internal penetration test reveals that a web application running on a Compute Engine instance can successfully query arbitrary metadata endpoints and access sensitive instance metadata values. How should you mitigate this security vulnerability?

options.text: Update the VPC firewall rules to block egress traffic to the metadata IP address 169.254.169.254.
Enforce Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2) on the Compute Engine instance to require session-token-based metadata requests.
Remove all service accounts attached to the Compute Engine instance.
Disable the metadata server entirely by modifying the instance startup script.

questions.explanation: Enforcing IMDSv2 requires attackers to possess the session token, effectively neutralizing standard Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks aimed at stealing metadata.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC firewall rules cannot block traffic to the internal metadata IP address, as it is handled at the hypervisor level.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Removing the service account prevents the instance from calling Google Cloud APIs, which may break required application functionality.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Disabling the metadata server completely breaks core functionality such as SSH key management, startup scripts, and service account token generation.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A production microservice running in a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster is failing to authenticate when calling Secret Manager to retrieve database credentials. The pod logs show authentication failures. Which configuration should you check first?

options.text: Verify that Workload Identity is configured and that the Kubernetes service account is correctly bound to a Google service account with Secret Manager Secret Accessor role.
Recreate the GKE cluster with legacy authorization enabled.
Ensure that the cluster master node has a public IP address assigned.
Grant the cluster's default node service account the Project Editor role.

questions.explanation: GKE Workload Identity securely links Kubernetes service accounts in your cluster to Google Cloud service accounts, allowing pods to authenticate seamlessly to APIs like Secret Manager without storing keys.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Legacy authorization is deprecated and insecure, and it does not resolve Google Cloud IAM authentication issues for pods.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cluster master public IP addresses are unrelated to pod-level authentication against Google Cloud APIs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Granting broad roles like Project Editor violates the principle of least privilege and is not the correct mechanism for pod-level secret access.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team reports that an unauthorized user was able to access a shared development project and modify production IAM policies. Upon investigation, you discover that project-level primitive roles were assigned. How should you remediate this security gap permanently?

options.text: Disable the IAM API across all projects in the organization.
Replace all primitive roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) with predefined or custom IAM roles adhering to the principle of least privilege, and enforce Organizational Policies to restrict role assignments.
Enable VPC Service Controls on the development project.
Delete the user accounts from Google Cloud Identity and recreate them.

questions.explanation: Primitive roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) provide broad, legacy access levels. Best practices mandate using predefined or custom roles tailored to specific job functions combined with Organization Policies.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Disabling the IAM API will break all access management and administrative operations across the environment.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC Service Controls protect against data exfiltration across network perimeters, but they do not replace proper IAM role governance.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Deleting and recreating user accounts does not address the underlying issue of overly permissive IAM role assignments.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are troubleshooting a deployment failure where a CI/CD pipeline service account fails to deploy resources to a target project. The service account resides in Project A, but the deployment target is Project B. Where must the IAM role be granted?

options.text: At the organization level, assigned to the user who triggered the pipeline.
By downloading a private key from the service account in Project B and uploading it to Project A.
In Project A, assigned to the project number of Project B.
On the specific resources or at the project level of Project B, assigned to the service account email from Project A.

questions.explanation: When a service account in one project needs to access or modify resources in another project, IAM bindings must be established in the target project referencing the service account principal.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Granting permissions at the organization level violates least privilege, and pipelines typically execute using service accounts rather than direct user credentials.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Service account keys are discouraged due to security risks; cross-project access is handled natively via IAM policy bindings.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Permissions must be granted where the resources are being created or managed (Project B), not in the source project.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An auditor requests verification that a sensitive BigQuery dataset containing personally identifiable information (PII) has been accessed only by authorized personnel. Which service and log type should you examine?

options.text: Cloud Logging, reviewing Admin Activity audit logs for BigQuery dataset creation.
Compute Engine serial port logs.
Cloud Logging, specifically reviewing Data Access audit logs for BigQuery API calls.
VPC Flow Logs for the default network subnets.

questions.explanation: Cloud Audit Logs include Admin Activity, Data Access, System Event, and Policy Denial logs. Data Access logs must be explicitly enabled and are used to track who read or modified data within services like BigQuery.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Admin Activity logs record administrative actions such as creating datasets or modifying IAM policies, not data queries or reads.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Serial port logs capture console output from virtual machine instances, which is irrelevant to BigQuery access auditing.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC Flow Logs record network packet metadata, not application-level database queries or user identities accessing BigQuery.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your company's security policy states that all encryption keys used for encrypting data in Cloud Storage buckets must be fully managed by your security team via an external key manager, without Google ever holding the key material. Which encryption option should you implement?

options.text: Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK).
Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) configured with Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) and Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM).
Enabling default service account impersonation for Cloud Storage.
Google-managed encryption keys.

questions.explanation: Cloud EKM integrates Google Cloud services with external key management partners (such as Fortanix, Thales, or Vormetric), allowing encryption operations to be executed using keys stored outside Google's infrastructure.

wrongOptionNotes.A: CSEK requires the customer to provide and manage encryption keys for every read and write operation, rather than providing an integrated external key manager.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Service account impersonation relates to IAM authentication and authorization, not data encryption key management.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Google-managed encryption keys are fully managed by Google, which does not satisfy the requirement for external key management.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A junior administrator attempts to create a new Compute Engine instance with an external IP address attached, but the creation fails with a policy violation error. Upon checking organization policies, you find a constraint restricting external IP addresses. How can the administrator successfully deploy the instance without violating compliance?

options.text: Deploy the instance without an external IP address, and configure Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) TCP forwarding or a Bastion Host with VPN to access it securely.
Temporarily disable the entire Organization Policy constraint, create the instance, and re-enable the policy.
Assign the Organization Administrator role to the junior administrator so the policy constraint is bypassed.
Attach a static public IP address instead of an ephemeral public IP address.

questions.explanation: Organization policies enforce hard constraints across cloud resources. When public IPs are prohibited, administrators must rely on internal-only architectures combined with secure tunneling tools like Identity-Aware Proxy.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling security policies violates compliance mandates and introduces security risks during the operational window.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Organization policies apply to all principals in the scope regardless of individual administrative roles unless specific exceptions or exemptions are configured.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Both static and ephemeral external IP addresses violate organization policies that restrict public IP attachments on instances.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An application running on a Compute Engine instance needs to connect to a PostgreSQL database hosted in an on-premises datacenter via a Cloud VPN tunnel. However, the database connection fails. Network troubleshooting confirms that the VPN tunnel is established and passing traffic. What security and networking component should you verify next?

options.text: Enable uniform bucket-level access on all project storage buckets.
Verify that Google Cloud VPC firewall rules allow egress traffic to the on-premises database subnet and that on-premises firewall rules permit ingress traffic from the Google Cloud instance IP.
Check that the Compute Engine instance has the Project Editor IAM role assigned.
Rotate the service account keys attached to the Compute Engine instance.

questions.explanation: Troubleshooting hybrid connectivity requires verifying both the underlying network paths (VPN/Interconnect) and stateful packet filtering controls (VPC firewall rules and on-premises firewalls).

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Storage bucket access settings have no impact on hybrid network routing or database connectivity over Cloud VPN.
