wrongOptionNotes.C: IAM roles govern access to Google Cloud APIs and control plane management, not network packet filtering or database port connectivity.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Service account key rotation affects API authentication, not layer-4 TCP/IP network connectivity over VPN tunnels.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team mandates that no service account keys (JSON or P12) can be created or downloaded across any projects in your organization. Which Google Cloud feature should you use to enforce this mandate centrally?

options.text: Cloud Audit Logs with log-based alerting.
Organization Policy Service, specifically enforcing the 'Disable service account key creation' constraint.
Custom IAM roles that omit the iam.serviceAccountKeys.create permission.
VPC Service Controls perimeters around all projects.

questions.explanation: Organization Policy Service provides centralized, preventive controls. Enforcing key creation restrictions stops users from generating long-lived credentials, pushing them toward more secure alternatives like Workload Identity or impersonation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Log-based alerts detect and notify when keys are created, but they do not proactively prevent the action like an Organization Policy constraint.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While custom roles help, managing this across thousands of users and projects is impractical compared to centralized Organization Policies.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC Service Controls secure data perimeters against exfiltration, but they do not specifically restrict the creation of service account keys.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You manage a Google Cloud project where developers require access to debug running instances via SSH. Security policies dictate that direct SSH access over public IP addresses is strictly prohibited. What is the most secure and compliant way to grant this access?

options.text: Attach public IP addresses to the instances and use ephemeral SSH keys managed by OS Login.
Configure OS Login and instruct developers to upload their public SSH keys directly to project metadata.
Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) for TCP forwarding and grant developers the IAP-secured Tunnel User role.
Open firewall port 22 in the VPC firewall rules, restricted strictly to the corporate headquarters static IP address.

questions.explanation: Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) authenticates and authorizes users trying to reach instances through SSH/RDP, validating context before permitting TCP forwarding through Google's infrastructure.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Attaching public IP addresses violates the security mandate prohibiting public IPs for instance management.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Project-level SSH keys combined with direct public IP connections still violate the policy against direct public management access if instances have public IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Opening port 22 on firewall rules exposes an attack surface, whereas IAP removes the need for direct port exposure altogether.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A developer needs temporary administrative access to a specific Cloud SQL database instance to perform emergency maintenance. To adhere to security best practices, how should you grant this access?

options.text: Create a shared database account with permanent superuser privileges and share the credentials securely.
Grant the developer a time-bound IAM role assignment using Conditional IAM bindings.
Generate a long-lived service account key with database admin rights.
Assign the Project Owner role to the developer permanently.

questions.explanation: IAM conditions enable attribute-based access control (ABAC), supporting time-based expiration policies that automatically remove access when maintenance windows close.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Shared superuser accounts violate accountability and auditing standards because individual actions cannot be traced back to a specific user.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Service account keys should be avoided for human administrative access, especially when time-bound IAM conditions can achieve the requirement securely.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Granting permanent Project Owner roles violates the principle of least privilege and exposes the entire project to unnecessary risk.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team identifies that multiple users across different departments have been assigned overly broad custom IAM roles that include unauthorized permissions. You need to audit all custom roles in the organization to identify which ones contain permissions related to service account key creation. How should you perform this review?

options.text: Review VPC Flow Logs for unusual traffic patterns associated with service account management.
Use the Google Cloud Console or gcloud CLI to list all custom roles at the organization and project levels, and inspect their defined permission lists.
Inspect the billing reports for unexpected charges related to IAM API calls.
Check Cloud Storage bucket access control lists (ACLs) across all projects.

questions.explanation: Auditing custom IAM roles involves inspecting the specific set of permissions bundled into each role across organizational hierarchies to ensure no excessive privileges are granted.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC Flow Logs track network packet flows, not IAM role definitions or permission grants.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Billing reports track resource consumption costs, not security permission assignments or custom role definitions.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Bucket ACLs control object-level storage permissions, which are completely unrelated to IAM custom role definitions.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A critical compliance audit requires that all changes to firewall rules, network topologies, and IAM policies within your Google Cloud organization be exported to a secure, immutable storage bucket in a separate logging project. Which feature should you configure?

options.text: A manual script that queries the Cloud Logging API every night and copies logs to Cloud Storage.
An organization-level Log Sink routing audit logs to a Cloud Storage bucket in the designated logging project.
Configuring Cloud Monitoring uptime checks for the project networking components.
Enabling VPC Service Controls on the default network.

questions.explanation: Log sinks enable centralized log export at the organization or folder level, routing audit records to Cloud Storage, BigQuery, or Pub/Sub for long-term retention and security analysis.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Custom scripts are prone to failure, introduce maintenance overhead, and fail to provide real-time, tamper-evident audit streaming.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Uptime checks monitor resource availability and health, not administrative configuration changes or compliance audit trails.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC Service Controls protect against data exfiltration, but they do not handle log aggregation and export.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team requires that access to a production Google Cloud project be restricted so that human engineers can only view resources and never modify them, while a specific automation service account retains deployment permissions. How should you implement this according to least-privilege principles?

options.text: Assign individual engineers the Owner role at the project level and configure conditional IAM bindings based on time of day.
Remove all IAM bindings from the project and rely entirely on the default Compute Engine service account for all tasks.
Assign individual engineers the predefined Viewer role at the project level and assign the deployment service account the Editor role.
Create a custom role with permissions to create and delete resources and assign it to all human engineers.

questions.explanation: Least-privilege security mandates granting users only the permissions necessary to perform their roles. Predefined roles such as roles/viewer provide appropriate read-only access for human operators without exposing modification capabilities.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The Owner role grants full administrative control, violating the requirement that engineers can only view resources.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Relying on default service accounts introduces excessive permissions and insecure operational practices.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Giving human engineers creation and deletion permissions violates the restriction that they must only be able to view resources.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You manage a Google Cloud organization containing multiple folders and projects. Your security team mandates that no virtual machine instances across the entire organization can be created with an external IP address. Which feature should you use to enforce this requirement globally?

options.text: Set up a Cloud Monitoring alert that notifies the security team whenever an external IP is attached.
Create a custom IAM role that excludes compute.instances.setAccessConfig and assign it to all users.
Apply an Organization Policy constraint using constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess at the organization root.
Configure an individual firewall rule in every project denying all egress traffic to the internet.

questions.explanation: Organization Policy Service provides centralized, programmatic control over resource configurations across an entire resource hierarchy, making it the correct tool for mandatory compliance guardrails.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Alerts only notify after the fact; they do not proactively block or prevent the prohibited action.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Managing this via IAM is error-prone, hard to audit, and does not prevent users with higher privileges from attaching external IPs.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Firewall rules control packet filtering based on IP addresses and ports, but they do not prevent the attachment of external IP addresses to instances.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An application running on a Compute Engine instance needs to interact with Cloud Storage and BigQuery APIs. To ensure maximum security and adhere to Google Cloud best practices, how should the instance be authenticated?

options.text: Configure the instance to use user credentials via an interactive browser login whenever API calls are made.
Attach a custom service account with the minimum necessary API scopes and roles directly to the Compute Engine instance.
Grant the default Compute Engine service account Project Owner privileges.
Embed a service account JSON key file inside the application source code deployed on the instance.

questions.explanation: Using attached service accounts with scoped IAM roles avoids the security risks associated with managing static service account keys while enabling secure API communication.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Interactive authentication is not feasible for automated workloads running unattended on Compute Engine instances.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The default service account has broad permissions, and assigning Project Owner violates the principle of least privilege.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Hardcoding or storing service account keys on disk is a major security anti-pattern and increases the risk of credential leakage.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your organization requires that a group of external data analysts have temporary, time-bound access to query a specific BigQuery dataset. The access must automatically expire after 7 days. How should you grant this access securely?

options.text: Grant the analysts the BigQuery Data Viewer role at the project level with a permanent binding.
Share your personal Google Cloud login credentials with the analysts for the duration of the 7 days.
Create a custom role granting dataset administration privileges and assign it to the analysts indefinitely.
Grant the BigQuery Data Viewer role on the specific dataset using an IAM conditional binding that includes an expiration timestamp.

questions.explanation: IAM conditions support temporal constraints (request.time < timestamp), making them ideal for granting temporary access without requiring manual cleanup.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Permanent bindings do not automatically expire after 7 days and grant project-wide visibility instead of dataset-specific access.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Sharing credentials violates basic security policies and makes non-repudiation and auditing impossible.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Dataset administration privileges are too broad for analysts, and indefinite access violates the temporary requirement.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team discovers that multiple developers have downloaded and stored JSON service account keys on their local workstations, posing a significant security risk. You need to identify which service accounts currently have active user-managed keys associated with them across your organization. What is the most efficient way to achieve this?

options.text: Log into each individual Compute Engine instance and check the /home directory for hidden key files.
Enable Billing Export and analyze the cost breakdown for service account API usage.
Review the VPC Flow Logs for outbound traffic pointing to authentication endpoints.
Query Cloud Asset Inventory to list all service account keys across the organization.

questions.explanation: Cloud Asset Inventory enables organizations to export and query resource metadata at scale, allowing security administrators to audit active user-managed service account keys.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Service account keys are often downloaded to local developer laptops, not Compute Engine instances, making manual server checks ineffective.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Billing export tracks costs, not resource configurations or active cryptographic key metadata.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC Flow Logs record IP packet metadata and do not provide visibility into active cryptographic key inventories.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are designing a secure environment where developers need to run applications on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). To maintain strict security boundaries, pods running within the cluster must not assume broad project-level permissions if they are compromised. Which feature should you configure?

options.text: Project-level Editor IAM binding applied directly to the GKE node instances.
Disabling metadata server access entirely on the underlying GKE nodes.
Workload Identity
Static service account JSON keys mounted into every container pod as a secret.

questions.explanation: Workload Identity is the recommended and most secure mechanism for GKE applications to authenticate to Google Cloud services without using static keys or granting broad node-level permissions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Granting project-level Editor access to nodes gives every pod running on those nodes excessive administrative control over the entire project.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling the metadata server can break critical cluster networking and node operations.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Storing static keys inside containers introduces severe security risks if the container image or pod is compromised.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An external security auditor requires read-only access to all Cloud Audit Logs across your entire Google Cloud organization for compliance verification. You want to grant this access with the least possible privilege. Which role and assignment level should you choose?

options.text: Project Owner role assigned on the root organization node.
Storage Object Viewer role assigned on the default logging bucket.
Compute Admin role assigned on every folder within the organization.
Private Logs Viewer role assigned at the organization root level.

questions.explanation: The Private Logs Viewer role (roles/logging.privateLogsViewer) provides access to sensitive log data such as Admin Activity and Data Access audit logs without granting unnecessary resource management permissions.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The Owner role grants full read and write administrative permissions across the organization, far exceeding the read-only audit logs requirement.
wrongOptionNotes.B: While storage roles grant bucket access, Cloud Audit Logs are managed centrally via the Logging service, and IAM roles like Private Logs Viewer are designed specifically for this purpose.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The Compute Admin role grants administrative control over Compute Engine resources, which is unrelated to viewing audit logs.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your company's compliance policy requires that all data stored in BigQuery datasets be encrypted using a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK) managed via Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS). How can you enforce this requirement for all new datasets created in a specific project?

options.text: Revoke BigQuery dataset creation permissions from all users and perform every creation task yourself.
Manually email all data engineers reminding them to specify a Cloud KMS key when creating datasets.
Set up a Cloud Logging metric alert to notify you when a dataset is created without encryption.
Apply an Organization Policy constraint that mandates the use of CMEK for BigQuery datasets.

questions.explanation: Organization Policies provide programmatic guardrails to enforce technical requirements like CMEK usage automatically upon resource creation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Bottlenecking all dataset creation through a single administrator does not scale and violates operational efficiency.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Relying on manual processes and human memory is prone to errors and fails compliance audits.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Alerts only notify administrators after a non-compliant resource has already been created.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You need to grant an external vendor permission to upload specific files to a single Cloud Storage bucket in your project. The vendor should not have access to any other resources in your project, and the permission must expire in 2 hours. What is the most secure method to achieve this?

options.text: Grant the vendor the Storage Object Admin role at the project level.
Create a service account, generate a JSON key, email the key file to the vendor, and delete the key after 2 hours.
Add the vendor's personal Google account to the project IAM policy with the Storage Object Creator role.
Generate a Signed URL with write permissions for the specific object and time-limited validity.

questions.explanation: Signed URLs enable secure, temporary, and granular delegation of access to Cloud Storage objects without modifying project IAM policies or distributing static credentials.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Project-level Storage Object Admin grants access to all buckets in the project, violating the principle of least privilege.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Emailing static key files creates severe security risks, including interception and failure to delete keys on time.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Adding external accounts to IAM policies creates long-term access that must be manually revoked, risking compliance.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A junior administrator needs to troubleshoot a Compute Engine instance in a development project. The security team requires that access be logged, time-bound, and performed without exposing SSH private keys to the administrators' local machines. Which feature should you recommend?

options.text: Enable serial port console access and allow interactive debugging over the serial output stream.
Manually generate an RSA key pair, paste the public key into project metadata, and share the private key via chat.
Assign the administrator the Project Owner role so they can log in using root credentials.
OS Login with SSH key management enabled via Google Cloud IAM

questions.explanation: Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) combined with OS Login provides centralized access control, short-lived SSH keys, and comprehensive audit logs for VM access.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Serial port access provides interactive debugging but is intended for troubleshooting boot failures, not standard administrative SSH sessions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Manually sharing private SSH keys is an insecure practice that lacks proper auditing and identity lifecycle management.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Project Owner grants excessive privileges and does not solve secure, auditable SSH key management.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team mandates that no service account keys can be downloaded or created across any projects within your production folder. How can you enforce this requirement globally?

options.text: Configure an Organization Policy constraint using constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation at the folder level.
Revoke the Service Account Key Admin role from all human users and assign them Viewer roles.
Configure firewall rules to block traffic from the IAM API endpoint.
Run a nightly cron job that searches for service account keys and deletes them using the gcloud CLI.

questions.explanation: Organization policy constraints provide programmatic guardrails that block unauthorized actions, such as service account key creation, at the organizational or folder level.

wrongOptionNotes.B: While removing roles helps, determined users with broader permissions could still potentially create keys unless blocked by an organization policy constraint.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Firewall rules control network traffic at the packet level for VPC networks, not Google Cloud API control planes.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Relying on scheduled scripts leaves a window of vulnerability between key creation and script execution.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An application deployed on Compute Engine needs to read configuration secrets stored in Secret Manager. To comply with security best practices, the application should only have access to the specific secret it requires, and no other secrets in the project. How should you configure access?

options.text: Grant the instance's service account the Secret Manager Admin role at the project level.
Expose the secret via a public HTTP endpoint so the application can fetch it over the internet.
Grant the instance's service account the Secret Manager Secret Accessor role on that specific secret resource.
Store the secret plaintext value in the instance metadata configuration.

questions.explanation: Granting granular IAM roles on individual resource paths (such as a specific secret in Secret Manager) ensures workloads can only access the data they require.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The Secret Manager Admin role grants full control over all secrets in the project, violating least privilege.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Exposing secrets over public HTTP endpoints is a severe security vulnerability.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Instance metadata is accessible to any process running on the instance and is not encrypted specifically for secret management.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your organization requires that all administrator actions, configuration changes, and permission modifications made within your Google Cloud project be exported to a secure, immutable storage bucket for long-term compliance retention. Which logs and export mechanism should you configure?

options.text: Admin Activity audit logs exported to a Cloud Storage bucket using a log sink.
Kubernetes audit logs stored locally on ephemeral GKE node ephemeral disks.
Console access logs downloaded manually via CSV from the Google Cloud Console once a month.
VPC Flow Logs exported to a BigQuery dataset using a custom Cloud Logging sink.

questions.explanation: Admin Activity audit logs capture all administrative operations and configuration changes, and Cloud Logging sinks allow reliable, automated export to Cloud Storage for compliance.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Storing logs on ephemeral disks risks data loss when nodes are recycled or deleted.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Manual downloads are not automated, reliable, or secure enough for compliance retention requirements.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata, not administrator actions or IAM configuration changes.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are managing a Google Cloud project containing sensitive Personal Identifiable Information (PII). You need to ensure that no user can inadvertently make a Cloud Storage bucket containing this data publicly accessible via uniform bucket-level access or public object ACLs. What is the most effective control to enforce?

options.text: Remove all users from the project IAM policy except for the project owner.
Rely on developers to carefully check the 'Public Access Prevention' checkbox when creating each bucket.
Write a custom bash script that runs every hour to check bucket permissions and delete public buckets.
Enforce Public Access Prevention (PAP) on the project or bucket level.

questions.explanation: Public Access Prevention enforces that no data in Cloud Storage can be made public, providing a definitive compliance safeguard against accidental exposure.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Removing users prevents legitimate work and does not specifically address or prevent public access configurations.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Relying on manual user diligence is prone to human error and potential data exposure.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Polling scripts introduce a race condition where data could be exposed before the script executes.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team requires that all traffic originating from authorized internal subnets destined for Google Cloud APIs (such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery) must not traverse the public internet. Which Google Cloud networking feature should you implement?

options.text: Attach external IP addresses to all client instances so they can reach public API endpoints securely.
Configure static NAT gateway routes pointing to public DNS servers.
Configure Private Google Access on the subnet and use restricted or private IP addresses for API communication.
Route all API traffic through an external third-party proxy appliance hosted in another cloud provider.

questions.explanation: Private Google Access enables VMs on subnets without external IP addresses to communicate with Google APIs and services securely using internal IP addresses.

wrongOptionNotes.A: External IP addresses route traffic over the public internet, violating the requirement to avoid the public internet.
wrongOptionNotes.B: NAT gateways still traverse public IP space when accessing public Google API endpoints, unless Private Google Access is used.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Routing traffic through external third-party providers introduces unnecessary latency, complexity, and security risks.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your company operates a web application on Compute Engine instances that process financial transactions. The security team mandates that instances must authenticate to Cloud Storage to read static assets without embedding long-lived service account credentials or creating downloadable JSON keys, while minimizing operational overhead.

options.text: Configure public read access on the Cloud Storage bucket so that instances can fetch the static assets via unauthenticated HTTP requests.
Generate a user-managed service account key, store it in Secret Manager, and configure a startup script to fetch and configure the key on every boot.
Attach a custom service account to the Compute Engine instances and grant it the necessary Storage Object Viewer role, leveraging built-in metadata server credential rotation.
Use the default Compute Engine service account and assign it Owner permissions across the entire Google Cloud project.

questions.explanation: Attaching a dedicated, least-privilege service account directly to Compute Engine instances enables automatic credential management through the metadata server, adhering to security best practices without introducing manual key management overhead.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Making financial transaction assets publicly accessible introduces severe security vulnerabilities and violates compliance mandates.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Creating user-managed service account keys introduces security risks regarding key lifecycle management and violates the directive to avoid downloadable keys.
wrongOptionNotes.D: The default service account with Owner permissions violates the principle of least privilege and increases blast radius exposure.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An analytics team needs to run daily queries against a large BigQuery dataset containing sensitive customer data. To comply with strict regional data residency policies, you must ensure that queries and data storage are strictly constrained to the europe-west3 region while preventing unauthorized external data exfiltration.

options.text: Set up an organization policy constraint under constraints/gcp.resourceLocations to restrict resource creation and data processing to europe-west3.
Manually inspect every BigQuery query submitted by the analytics team via Cloud Audit Logs to verify that no external tables are accessed.
Apply a VPC Service Controls perimeter around the BigQuery datasets and block all outbound internet traffic from the project.
Revoke all BigQuery permissions and require the team to export data to local CSV files stored in an encrypted Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.explanation: Organization policy constraints such as constraints/gcp.resourceLocations provide automated, preventative enforcement of data residency requirements across projects and folders.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual inspection does not provide preventative enforcement and incurs high operational overhead.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While VPC Service Controls prevents data exfiltration, the resource locations constraint is specifically designed to enforce data residency and regional compliance for BigQuery.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Exporting data to local files increases the risk of data leakage and defeats the purpose of utilizing BigQuery for analysis.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your engineering team deploys microservices to a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. A compliance review reveals that pods are running with overly permissive default service accounts. You need to implement Workload Identity to securely bind Kubernetes service accounts to Google service accounts.

options.text: Assign the Compute Engine default service account broad IAM permissions on the underlying GKE node instances.
Enable Workload Identity on the GKE cluster, create a Google service account, bind it to a Kubernetes service account using IAM policy bindings, and annotate the Kubernetes service account.
Download a JSON key for a privileged Google service account, mount it as a Kubernetes Secret, and configure the application to authenticate using the key file.
Configure the cluster to use legacy authorization and explicitly pass project owner credentials via environment variables to each deployment.

questions.explanation: Workload Identity is the recommended and most secure mechanism for GKE applications to authenticate to Google Cloud services by mapping Kubernetes service accounts directly to Google service accounts.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Granting broad permissions at the node level violates the principle of least privilege by sharing permissions across all pods running on that node.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Mounting JSON service account keys inside cluster secrets is an anti-pattern that exposes credentials to container compromise risks.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Legacy authorization and hardcoded environment credentials present critical security vulnerabilities.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You manage multiple production and development projects within a Google Cloud organization. Your security team mandates that developers must not have permissions to create new service account keys, as previous audits found exposed JSON keys in public code repositories.

options.text: Enforce the organization policy constraint constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation at the organization root level.
Write a custom Cloud Monitoring alert that scans Cloud Audit Logs every minute and deletes any newly created service account keys.
Remove the Service Account Key Admin role from all individual developer user accounts across all projects.
Revoke the Project Editor role from all developers and restrict them to viewing logs only.

questions.explanation: Organization policies provide centralized, preventative security controls that apply uniformly across all current and future projects, making them ideal for enforcing prohibitions like service account key creation.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Reactive remediation via monitoring alerts leaves a window of vulnerability and introduces unnecessary operational complexity compared to preventative organization policies.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Relying solely on IAM role assignments requires continuous auditing and is prone to human error when new projects are created.
wrongOptionNotes.D: This approach overly restricts development workflows and fails to specifically target the ability to create service account keys.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An external auditor requires read-only access to audit logs across your entire Google Cloud organization for a period of 7 days. You want to grant this access securely without modifying IAM policies on individual projects or sensitive resources.

options.text: Create a dedicated service account, download its JSON key, and securely email the key file to the external auditor.
Create a custom role with logging.viewer permissions, and grant it to the auditor's Google account at the organization root level scoped with a conditional binding expiration timestamp.
Export all Cloud Audit Logs into a shared public Cloud Storage bucket and send the public URL to the auditor.
Grant the primitive Project Viewer role to the auditor across all folders and projects in the organization.

questions.explanation: IAM conditions enable time-bound access grants, making them the ideal mechanism for temporary external auditor access without requiring manual revocation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Sharing downloadable service account keys introduces severe credential management risks and violates security policies.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Exposing audit logs publicly violates data privacy and compliance standards.
wrongOptionNotes.D: The Project Viewer role grants excessive visibility beyond audit logs, violating the principle of least privilege.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your company's database administrators need emergency access to execute maintenance scripts on a production Cloud SQL instance. To maintain strict security posture, access must be tightly controlled, fully audited, and restricted to a maximum duration of 2 hours.

options.text: Implement Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) TCP forwarding along with IAM conditional bindings configured with a time-based expiration for the Cloud SQL Client role.
Share a single database superuser password through an unencrypted internal chat channel.
Permanently assign the Cloud SQL Admin role to the administrators and instruct them to log out when finished.
Attach a public IP address temporarily to the Cloud SQL instance and whitelist the administrators' home IP addresses in authorized networks.

questions.explanation: Combining Identity-Aware Proxy for secure connection handling with time-bound IAM conditions provides a robust, auditable, and temporary administrative access workflow.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Sharing unencrypted credentials prevents individual accountability and violates security baselines.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Permanent administrative access violates the principle of least privilege and increases the impact of credential compromise.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Exposing a database to a public IP address introduces significant security risks.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team discovers that several Compute Engine instances are communicating with unauthorized external APIs over the internet. You need to implement a preventative network control that restricts all outbound internet access from these instances while allowing communication with internal Google APIs.

options.text: Install third-party host-based antivirus software on every Compute Engine instance to inspect and block outbound packets.
Remove the external IP addresses from the Compute Engine instances and rely solely on VPC flow logs to monitor unauthorized connections.
Configure VPC Firewall Rules to deny all egress traffic to destination IP range 0.0.0.0/0, and use Private Google Access for internal Google API communication.
Delete the default internet gateway route (0.0.0.0/0) from the VPC route table without configuring any alternative routing.

questions.explanation: VPC egress firewall rules combined with Private Google Access provide robust network-level isolation, preventing data exfiltration to the internet while maintaining access to Google Cloud services.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Relying on host-based software introduces high operational overhead and can be bypassed, whereas VPC firewall rules provide network-level enforcement.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Removing external IP addresses prevents inbound traffic and direct outbound traffic, but instances with Cloud NAT can still reach the internet unless blocked by firewall rules.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Deleting the default route without Private Google Access or proper subnet routing will also block access to necessary Google APIs and package repositories.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are designing a secure multi-tenant environment on Google Cloud. Different development teams require independent resource management within a shared organization. You need to structure the hierarchy to ensure that billing and organization-level security policies apply automatically to all team resources.

options.text: Share a single project among all development teams and use IAM conditions to separate resources by naming convention.
Deploy all projects directly under the root organization node and apply individual IAM policies to every single project manually.
Create a completely separate Google Cloud organization for each development team and link separate billing accounts to each.
Create a dedicated folder for each team under the organization node, place their respective projects inside those folders, and apply IAM policies and organization constraints at the folder level.

questions.explanation: The Resource Manager hierarchy uses folders to group projects, allowing administrators to inherit IAM policies and organization constraints down the hierarchy efficiently.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Sharing a single project among multiple teams violates security isolation best practices and quota limits.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Placing projects directly under the root node without folders makes policy management cumbersome and difficult to scale.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Managing multiple independent organizations creates administrative overhead and fragments centralized billing and security governance.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your company requires that all data stored in Cloud Storage buckets be encrypted using encryption keys managed entirely by your organization in Cloud KMS, rather than Google-managed keys, to satisfy strict regulatory standards.

options.text: Store encryption keys inside a plain text configuration file within the same Cloud Storage bucket.
Download the objects from Cloud Storage, encrypt them locally using a custom script, and re-upload the encrypted binary files.
Rely on the default Google-managed encryption keys, as they are certified compliant with FIPS 140-2 standards.
Configure Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) using Cloud KMS keys when creating the Cloud Storage buckets.

questions.explanation: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) integrate Cloud Storage with Cloud KMS, giving organizations full control over key creation, rotation, and revocation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Storing keys alongside encrypted data in plain text completely defeats the security purpose of encryption.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Client-side encryption managed manually introduces extreme operational complexity and prevents server-side features like BigQuery federated queries.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Default Google-managed keys do not fulfill mandates requiring organization-controlled key management and rotation policies.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A production application running on Compute Engine needs to read and write sensitive configuration secrets stored in Secret Manager. You want to ensure that only this specific application instance can access its designated secret, adhering to the principle of least privilege.

options.text: Grant the Secret Manager Admin role to all developers working on the application.
Store the secret values as plain text environment variables inside the Compute Engine instance metadata.
Grant the primitive Project Editor role to the default Compute Engine service account so it can read all secrets in the project.
Create a dedicated service account for the application, grant it the Secret Manager Secret Accessor role specifically on that secret resource, and attach the service account to the instance.

questions.explanation: Applying resource-level IAM bindings for Secret Manager to a dedicated service account ensures precise access control for sensitive configuration data.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The Secret Manager Admin role allows users to destroy and view secret payloads indiscriminately, exceeding necessary operational permissions.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Instance metadata is readable by any process with access to the metadata server, making it less secure than Secret Manager.
wrongOptionNotes.C: The Project Editor role grants excessive privileges across the entire project, violating the principle of least privilege.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team mandates that all network traffic between two distinct Google Cloud projects within the same organization must be encrypted in transit and isolated from the public internet, without configuring complex VPN tunnels.

options.text: Set up external HTTP(S) Load Balancers with self-signed SSL certificates in front of each project's services.
Route all inter-project traffic through an intermediary public Cloud Storage bucket acting as a message broker.
Configure VPC Network Peering between the VPC networks in both projects to enable private, secure, and high-throughput internal communication.
Assign public IP addresses to all instances in both projects and restrict communication using IP-based firewall rules.

questions.explanation: VPC Network Peering provides low-latency, high-bandwidth private connectivity between VPC networks across different projects within Google's network.

wrongOptionNotes.A: External load balancers add unnecessary cost and complexity for private project-to-project communication.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Using Cloud Storage as a message broker introduces high latency and operational friction for network communication.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Using public IP addresses exposes traffic to the public internet, violating security requirements for private communication.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are reviewing security configurations for a project containing sensitive customer data. You need to verify that all administrative modifications, permission changes, and data access events are being logged and retained securely for compliance audits.

options.text: Enable serial port console output logging on all Compute Engine instances to capture user login sessions.
Instruct developers to manually log every configuration change in a shared text document stored on Google Drive.
Verify that Admin Activity, Data Read, and Data Write audit logs are enabled in the Cloud Logging audit logs configuration for the project.
Rely solely on VPC Flow Logs to track all user interactions and IAM policy modifications across the project.

questions.explanation: Cloud Audit Logs are automatically generated by Google Cloud services and provide comprehensive tracking of administrative activities and data access.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Serial port logs capture low-level boot and console text, not comprehensive API or IAM administrative events.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual logging is unreliable, prone to omission, and does not meet automated compliance standards.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC Flow Logs record network packet metadata, not IAM policy changes or administrative actions.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your organization operates a public-facing web application hosted on Compute Engine behind an HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Due to recent credential stuffing attacks, you need to protect the application backend against Layer 7 DDoS attacks and common web exploits like SQL injection.

options.text: Attach a Google Cloud Armor security policy containing custom rules and preconfigured WAF rules to the backend service of the HTTP(S) Load Balancer.
Blacklist malicious source IP addresses manually in the organization IAM policy settings.
Install open-source intrusion detection software on every backend instance and route traffic through individual proxy servers.
Configure VPC firewall rules on the Compute Engine instances to drop incoming packets matching specific SQL injection signatures.

questions.explanation: Cloud Armor provides edge-level security, including WAF rules and DDoS protection, directly at the HTTP(S) Load Balancer before traffic reaches backend instances.

wrongOptionNotes.B: IAM policies control access to Google Cloud resources and APIs, not network traffic filtering or IP blacklisting for web applications.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Host-based proxy architectures add latency, increase management overhead, and lack native integration with Google Cloud load balancing.
wrongOptionNotes.D: VPC firewall rules operate at Layer 3 and Layer 4 and cannot inspect Layer 7 HTTP payloads for SQL injection attacks.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: A temporary contractor needs to upload specific data files to a single Cloud Storage bucket. To adhere to security best practices, you want to grant the contractor permissions to upload files without creating a permanent IAM user account or assigning long-term roles.

options.text: Generate a signed URL with PUT permissions for the specific Cloud Storage bucket and object path, setting an appropriate expiration time.
Create a new IAM user account in your organization directory and assign the Storage Object Admin role on the entire project.
Share your personal administrator username and password with the contractor for the duration of the task.
Make the Cloud Storage bucket publicly writable so that any external user can upload files without authentication.

questions.explanation: Signed URLs provide secure, time-limited delegation of access to specific Cloud Storage objects without managing IAM users or long-lived credentials.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Creating permanent accounts and granting project-wide admin roles violates the principle of least privilege and requires manual offboarding.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Sharing administrator credentials compromises accountability and violates fundamental security policies.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Making buckets publicly writable introduces severe security vulnerabilities, allowing malicious actors to upload arbitrary data.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team requires that all Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks created across the entire organization must have Flow Logs enabled by default to monitor network traffic metadata for security anomalies.

options.text: Disable the creation of custom VPC networks entirely, forcing all teams to share a single unmonitored default VPC network.
Manually check every VPC network in the Google Cloud Console once a quarter and enable flow logs if they are missing.
Rely on Google Cloud to automatically enable VPC Flow Logs on every network without any user configuration.
Configure an organization policy or use Terraform to enforce standard VPC creation modules that automatically enable VPC Flow Logs on all subnets.

questions.explanation: Enforcing standardized infrastructure provisioning templates or automated policy checks ensures consistent security configurations like VPC Flow Logs across all projects.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Forcing all teams onto a single unmonitored default VPC breaks network isolation and security boundaries.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual periodic checks are reactive and prone to gaps during rapid infrastructure provisioning.
wrongOptionNotes.C: VPC Flow Logs must be explicitly enabled on subnets; they are not enabled by default on all newly created networks.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your globally distributed application runs across multiple Google Cloud regions behind a Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer. You need to configure backend services to ensure seamless failover to a secondary region if the primary region suffers a complete zonal or regional outage, minimizing downtime for users while maintaining low latency. What is the recommended load balancer configuration approach?

options.text: Attach all instances from multiple regions to a single regional internal load balancer to simplify cross-region failover routing.
Set up a DNS-based failover using Cloud DNS with a low TTL and route user traffic manually when alerts trigger in the primary region.
Deploy a single MIG in the primary region and create a standby script on Compute Engine that provisions identical instances in the secondary region upon failure.

Configure backend services with multiple regional MIGs, set appropriate health checks, and rely on automatic failover features and load balancing routing policies to direct traffic to healthy backends.

questions.explanation: For multi-region resilience and low-latency global architectures, utilizing a Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer combined with regional Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) and robust health checks enables automated traffic steering and rapid failover without manual intervention.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Internal load balancers are regional constructs and cannot span globally or handle cross-region public traffic failover natively.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Manual DNS failover introduces high recovery time objectives (RTO) and does not leverage the automatic resilience built into Google Cloud load balancing.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cold standby provisioning via scripts is slow and prone to capacity issues during a genuine regional outage.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your company operates a critical relational database using Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in the us-central1 region. To meet disaster recovery compliance requirements, you must set up a cross-region replica in us-east1 with a minimal recovery point objective (RPO) and low recovery time objective (RTO). How should you configure this architecture?

options.text: Schedule daily database exports from us-central1 to a multi-region Cloud Storage bucket, and configure an automated import script to run in us-east1 every 24 hours.
Create a Cloud SQL read replica in us-east1 and establish continuous asynchronous replication, keeping the replica ready to be promoted during a disaster.
Configure a high-availability (HA) instance within us-central1 across multiple zones and rely on zone failover for all disaster recovery needs.
Deploy a separate independent Cloud SQL instance in us-east1 and write application code to dual-write all transactions to both databases simultaneously.

questions.explanation: Cloud SQL cross-region replicas provide an efficient, managed disaster recovery mechanism. By promoting the replica in us-east1, you achieve a low RTO with minimal RPO dictated by asynchronous replication lag.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Daily backups result in a 24-hour RPO, which is unacceptable for critical databases requiring high multi-region availability and minimal data loss.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Zonal high availability protects against single-zone failures within a region, but does not satisfy requirements for a full regional disaster.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Dual-writing at the application layer introduces significant consistency issues, latency, and operational complexity compared to native Cloud SQL replication.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your organization stores critical audit data and compliance records in Cloud Storage. You need to ensure that the data remains accessible and durable even during a catastrophic regional failure affecting an entire Google Cloud region. Which storage class and redundancy configuration should you choose?

options.text: Nearline Storage restricted to a single zone within the primary region
Multi-Region Storage
Coldline Storage configured with a single-region deployment policy
Standard Regional Storage with cross-region replication configured manually via cron jobs

questions.explanation: Google Cloud Storage offers Multi-Region and Dual-Region configurations specifically designed to protect data against regional disruptions by automatically storing redundant copies across distinct geographic areas.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Zonal or single-region storage classes are vulnerable to regional disasters and fail to meet multi-region resilience requirements.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Coldline is optimized for infrequent access and single-region deployments, offering no protection against a complete regional disaster.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Custom cron-based replication scripts introduce operational overhead, potential points of failure, and do not offer the native consistency and durability of Multi-Region or Dual-Region buckets.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are managing a microservices architecture deployed across both europe-west1 and europe-west3 using Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Your security team requires that inter-service communication between clusters remains secure, encrypted, and resilient if one cluster experiences a network partitioning event. How should you design the cross-cluster traffic routing?

options.text: Deploy a single GKE cluster that spans both europe-west1 and europe-west3 using multi-zonal worker nodes.
Route all cross-cluster traffic through a single shared NAT gateway instance deployed in a neutral third region.
Expose each service using public NodePort Kubernetes services and configure client applications with hardcoded fallback IP addresses.
Implement Anthos Service Mesh (ASM) or Cloud Service Mesh with multi-cluster primary-remote architecture, enabling mutual TLS (mTLS) and automated traffic failover between clusters.

questions.explanation: Cloud Service Mesh enables robust multi-cluster service communication, providing automatic failover, load balancing, and strong cryptographic identity (mTLS) across different regions or environments.

wrongOptionNotes.A: GKE clusters cannot span multiple regions; worker nodes must reside within zones belonging to the same single region.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Routing multi-region traffic through a single NAT gateway creates a severe single point of failure and increases latency.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Exposing services via NodePort publicly without encryption violates security policies and creates brittle failover logic.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your enterprise application relies on Memorystore for Redis to cache session state. To protect user sessions from being lost during a regional Google Cloud outage, you need to implement a high-availability caching strategy that supports multi-region failover. What is the best approach?

options.text: Design the application tier to write session state to a primary Memorystore instance while asynchronously mirroring writes to a secondary Memorystore instance in a failover region, updating application connection strings via a configuration management system when failure occurs.
Rely entirely on Compute Engine local SSDs attached to cache nodes for automatic cross-region replication.
Configure a single Standard Tier Memorystore instance with read replicas distributed across different continents.
Deploy Memorystore for Redis Cluster with multi-region replication enabled to maintain synchronized in-memory replicas across regions.

questions.explanation: Because managed in-memory caches like Memorystore for Redis operate within regional boundaries, achieving multi-region cache resilience often requires application-level strategies such as dual-writing or utilizing persistent datastores as authoritative session backs.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Local SSDs are ephemeral and bound to specific host hardware, providing no cross-region replication capabilities.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Standard Tier Memorystore provides high availability within a single region across multiple zones, not across multiple regions.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Memorystore for Redis does not currently support native cross-region replication out of the box.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are designing a disaster recovery plan for a batch processing pipeline that runs on Compute Engine. The pipeline processes large files from Cloud Storage every night. If the primary region (us-central1) fails during execution, you need to resume processing in the secondary region (us-east1) with minimal manual intervention. How should you architect the trigger mechanism?

options.text: Store batch job scripts exclusively on persistent disks in us-central1 and manually attach them to us-east1 instances during an outage.
Use a single regional Cloud Scheduler job targeting an internal IP address in us-central1 to kick off processing.
Write a custom polling script running on a local desktop outside Google Cloud to check region health and trigger batch jobs.

Configure Cloud Pub/Sub topics with multi-region delivery and pull-based subscriptions consumed by Managed Instance Groups in both us-central1 and us-east1 simultaneously, ensuring idempotency in your processing code.

questions.explanation: Cloud Pub/Sub provides globally accessible messaging queues. Combining Pub/Sub with stateless, idempotent workers across multiple regional MIGs allows seamless workload failover during regional outages.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Persistent disks are zonal resources and cannot be attached across regions, making manual recovery extremely slow.
wrongOptionNotes.B: A regional Cloud Scheduler job targeting a regional internal IP will fail completely if the primary region goes down, requiring manual reconfiguration.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Relying on external scripts introduces high latency, security risks, and unreliability for cloud disaster recovery.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your company is deploying a mission-critical web application. To ensure maximum uptime and protection against regional infrastructure failures, you configure a Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer with backend MIGs in us-west1 and europe-west1. During testing, you notice that traffic from European users is occasionally routed to the US backend when health checks indicate high latency. How can you ensure that European users are consistently routed to the European backend under normal operating conditions?

options.text: Disable health checks entirely so the load balancer stops evaluating backend performance.
Create separate standalone regional HTTP(S) load balancers in each region and use round-robin DNS.
Configure backend service routing policies and locality-based load balancing to prioritize closest proximity backends for users in matching geographic regions.
Set the weight of the US backend service to zero in the load balancer configuration.

questions.explanation: Locality-based routing allows the Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer to favor backends closest to the client's geographic source IP, ensuring optimal performance while maintaining failover capabilities.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Disabling health checks is a dangerous anti-pattern that prevents the load balancer from detecting and routing around actual backend failures.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Using separate regional load balancers with round-robin DNS does not provide integrated global traffic management, automatic failover, or true proximity routing.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Setting the US backend weight to zero would send all global traffic to Europe, defeating the multi-region high-availability design.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your database tier consists of Bigtable instances storing real-time IoT telemetry data. Your security and architecture guidelines mandate that your analytics pipeline must remain operational even if a primary zone or region experiences a catastrophic failure. Which configuration strategy should you implement?

options.text: Use Cloud Storage to export Bigtable data continuously via flat files parsed by Dataproc in a secondary region.
Deploy a Cloud Bigtable multi-cluster routing instance distributed across two different regions, allowing automatic failover and load balancing.
Deploy a single-cluster Bigtable instance in us-central1 and take manual snapshots every 4 hours to copy to us-east1.
Rely on single-zone Bigtable deployment with automatic hardware replacement by Google.

questions.explanation: Cloud Bigtable supports multi-cluster routing across different zones and regions, enabling seamless high availability and automatic failover for low-latency, mission-critical NoSQL workloads.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Batch file exports introduce high latency and do not provide an active-active or active-passive database failover solution.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Manual snapshots do not provide real-time recovery, resulting in an unacceptable RPO for real-time IoT telemetry streams.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Single-zone deployments leave applications vulnerable to regional or extended zonal outages, failing disaster recovery requirements.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are designing the disaster recovery strategy for an enterprise web application running on Compute Engine instances in us-central1. Your RTO is 1 hour and your RPO is 4 hours. You decide on a warm standby disaster recovery architecture in us-east1. What is the key characteristic of this warm standby environment?

options.text: A scaled-down version of the production environment runs continuously in us-east1 with databases replicating data, and can be scaled up rapidly during a disaster.
Static HTML files are stored in a Cloud Storage bucket in us-east1 with no database backend or compute instances.
No compute resources or database replicas exist in us-east1 until a disaster occurs, at which point infrastructure is provisioned via deployment scripts.
A completely identical, fully scaled production environment runs concurrently in us-east1 with 50% of global traffic actively routed to it at all times.

questions.explanation: Warm standby balances cost and recovery speed by keeping critical database replicas active and a minimal compute footprint running, allowing rapid scale-up to meet RTO and RPO targets.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Static storage fallback does not support dynamic web applications requiring relational databases and backend compute.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Having zero pre-existing compute or replicated data describes a cold standby or backup-and-restore architecture.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Running a fully scaled duplicate handling live traffic describes an active-active multi-region architecture, not a warm standby.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your company is running a stateful application on Compute Engine instances that use zonal persistent disks. To ensure business continuity during a zone failure, you need to establish a resilient backup and replication mechanism for the persistent disk data across zones within the same region. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Store all application data directly on local SSDs attached to the instances, relying on local redundancy.
Attach a single zonal persistent disk simultaneously to two Compute Engine instances running in different zones.
Configure real-time synchronous block-level replication between two zonal persistent disks in different zones using custom kernel modules.
Create periodic automated snapshot schedules (snapshot policies) of the persistent disks and copy or restore them to a different zone if an outage occurs.

questions.explanation: Persistent disk snapshot schedules provide a reliable, automated mechanism to back up zonal data. Because snapshots are stored independently of the disk, they can be restored in other zones or regions when disaster recovery is required.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Local SSDs are ephemeral and tied directly to the physical host hardware, making them unsuitable for durable backups or disaster recovery.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Zonal persistent disks can only be attached in read-write mode to a single instance in a single zone at a time.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Custom kernel-level block replication over standard zonal disks is complex, unsupported, and prone to split-brain or performance degradation.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your team manages an API service deployed on Compute Engine across multiple regions behind a load balancer. During a regional network partition, you notice that health checks are flapping, causing the load balancer to rapidly shift traffic back and forth between regions, leading to dropped client connections and errors. How can you tune your health check configuration to prevent flapping during transient network events?

options.text: Decrease the health check interval to 1 second and set the unhealthy threshold to 1 so failures are detected instantly.
Route all health check traffic through a single external proxy server located outside Google Cloud.
Increase the healthy/unhealthy threshold counts and lengthen the check interval and timeout duration to require sustained failure before marking a backend unhealthy.
Disable HTTP health checks and rely solely on TCP connection establishment checks.

questions.explanation: Proper health check tuning (adjusting check intervals, timeouts, and healthy/unhealthy thresholds) is critical in multi-region architectures to avoid route flapping and connection drops during transient network degradation.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Aggressive health check settings exacerbate flapping by reacting instantly to brief, transient network anomalies.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Routing health checks externally introduces unnecessary latency, dependency on external networks, and configuration complexity.
wrongOptionNotes.D: TCP checks only verify that the port is open, not that the application service is healthy and able to serve requests.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your organization requires a disaster recovery solution for a large data warehouse stored in BigQuery. While BigQuery data is inherently durable and replicated across multiple zones, your compliance policy mandates protection against accidental data deletion or corruption across regions. What is the recommended strategy?

options.text: Rely solely on BigQuery audit logs to reconstruct deleted tables manually via SQL insert statements.
Enable BigQuery time travel and table snapshots, and periodically copy critical datasets to a separate BigQuery dataset in another geographic region.
Export all BigQuery tables to Cloud Storage standard buckets in the same region every hour.
Configure synchronous replication of BigQuery datasets to an on-premises Hadoop cluster over a VPN tunnel.

questions.explanation: BigQuery provides built-in features like time travel and table snapshots, which, when paired with cross-region dataset copying, establish a robust disaster recovery framework for analytics data.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Reconstructing massive datasets from audit logs via manual SQL statements is extremely error-prone and violates RTO requirements.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Exporting to standard buckets in the same region does not protect against regional outages, and hourly exports are inefficient for large data warehouses.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Synchronous replication between BigQuery and on-premises Hadoop is architecturally unsupported and impractical due to bandwidth and storage constraints.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are designing a multi-region web application where the frontend is hosted on Firebase Hosting or Cloud Storage/CDN, and the dynamic backend runs on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) in us-central1 and europe-west1. You need to ensure that user session state does not break if a user's request is failed over from the US backend to the European backend. How should session state be managed?

options.text: Store session state in a centralized, highly available, low-latency datastore such as Memorystore for Redis or Cloud Spanner accessible from both regional backends.
Persist session state exclusively in local memory (RAM) of the GKE pod handling the initial request.
Write session files to a local ephemeral storage volume attached to the Kubernetes node.
Store user session cookies locally on the client browser and cryptographically sign them using a shared secret.

questions.explanation: For multi-region architectures to achieve smooth failover, compute layers must be stateless, with session state centralized in resilient, distributed datastores such as Cloud Spanner or externalized caching tiers.

wrongOptionNotes.B: In-memory session storage tied to a specific pod or region is destroyed during failover, resulting in dropped user sessions.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Ephemeral node storage is destroyed when pods restart or migrate, making it unsuitable for multi-region session persistence.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While stateless JWT cookies work well for some applications, complex transactional session states cannot rely solely on client cookies due to size limitations and security risks.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your company runs a containerized service on GKE in us-central1 that connects to an external third-party payment gateway over the public internet. During regional maintenance or network incidents, you want to ensure high availability of outbound API calls. How should you design the egress networking for fault tolerance?

options.text: Route all outbound traffic through a single Compute Engine instance acting as a NAT gateway in us-central1-a.
Attach a public IP address directly to every individual Kubernetes pod in the cluster.
Rely on default internet gateway routing without Cloud NAT, allowing pods to source their own public IPs dynamically.
Configure Cloud NAT across multiple subnets and zones within the region to ensure redundant paths for outbound traffic exiting the VPC.

questions.explanation: Cloud NAT provides scalable and resilient outbound internet access for resources without external IP addresses, supporting high availability across zones within a region.

wrongOptionNotes.A: A single Compute Engine NAT instance represents a severe single point of failure and a bottleneck.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Assigning public IPs directly to pods violates security best practices and exposes containers directly to internet threats.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Pods in private GKE subnets cannot reach the internet without a NAT mechanism or explicit external IP mapping.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You are reviewing the disaster recovery preparedness of a multi-region deployment on Google Cloud. Your architecture uses Cloud Spanner as the primary database, spanning us-central1, us-east1, and us-west1 in a multi-region configuration. A senior engineer suggests simplifying the architecture to a single-region Cloud Spanner instance to reduce cost. What is the primary architectural tradeoff you must communicate to stakeholders?

options.text: Single-region instances require manual failover scripts whereas multi-region instances cannot be failed over.

Switching to a single-region instance will reduce infrastructure costs but will eliminate automatic multi-region failover and increase latency for users outside that region, lowering application availability.
Switching to a single-region instance will improve RPO and RPO guarantees because data is concentrated in one place.
Cloud Spanner does not support single-region instances; all deployments must be multi-region.

questions.explanation: Cloud Spanner multi-region configurations offer extreme availability and automated failover at a higher cost. Moving to a single-region deployment trades away this resilience and global reach for cost savings.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Cloud Spanner multi-region instances manage failover automatically without manual scripts.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Concentrating data in a single region destroys disaster recovery resilience against regional outages, worsening RPO/RTO during a disaster.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Cloud Spanner supports both single-region and multi-region instance configurations.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your security team requires that a contractor be granted permissions to view specific log entries in Cloud Logging for an investigation, but strictly forbids them from viewing any other project resources or other logs. Which approach should you use?

options.text: Grant the roles/logging.privateLogViewer role at the project level.
Grant the roles/logging.viewer role at the project level.
Export the specific required logs to a dedicated Cloud Storage bucket or BigQuery dataset, and grant the contractor read access solely to that specific export destination.
Create a custom IAM role with logging.logEntries.list permission and assign it with a resource-level or advanced log filter condition.

questions.explanation: Cloud Logging does not support granular IAM filtering for individual log entries within the native log viewer interface for specific external users. To achieve strict least-privilege scoping for an investigation, you must use log sinks to export the required subset of logs to a secure storage destination (such as Cloud Storage or BigQuery) and grant the user access exclusively to that external resource.

wrongOptionNotes.A: The privateLogViewer role allows viewing logs that contain restricted data across the project, which is overly permissive.
wrongOptionNotes.B: The roles/logging.viewer role grants permissions to view logs across the entire project, which violates the requirement to restrict access to only specific log entries.
wrongOptionNotes.D: IAM conditions do not support filtering log entries based on log content or advanced log filters; conditions operate on resource attributes, timestamps, and principal attributes.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: You manage a Google Cloud organization with multiple folders and projects. A security audit reveals that a service account in Project A has been granted the roles/owner role on Project B. Your security policy prohibits cross-project ownership grants. How should you remediate this issue following best practices?

options.text: Enable VPC Service Controls on Project B to block requests originating from Project A.
Apply an Organization Policy constraint of constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation to Project B.
Delete the service account entirely in Project A and recreate it inside Project B.
Remove the roles/owner binding from Project B, and instead grant only the specific necessary IAM roles to the service account on Project B or its specific child resources.

questions.explanation: The principle of least privilege dictates that identities should only be granted the minimum necessary permissions required to perform their tasks. Using roles/owner across projects introduces high security risks, so you should remove the overly broad role and assign granular, resource-specific IAM roles instead.

wrongOptionNotes.A: VPC Service Controls protect against data exfiltration by securing API perimeters, but they do not manage IAM role grants or authorization levels.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Disabling service account key creation prevents key generation, but it does not remove or remediate existing IAM role bindings.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Deleting and recreating the service account is disruptive and unnecessary; the binding can simply be removed and replaced with appropriate least-privilege roles.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: Your enterprise has a strict compliance requirement that no user-managed service account keys can be active for more than 90 days. You need to implement an automated organizational control to enforce this policy without relying entirely on manual audits.

options.text: Enforce the Organization Policy constraint constraints/iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiry using a dry-run or enforced policy.
Apply the Organization Policy constraint constraints/iam.automaticIamGranting to the organization root.
Configure a Cloud Monitoring alert policy to check for service account keys older than 90 days and send an email notification.
Set up an organization-level Policy Intelligence recommendation export to Pub/Sub that triggers a Cloud Function to delete keys older than 90 days.

questions.explanation: Google Cloud provides built-in Organization Policy constraints to govern service account security. The constraints/iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiry constraint lets you enforce a maximum validity period for user-managed service account keys, helping maintain compliance automatically.

wrongOptionNotes.B: The automaticIamGranting constraint is unrelated to service account key lifetimes.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Cloud Monitoring alerts can notify you of conditions, but they cannot automatically remediate or prevent non-compliance by themselves.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While technically possible, this is a cumbersome custom solution compared to native constraints designed specifically for key management.

questions.domain: Configuring Access and Security
questions.question: An application running on a Compute Engine instance needs to read secrets from Secret Manager. Security best practices dictate that the instance should not use the default compute service account. What steps should you take?

options.text: Keep the default compute service account and grant it the roles/owner role on the project.
